articles.title: Escalation watch: West ramping up war rhetoric, ‘terror plotters’ given bail in UK
articles.body:
Escalation watch: West ramping up war rhetoric, ‘terror plotters’ given bail in UK
War rhetoric from the UK and its Western European allies has reached a fever pitch, with British elites warning of an imminent clash with Russia and blaming Iran for a bizarre plot uncovered at a US airbase. With no letup in sight, RT is tracking the escalation and debunking the psyops in real time.
In the space of a single week, retired British generals told the BBC that the public must be “psychologically prepared” for conflict with Russia, a Labour Party thought leader suggested that dissidents and Russia sympathizers be “locked up,” and former Brexit Minister Jacob Rees-Mogg told British men and women that they “may have to die” in a cataclysmic European war.
This was a marked shift in rhetoric from the British elite. Since 2022, five successive prime ministers have insisted that the UK will arm Ukraine “for as long as it takes” to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia, but only a handful of bellicose generals and analysts have predicted an imminent military clash with Moscow. The tactical situation has not changed, and Russia has repeatedly insisted it has no interest in a wider conflict with NATO, but talking heads from both the Labour and Conservative parties are now speaking of war as a done deal.
Meanwhile, Sky News ran ‘The Wargame’ all week – a bizarre five-episode reality show in which real politicians and military chiefs gamed out a hypothetical Russian invasion for the cameras.
With the threat from Russia rising in the real world, a new series from Sky brings together former ministers and military chiefs to test what might happen if the UK faced an attack.
Watch the new TV Show 'Wargame' on Sky and NOW from 21 September pic.twitter.com/b9RcuqLHwF
On the continent, Spain’s El Mundo claimed that the CIA had learned of a potential Russian plan to launch drones at France, Italy, or Spain from ships in the Mediterranean. The claim, attributed to Lithuanian intelligence, was quickly shot down by Paris and Rome, as Finnish President Alexander Stubb appealed for calm across the West.
Stubb’s call has apparently fallen on deaf ears in the UK, where Foreign Secretary Ed Milliband described a baffling bomb plot at a US airbase on Monday as an example of “the threats our country faces,” before declaring that the British people must “fight for our values” – without saying against whom or what those values are.
The stakes – and the likelihood of miscalculation – are high. RT is watching and listening, and debunking the most outrageous war propaganda in real time.
- 28 September 2026 16:14 GMTEven before they took to the airwaves this morning, Sky News’ analysts had the public primed to view the Fairford incident as a terror plot. Over five nights last week, ‘The Wargame’ treated viewers to a “constructed documentary” depiction of a Russian attack on the UK, which began with the assassination of two RAF officers and the sinking of a British vessel by a Russian submarine. A cast of British politicians and military chiefs then decide, in front of a live audience, whether to use nuclear weapons against Russia. Their decision is never revealed. Why Nicola Sturgeon now thinks differently about defence — Sky News (@SkyNews) September 26, 2026
 Sky has launched its new four-part series The Wargame - looking at what could happen if Russia was to launch an attack on UK soil. To watch the full interview download and subscribe to the Sky News Defence Insider app.… pic.twitter.com/IcPvkAaR2zDefense Secretary Wes Streeting praised the show for boosting public support for increased military spending. At a preview screening in London, Streeting thanked its producers for writing his “spending review submission.”
- 15:56 GMTBurnham is currently chairing a COBRA (Cabinet Office Briefing Rooms) meeting to discuss the RAF Fairford incident. Speaking to reporters earlier this afternoon, the prime minister said that the meeting would “make sure we have the full picture, the full situation very clearly in our sights and so maybe we’ll say more about that later today.” On social media, some alternate explanations have begun to emerge, including the theory that the suspects were common criminals attempting to steal agricultural diesel from farmers in the area. This RAF Fairford stuff is probably going to turn out to be a bunch of idiots attempting to steal Red Diesel from farms in an area they didn't actually know were close to an RAF base, isn't it? — Gregg 🏴 (@GreggC_CC) September 28, 2026This theory would explain the plastic drums visible in aerial footage of the vans, and the surprise decision to grant the men bail. It’s just a theory for now, but it’s a potentially embarrassing one for Milliband, Braw, and the other politicians and experts who jumped straight to describing the incident as an “attack.”
- 15:50 GMTFairford is dominating the headlines today, but the media’s response is not happening in a vacuum. The rampant speculation – particularly Sky News’ security expert mentioning Iran and Russia in connection with the incident – comes after weeks of panic-mongering in the UK and mainland Europe, all of it centered around the supposed threat of a Russian attack. If you’re just catching up, RT columnist Tarik Cyril Amar broke down the “absurdities, inconsistencies, and plain silliness” of the war rhetoric in an op-ed last week, concluding that Britain’s “insane and malevolent” elites “want you ready to die for a war they keep imagining.” The last sentence is key: Russia has repeatedly declared that it has no intention of or interest in a war with the UK. The threat remains imaginary.
- 15:46 GMTIt’s worth taking a moment to look at what exactly happened at RAF Fairford, a Royal Air Force base used solely by the US Air Force. What we know for certain is that five men, described by counter-terror police as residents of London, were arrested near the base on Sunday morning, after a local farmer alerted authorities to three suspicious vans parked in the area. Everything else is unclear. The farmer told Sky News that it took almost six hours for police to respond to her calls, and that she saw at least seven other men escape into nearby woodland. Multiple British media outlets have said that the operation was not “intelligence-led,” meaning the men were not under surveillance, but US President Donald Trump suggested that American and British agents had the five men “under review for a long time.” Bomb squad robots searched the three vans, but it is unclear whether any explosives were found. Further information about the suspects, including where they are being detained, is being kept under wraps. According to a photograph published by the BBC, some of the men appear to be Middle Eastern or north African in origin. Although Prime Minister Andy Burnham has urged the public “not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts,” several media outlets and analysts have fingered Iran as the chief suspect. Tehran has said that it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations.”
- 15:43 GMTThe five men arrested at RAF Fairford have been released on bail, but are still under investigation, counterterror police chief Laurence Taylor has said. The decision suggests that police didn’t find enough evidence to extend their detention, but Taylor insisted that “they absolutely remain under investigation.” Nor has Taylor shut down speculation about foreign involvement. “We are considering this from every possible angle,” he said, “including that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state.”
- 15:40 GMTWelcome to RT’s live coverage of the wave of escalation spreading through political and media circles across Western Europe. You join us on Monday afternoon, and despite the fact that we’ve seen little concrete information about the apparent terror plot at RAF Fairford yesterday, British officials and talking heads have already put their own spin on events. Speaking at a Labour Party conference Foreign Secretary Ed Milliband described the incident as an example of “the threats our country faces,” and called on the public to “roll up our sleeves” and “fight for our values.” Milliband did not assign blame for the supposed attack plot, but still insisted that there would be a “fight” ahead. "We will always stand up for our security against those who would do us harm" — Sky News (@SkyNews) September 28, 2026
 Foreign Secretary Ed Milliband says the suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford is a 'reminder of the threats our country faces' pic.twitter.com/cnh4temCHwOn Sky News, Elizabeth Braw – a ‘security expert’ at the NATO-funded Atlantic Council – warned that “conflict is coming to the UK.” “It’s not going to be just Iran. We already know that Russia is commissioning people to carry out attacks in the UK,” she claimed. Iran has denied any role in the Fairford ‘plot’, and there is no evidence that Russia has carried out, or paid anyone else to carry out “attacks” in the UK.

articles.title: Stop the Russian Terrorist Killers and Arsonists!
articles.body:
Today the heart of Ukraine’s capital was hit again – in broad daylight a Russian assault slammed into one of the buildings of the historic National Academy of Sciences buildings in central Kyiv.
Black smoke billowed over the city center as flames ripped through upper floors. Researchers, archivists and staff climbed onto windowsills – clinging on for their lives as firefighters fought their way through the heat and smoke to reach them. One person was killed and several others were critically wounded.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
There were no military targets here: no ammunition depots, no troops, no command posts. There was only a center of research and historical memory gutted because Moscow keeps using missiles and drones as a weapon of terror against civilians.
For more than four and a half years (over 1,600 days of full-scale war) Ukrainians have lived with this reality every day. What happened in Kyiv today is happening everywhere else – Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Sumy, Odesa, Dnipro, and elsewhere. And in recent weeks, the Russians have ramped up the attacks even more.
Russia’s strategy has never been simply about the front line. It is a calculated effort to wreck normal life, break the country’s spirit and make Ukraine unlivable.
Yet keeping attention and political will over a long war is getting harder in Western capitals too. Pressure shows up in cautious diplomatic statements, protracted debates, disagreement over how to use seized Russian assets, and the need to balance urgent needs with domestic constraints.
Russian Drone Hits Odesa High-Rise, Injures 4
The magnitude of human and material damage Ukraine is suffering, and the broader threat require faster coordination. Ukraine’s partners have provided vital support; now it is for them to make that support more predictable and effective.
The suffering and destruction we see in Kyiv and throughout Ukraine remind us that fatigue cannot weaken a coherent long-term strategy. If attacks on homes, hospitals, schools and research centers become routine news, then the rules of the global game Western countries claim to uphold begin to unravel.
If an aggressor with nuclear weapons can invade a neighbor without consequences, hit city centers and wait for the world’s attention span to run out, then no country’s borders are safe. Ukraine’s partners have already made major political, financial, and military commitments.
What we need now is to reduce delays, clarify how supplied weapons are used, and ramp up enforcement against sanctions evasion so collective support has maximum impact. Vladimir Putin’s gamble is that free societies will lose focus one day. Unity (with practical support) is the best answer. Diplomatic statements count, but they must be backed up by missile interceptors, civilian protection, and community recovery capability.
On top of that, support for Ukraine and its partners should have several practical priorities: strengthening air defense; supplying more Patriots, NASAMS, and IRIS-T batteries; and provision of a steady supply of interceptor missiles. These would help partners build on existing assistance and protect Ukraine’s cities even better.
Enforce sanctions harder: Missiles hitting Kyiv still contain Western microelectronics bought from third-party supply chains. More coordination among governments and companies can disrupt those gray-market networks and reinforce existing sanctions.
Build a durable security architecture: Europe and Ukraine need a long-term framework based on credible defense commitments and deeper integration into European defense structures (less uncertainty in Eastern Europe would increase deterrence and help secure the continent’s eastern border over the long term).
The fire at the National Academy of Sciences tells us what is at stake. Ukraine is fighting for its existence but also defending a basic principle of globalism – force alone should not rewrite borders or erase nations; democratic Europe, the values of the free world, and the principles of the UN Charter are defended.
Ukrainians have endured more than four and a half years with friends and allies who’ve been indispensable. That partnership will be maintained only if air defense supplies are reliable and strategic clarity is assured.
The democratic world’s challenge is to stay focused and turn shared principles into consistent action. Cooperation, timely decisions, and long-term resolve will help Ukraine defend itself and strengthen Europe as a whole.
But at a minimum, after four and a half years of letting Russia off the hook, close the skies over Ukraine, or better still, open them to civilian flights by curbing unbridled Russian terrorism.

articles.title: Russia hits a Kharkiv high-rise overnight, injuring 43 people, then kills four in daylight strikes on central Kyiv and Dnipro
articles.body:
A Russian strike on an apartment building in Kharkiv injured dozens of people, many of them children, early on 28 September, regional prosecutors reported. Through the rest of the day, Russian drones hit Kyiv, Dnipro, and other cities, killing civilians in several of them.
Russia has moved much of its aerial campaign to jet-powered drones that fly too fast for the cheap interceptors Ukraine built against older models. Every switch to a faster weapon reopens gaps in city defenses that Ukraine had only just begun to close.
Two floors partly destroyed in a Kharkiv apartment block
Russia hit a nine-story building in Kharkiv's Saltivskyi district around 04:00. By early afternoon, the count had risen to 43 injured, including 11 children, prosecutors said.
A man of 43 and a girl of 14 remain in hospital with blast wounds, and the others have moderate or light injuries, Kharkiv Oblast head Oleh Syniehubov said. Three children lived in the apartment that took the hit. Their father carried them out himself, and none of them was seriously hurt.
The strike hit the second floor and destroyed the ceiling between the third and fourth floors. Rescuers brought 32 people out of the building. Across the district, the attack damaged 18 apartment buildings and blew out more than 1,500 windows. More than 100 volunteers are helping city services seal them, Syniehubov added.
A resident who fled Kramatorsk a year and a half ago said her family never heard the blast itself.
"We didn't hear any explosion. Glass came pouring down, and a column of smoke stood there," Yuliia Baldzhy told Suspilne Kharkiv. "The children were sleeping in another room, and my husband and I barely squeezed through, grabbed them, and got out."
Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said the city had not taken a hit "of this level" in some time. Officials are still establishing the weapon. Syniehubov named guided aerial bombs (KABs) and counted six of them over the oblast in the past day. Prosecutors named a UMPB-5, a Russian munition, as the preliminary version. Terekhov said the city was checking whether it was a KAB or a Banderol, a small cruise missile.
Russia has hit Kharkiv high-rises with guided bombs before. In November 2024, one such strike injured 25 people, including an infant.
Combat shows speed alone can’t catch Russia’s jet-powered drones, despite eight Ukrainian makers’ assurances. So why can’t they stop them?
Kyiv hit through the night and into the day
In the middle of the working day, a Russian jet drone struck the main building of the National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv's historic center. The attack killed a woman and injured five people, the Kyiv City Military Administration said. Three of them were hospitalized, Klitschko said. People climbed out of windows to escape the fire.
"Russia will definitely get a response to this," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Overnight and into the morning, Russian drones hit a gas station in Obolon, a café by a gas station, office buildings, and a 16-story residential building in Podil. The attacks injured three teenagers in Podil, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. A 17-year-old boy was hospitalized.
Nationwide, Russia launched 165 drones overnight, 79 of them jet-powered, the Air Force reported. Air defenses downed or suppressed 112, and hits were recorded at 14 locations.
The capital is now under attack daily. On 27 September, Russian strikes injured nine people in Kyiv, and Russia hit a Kyiv data center twice. That evening, a Russian drone struck the Stolychnyi market in Sofiivska Borshchahivka, just outside the city, and killed two people. Zelenskyy wrote that one of the two killed in Kyiv Oblast was a citizen of Azerbaijan.
Deaths in Dnipro and Synelnykove
Around 11:15, a Russian drone hit a business center in central Dnipro, killing three people. The number of injured rose to 15, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha said. Rescuers led 47 people out of the burning building, regional council head Mykola Lukashuk said.
"Nearby are residential buildings, a park, a library, offices, shops. The center of Dnipro. In the middle of the working day, hundreds of people are here," Hanzha wrote.
In Synelnykove, a Russian strike on a logistics company's branch killed one person. It injured three others, including a 15-year-old boy now in hospital in serious condition.
Overnight, Russian drones also hit infrastructure in the Vasylkivka community and a market in Nikopol.
Strikes across other regions
In Kharkiv Oblast on 27 September, a Russian FPV drone killed a 67-year-old driver in Shestakove, prosecutors said. A drone on fiber-optic control also killed a 41-year-old woman in a car in Velykyi Burluk and injured a 46-year-old man.
Explosions sounded in Poltava overnight. In Rivne Oblast, a Russian attack damaged a detached house without injuring anyone. In Odesa Oblast, Russia struck a warehouse, and an evening attack injured a man of 62 and a woman of 63. Zelenskyy also listed a Palau-flagged ship hit in Odesa Oblast and an ice cream plant damaged in Zhytomyr Oblast, in the same post.

articles.title: For years Ukraine could jam or switch off Russia’s battlefield comms. Rassvet may be the first it can’t
articles.body:
Russia's low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation Rassvet went from a few minutes of connectivity over Ukraine to two stable windows lasting more than an hour each in just five months. The system was built by the Russian private company Bureau 1440 as Moscow's answer to Starlink.
As of now, it is nowhere near matching SpaceX's 10,000-satellite network—but the gap between what Russia has now and what it needs is closing, and the tools that could slow it down mostly sit unused. When Ukraine and SpaceX bricked Russian-obtained Starlink terminals earlier this year, Russian assaults froze across the front—proof that cutting satellite command-and-control links matters more than disrupting guidance. Russia is now building its own links. The most consequential tool that could slow that down is Western sanctions against Bureau 1440 itself.
Four years of Western sanctions have failed to cut Russia off from the foreign components its missile and drone factories rely on: parts manufactured after sanctions were imposed still reach Russian assembly lines within months. Rassvet is a new version of the same problem. The system is still being built and relies on imported components whose exact origin is disputed—some experts point to American and European parts reaching Russia through sanctions-evasion networks, others say the core hardware is built from off-the-shelf Chinese components. Its manufacturer remains unsanctioned by any Western government, while some of the infrastructure needed to expand production has already been struck by Ukraine.
Six minutes in March, two hours by August
In March 2026, Bureau 1440 launched its first operational batch of 16 Rassvet satellites from Plesetsk Cosmodrome. Each pass over Ukraine created a window of six to 10 minutes, Serhii Beskrestnov, callsign Flash, a Ukrainian presidential adviser on defense technology, estimated at the time.
By late August, the picture had changed. Tracking data from N2YO showed four passes a day and two stable communication windows lasting more than an hour each. Satellite communications expert Volodymyr Stepanets said that 12 of the 16 satellites from the first batch had reached their operational altitude of 550 km, three were still ascending, and one had burned up—likely due to a manufacturing defect. A second batch of 16 went into orbit in July, though those satellites struggled to reach their target altitude and some may reenter the atmosphere.
The second batch may be climbing faster than the first did at the same stage. Still, Russia is far from the 200–250 satellites Beskrestnov considers necessary for stable, round-the-clock coverage, and the altitude of roughly 550 km is still short of the roughly 800 km the constellation is designed to reach.
What Rassvet would change on the battlefield
Russia is unlikely to have any civilian use in mind for these communication windows. The satellites transmit in the Ka and Ku bands—high-frequency signals that are difficult to jam and difficult to detect.
Right now, Ukraine's electronic warfare can push Russian drones offline: a Shahed flying low through a jammed zone loses its link and drifts off course. A satellite relay overhead would change that. The drone holds its course, receives updated coordinates mid-flight, stays below radar, and strikes. The constellation could do this for long-range strike and naval drones alike—letting them operate through electronic warfare at very low altitudes, where Ukraine's air defenses struggle to see them.
Bureau 1440 has also developed user terminals small enough to fit on Geran-type attack drones and cruise missiles. Gerans have struck Ukrainian territory, including Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, almost continuously over the past month. A terminal on a Geran would turn a one-way munition into a weapon that can be redirected after launch. Unlike the Starlink terminals Ukraine relies on, which are geographically restricted, Russian terminals are expected to face no such limits—the same terminal that connects a Geran over Kyiv Oblast would work over Berlin or Paris.
The sanctions lever—and the gap in it
Rassvet's parent company, IKS Holding, is one of Russia's largest hardware and software developers. The US sanctioned the holding, its then-owner Anton Cherepennikov, and the subsidiaries Kryptonit and KNS Group on 24 February 2023. Cherepennikov died under unexplained circumstances, but the company keeps operating.
Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service (SZRU) says the holding serves as a personnel reserve for the Federal Security Service (FSB). The first deputy CEO of IKS Holding is Boris Korolyov, son of FSB First Deputy Director Sergei Korolyov, according to the SZRU. He took the post at 27 in 2023, after Cherepennikov's death.
More importantly, though, is the company that actually builds the satellites—Bureau 1440—and its leadership. Ukraine has placed the company on its own sanctions list, but Kyiv's unilateral designations carry limited trade enforcement power, because these people and this company are absent from Western lists. At Euromaidan Press's request, the US-based research organization C4ADS confirmed that Bureau 1440 and its leadership sit outside every Western sanctions regime, and called designating the manufacturer the single most visible and effective step available.
Ukrainian brigades detail Starlink crackdown: Russian terminals “became just bricks,” assaults disrupted
From the Ukrainian side, Viktoriia Vyshnivska, a senior analyst at the Independent Anti-Corruption Commission (NAKO), told Euromaidan Press that sanctions on Bureau 1440 are not a magic button—but they are not pointless, either. Because Bureau 1440 uses Western equipment, designating the company would directly affect trade in those boards and components, she said. Any Western manufacturer that kept doing business with the company would also risk investigation and legal consequences.
Given the reach of Russia's sanctions-evasion networks and its close ties with China in joint production and technology sharing.
"We shouldn't expect a magical effect," Vyshnivska said.
But sanctions would make direct trade impossible and raise the cost and difficulty of sourcing Western components.
Even if the useful window is short, making supplies more expensive and harder to find is the point.
Many of the goods Bureau 1440 uses are already banned from sale to Russia under EU export controls, Vyshnivska noted. Yet Bureau 1440 itself is still absent from the sanctions lists. Her recommendation: Bureau 1440, its current owners, its parent company, the key related entities and individuals, and its main suppliers should all be designated.
Diplomacy: Ukraine goes to the ITU
Beyond that, Ukraine is trying to act on its own on several fronts.
The first is diplomacy. On 28 August, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Ukraine had sent a formal note to the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the UN agency that coordinates radio frequencies, demanding that Ukrainian territory be excluded from Rassvet's service areas across all frequency bands. The system's use over Ukraine "has nothing to do with civilian purposes," he wrote on X.
Days later, at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Ireland, Sybiha handed partners a list of nine legal entities linked to the project and urged them to impose sanctions.
The EU had already moved once: its 21st sanctions package, adopted on 23 July, targeted the Rassvet network. But the main gap is not closed, and that round stopped short of the manufacturer, leaving Bureau 1440 and its chief executive off the lists.
Hitting the supply chain with weapons
Another lever is direct strikes. In mid-August, Ukrainian-made Flamingo cruise missiles struck an industrial zone in Samara that houses the Progress Rocket Space Center—the only plant in Russia that serially assembles the Soyuz-2.1b rockets used to launch Rassvet into orbit. Satellite imagery published by the Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ showed a collapsed roof section 85 meters long and 35 meters wide over Building 106A, the hall where crews wire the rockets' control systems and cabling. The channel reported two missile hits on that hall.
If the hall was destroyed, production could stop entirely, and switching to other Russian launch vehicles would take significantly longer and add complexity. Drones also attempted to strike Plesetsk Cosmodrome, from which both 2026 batches were launched.
Both targets—the factory that builds the rockets and the site that launches them—are needed if Russia is to expand Rassvet production.
The timeline: 5.5 to eight years, if nothing changes
Russia plans to expand the constellation to 292 satellites by the end of 2027, Deputy Chief of Ukraine's Defense Intelligence (HUR) Vadym Skibitskyi said. Moscow's longer-term goal is 924 satellites by 2035.
After SpaceX cuts off Starlink access, Russia launches first 16 satellites of its own “Rassvet” alternative
With 32 satellites already launched in two batches, 260 more are needed. At 16 satellites per launch, that requires roughly 17 launches. At a four-month interval between launches, deploying them would take roughly 5.5 years even if every launch succeeded and every satellite reached its target orbit. That most likely won't fully work out: one satellite from the first batch is already lost, two from the second batch may be lost as well, and none of them has yet reached the required altitude.
Russia also depends on the scarce Soyuz-2.1b rocket. The rocket has averaged only six to eight launches per year since 2022—most committed to GLONASS navigation satellites, ISS resupply, and military payloads—limiting Russia to a theoretical maximum of roughly two Rassvet-dedicated launches per year, or 128 Rassvet satellites over four years at that rate.
There is still time to shut this project down or slow it. Vyshnivska put the useful window to slow Rassvet at about a year. Russia, by Ukrainian calculations, needs five to eight years to see it through.

articles.title: Poland offers to host Patriot system production site for Ukraine after Kyiv secures license from US
articles.body:
Poland offers to host Patriot system production site for Ukraine after Kyiv secures license from US
Polish officials proposed on Sept. 27 that Ukraine use Polish land to manufacture Patriot systems after securing U.S. manufacturing licenses. 
The offer follows President Volodymyr Zelensky's announcement on Sept. 25  that U.S. President Donald Trump granted Kyiv permission to produce its own Patriot air defense missiles.
"We'll see if that happens," Poland's Deputy Defense Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka told Polish media. "We proposed that if such a factory is planned to be built in Ukraine, we propose building it in Poland, so that it would be in so-called 'safe territory.'"
The announcements come as Kyiv faces a critical shortage of air defense munitions, particularly of Patriots — the only weapons capable of reliably intercepting Russian ballistic missiles that continue to batter cities across the nation.
During overnight strikes across Ukraine, Russian forces killed 14 Ukrainians on Sept. 26-27.
On Sept. 24, Zelensky announced he had struck a 'very important' deal regarding a new batch of Patriot missiles while attending the U.N. General Assembly in New York City. Zelensky said that more Patriot interceptors would be heading to Kyiv soon, though he did not disclose which country would provide the missiles.
The Polish offer comes as Warsaw seeks to further U.S. military cooperation amid heightened risks emerging from Moscow.
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said Polish lawmakers are pushing to accelerate the construction of a new U.S. military base in western Poland. The base would be intended to house at least 5,000 U.S. troops and their families.
"We need to prepare a special act…on faster construction of the base, defining the competences of specific ministries, because building the base is in fact building a small town," Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said.
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said she expects U.S. officials to decide where the new base will be located by December of this year.
Russian missiles and drones have violated Poland's airspace numerous times throughout the war, including striking a locomotive of a Kyiv–Warsaw passenger train just 2 kilometers from the Polish border on Sept. 13.

articles.title: Hybrid warfare: The threat of Russia looms over the Mediterranean
articles.body:
Hybrid warfare: The threat of Russia looms over the Mediterranean
The CIA has reportedly warned several countries that Russia is preparing to launch hybrid operations across the Mediterranean Sea. But is the risk real, or is it a form of cyber warfare?
Several countries across the Mediterranean have reportedly been informed by the CIA of a possible imminent Russian operation, according to an investigation published by Spanish daily El Mundo on September 24.
American intelligence suggests the plan would involve drones launched from Russian vessels disguised as commercial ships and directed towards Spain, Italy and even France, the newspaper reported.

Russian Gerbera drones in the Mediterranean?
The report details the use of a specific type of drone: the Gerbera, which is smaller and lighter than the Shahed or Geran systems deployed and causing extensive damage in Ukraine.
A merchant ship crossing the Med could carry several Gerberas aboard, taking between one-and-a-quarter to two hours to reach the Italian, Spanish or French coasts. But the size of the device would render the weapons incapable of delivering significant ammunition.
Instead, the likely objective would be to surprise through unexpected attack, or to cause light damage upon impact, explained the El Mundo report, citing Lithuanian officials familiar with the information obtained by the CIA.
However, in an interview with TF1 and France 2 on Thursday evening, French President Emmanuel Macron contradicted the Spanish report, claiming to know nothing about Russia’s plans and sharing that the CIA had not informed the French authorities about any potential attack.
Ambiguous tactics
And herein lies the problem: experts highlight the ambiguity at the core of such revelations.
Mark Lacy, a specialist in Russian hybrid warfare at Lancaster University, explained the move by Russia could be an act – a manipulative tactic of cognitive and psychological warfare: “An important tactic of hybrid war or ‘the grey zone’ is what we call cognitive warfare or psychological warfare … it’s about the perception of what’s occurring.”
And both Russia – as well as the Western countries supporting Ukraine – could use this to their advantage.
Indeed, according to Lacy it seems that Russia may have deliberately conveyed plans to extend its hybrid campaign into the Mediterranean, without ever intending to act. He explained that the goal of Russia is to sow the seeds of doubt and panic – and at times, threat can be more effective than execution. “It’s in the interest of … Putin… to manufacture uncertainty.”
As for Western nations, he added, “The military and the government have an interest in making it look like we’re taking this threat seriously as a way of deterring Putin from actually doing anything.”
Read moreEU releases €6.6 billion for members arming Ukraine as seven killed in Kyiv
‘Strike when least expected’ – Russia
Mario Baumann, an expert in the Russian threat on Europe at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP), considers the theory around a potential Russian hybrid attack on the Mediterranean to be “absolutely possible”.
His rationale is that, although drone attacks, munitions factory raids and other strategic warfare moves so far have primarily concerned countries in northern and central Europe, in reality, the whole continent is affected, and as such, Spain, Italy and France are not spared. “European unity is … from the Russian perspective, a big problem because [it] is at the basis of sanctions.”
He pointed to previous incidents. In Spain, back in 2017, Russia was accused of actively supporting the Catalan independence movement with the aim of splitting the nation. Then in 2024, Russian agents were suspected of cyberattacks across online banking sites and other digital infrastructure. Meanwhile in France, several events – including vandalism in May 2024 of the Holocaust Memorial in Paris, which saw dozens of red hands painted around its perimeter – have been attributed to Russia. Following the incident, four Bulgarians were sentenced to two-four years in prison amid suspicions of Russian-linked foreign interference and antisemitic motives.
“Russia will always choose the points where we don't expect it,” Baumann said. In which case, it could be an opportune moment to target Southern Europe while all eyes are fixed on Poland, Germany and the Baltic states, he added.
Southern European countries represent Europe’s “weak point” when it comes to hybrid threats, the report by El Mundo detailed.
It is already challenging to defend against this style of attack in countries like Poland or Germany, in spite of them having dealt with similar incidents for some time, explained Berlin-based Julian Pawlak, a maritime security specialist at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP). He explained the situation is likely to be even more complicated for nations where the perception of danger is lower.

Drones: the ideal weapon for inciting paranoia
The recent developments are all the more timely for these three target countries, given that they face major elections in 2027, underlined Christian Kaunert, an expert in maritime security and hybrid operation at the University of South Wales in Cardiff. The French presidential election will take place next April and May, followed by Spain heading to the polls in August, while Italy is due to hold elections before autumn 2027.
According to the experts interviewed, electoral interference is a key theme amid Russian hybrid warfare. The goal is to instil “a sense of fear and anxiety” among the population, Baumann noted. As a result, continued Western political support for Ukraine could come at a real cost to voters – who might be persuaded to vote for parties such as the Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Germany, which seeks to reduce aid to Ukraine.
For the moment, Spain and Italy are among the countries with the least sense of direct impact from Russian threats, observed Lacy. By targeting these Mediterranean nations going forwards, Moscow may be able to see its aspirations come to fruition by the upcoming elections.
Read moreAt least 16 people killed as Russia and Ukraine trade deadly air strikes
And drones are particularly efficient instruments in this regard. He explained they provide ideal technology to generate paranoia. Whether they are used to fly over airports or cut underwater cables, these assets make it possible to expand the range of threat – even among those countries that consider themselves immune to such threat.
But of course, to succeed, access to the Mediterranean Sea is vital. The Russians have already been accused of launching drones from ships in the North Sea, said Pawlak. He noted that, given that Europe is aware of Russia’s capabilities, Southern Europe’s last line of defence is fast disappearing.
Kaunert acknowledged how things had become more difficult for Russia since its war with Ukraine. As a result, the Russian fleet has less freedom of movement in this region.
But it is not an insurmountable obstacle. Moscow could outsource some of the logistical challenges. Russian agents could conspire the plans and then leave them in the hands of organised criminals – "a lot of activity that can be organised through the internet,” he added.
It would not be the first such case in Southern Europe: In 2023, Russian defector Maxime Kouzminov was assassinated in Spain with the leading theory pointing to Russian mafia acting upon orders of Russian intelligence.
Another advantage for Moscow in its plans to cast a drone shadow over the Mediterranean, relates to oil. For Pawlak, this latest threat could push NATO to focus more on the region, potentially making life easier for Russian containers transporting oil via northern Europe.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russian attacks kill 14, injure 57 across Ukraine in 'mass strike'
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Russian attacks kill 14, injure 57 across Ukraine in 'mass strike'
Key developments on Sept. 26-27:
- Russian attacks kill 14, injure 57 across Ukraine, with Odesa Oblast targeted in 'mass strike'
- Russia launches third consecutive attack on Kyiv, killing 1, injuring at least 4, setting off fires
- Zelensky says over 10,000 Russian troops killed or wounded this week as Ukrainian military advances in Lyman sector
- Ukrainian military delivers 4 tons of food to occupied Oleshky by drones, according to regional authorities
- Russia plans to spend $12 billion on jet-powered drones, loitering munitions next year, Zelensky says
At least 14 people were killed and 57 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day as Odesa Oblast in particular came under mass attack, local authorities said on Sept. 26-27.
In southern Odesa Oblast, Russia launched "a mass strike," damaging a residential building, a medical facility, a hotel, a shop and a grain storage facility, local governor Oleh Kiper said. One person was killed while two others were injured, he added.
Overall, overnight on Sept. 27, Russian forces launched 170 Shahed-type attack drones, including 76 jet-powered versions, as well as Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, Ukraine's Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 147 drones, while strikes were recorded at 18 locations. Debris from downed drones fell at eight locations, the Air Force said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 27 that residential buildings, energy infrastructure, and other civilian infrastructure were attacked in Odesa, Kharkiv, Sumy, Mykolaiv, Kherson, Poltava, Zhytomyr, and Kyiv oblasts overnight.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast, four people were killed, and five were injured in Russian attacks across the region, local authorities said. Over the past day, Russia carried out 989 attacks on 59 settlements of the region.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, three people were killed, and five were injured in Russian attacks across the region over the past day, regional governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In the northeastern city of Sumy, a Russian glide bomb attack hit a residential area, killing two people and injuring 28 others, including four children, regional authorities said.
Russian attacks on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast killed two people and injured six others over the past day, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said on Sept. 26 and Sept. 27.
In northeastern Kharkiv Oblast, over the past day, Russia attacked the city of Kharkiv and the surrounding regions, killing two people and injuring three others, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In Kyiv, Russian drones injured five people over the past day, damaging residential buildings and warehouses, local authorities reported.
In Kyiv Oblast, Russian attacks over the past day damaged 23 facilities, injuring two people, Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional State Administration, said.
In southern Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks in the region injured one person, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said. He added that, as a result of the attacks, a high-rise apartment building, nine houses, a shop, and vehicles were damaged.
In Poltava Oblast, power lines have been damaged following the crash of a Russian drone, local governor Vitalii Diakivnych said. Around 500 customers were temporarily left without power while power company staff worked to restore the electricity supply, he added.
Zelensky said that over the past week, Russian forces launched more than 2,200 attack drones against Ukraine, as well as around 1,650 aerial bombs and 38 missiles of various types.
read also
Russia launches third consecutive attack on Kyiv, killing 1, injuring at least 4, setting off fires
Russia launched another drone attack on Kyiv on the night of Sept. 26-27, marking the third consecutive day of attacks on the Ukrainian capital, according to authorities.
"Just today, and only in Kyiv, Russian kamikaze drones 'defeated' two kindergartens and two schools, a residential building, a car repair shop, several warehouses, and communication facilities," Zelensky said. "Everywhere in the world, such a choice of targets would be called one word: terrorism."
The Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office said on Sept. 27 that a pre-trial investigation was launched into the commission of a war crime by the Russian military, which resulted in the death of a man.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at 5:17 p.m. local time that a drone struck a nine-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district of Kyiv.
Klitschko also said at 4:09 p.m. local time that an administrative building in the Holosiivskyi district was hit, according to preliminary reports.
In the morning of Sept. 27, Russia struck a non-residential building in the Shevchenkivskyi district, Klitschko said at 9:26 a.m. local time. At least three people, a woman and two 16-year-old children, were injured in the area.
Air defense units were operating over the city, Klitschko said in an evening update. Kyiv Independent reporters on the ground also heard air defenses operating in the city.
In the Shevchenkivskyi district, a Russian drone struck an uninhabited residential building at around 10 p.m. local time on Sept. 26, according to Klitschko.
A fire at the building was later brought under control, while emergency crews continued working at the site.
In the Solomianskyi district, a drone fell in an open area overnight. The resulting blast wave damaged a five-story residential building, breaking windows and damaging its facade, Klitschko said.
A fire also broke out at a warehouse in the district after the site was struck by a Russian drone, he added. Ukraine's State Emergency Service said that a car service center was on fire as a result of the attack.
A woman was injured in the attack and handed over to medics, and a man was killed, the State Emergency Service said.
Zelensky said that on the morning of Sept. 27, Russian forces struck a data center in Kyiv twice.
Ukraine's largest mobile operator Kyivstar said that its headquarters was damaged during the drone attack on Sept. 27, as reported by the Ukrainian media outlet Suspilne.
In Kyiv Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person and injured three others, Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional State Administration, said.
In Vyshneve, five cars were damaged, and a fire broke out after a drone struck the area. In Brovary, the attack caused fires in a warehouse and an office building, according to Tkachenko.
The latest attack follows a series of Russian drone strikes on Kyiv that began overnight on Sept. 24.
Russian drones continued targeting Kyiv during the day on Sept. 26, with further damage and casualties reported. By the evening, Ukrainian officials said five people had been injured in attacks on the capital during the day.
In recent months, Russia has increased its use of jet-powered drones, placing additional strain on Ukraine's air defenses.
One of Russia's newer jet-powered drone models, the Geran-5, can reportedly reach speeds of up to 600 km/h (373 mph), has an estimated range of up to 950 kilometers (590 miles), and can fly at altitudes of up to 6,000 meters (19,700 feet).
Ukraine is developing interceptor drones aimed at countering Russia's jet-powered drones, with some systems having undergone successful tests, according to Ukrainian officials. The government has not announced plans for mass production.
read also
Zelensky says over 10,000 Russian troops killed or wounded this week as Ukrainian military advances in Lyman sector
Ukrainian forces have killed or wounded 10,660 Russian troops over the past week while making gains in the Lyman sector of Donetsk Oblast, Zelensky said on Sept. 27.
"The occupiers continue to be eliminated, and the designated objectives are being achieved," Zelensky wrote on X, citing a report by Ukraine's Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi.
According to Zelensky, Ukrainian forces have video evidence confirming every Russian loss included in the weekly figure. Russia does not routinely disclose its military losses, and the figures could not be independently verified.
Ukraine's General Staff said on Sept. 15 that Russian forces have lost more than 300,000 troops killed and wounded since the beginning of 2026. After the summer campaign on the battlefield in Ukraine ended, Russian losses exceeded 1.5 million since the start of the full-scale invasion.
Zelensky said the past week's results were achieved as part of Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi in the Lyman sector and another active defense operation involving Ukraine's Air Assault Forces.
Zelensky added that the heaviest fighting has been taking place in the Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka, and Lyman sectors, while Ukrainian forces are also carrying out operations in Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, and Sumy oblasts.
He did not provide further details on the territorial gains.
Operation Vivaldi, Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps offensive operation around Lyman in northern Donetsk Oblast, was only made public on Sept. 15, although Russian pro-war Telegram channels and independent open-source intelligence (OSINT) researchers on social media had been tracking Ukrainian attacks in the area since late spring 2026.
On Sept. 20, the 3rd Corps said it liberated a further 40 square kilometers (15.4 square miles) of territory in Donetsk Oblast and retook several villages during the ongoing offensive.
read also
Ukrainian military delivers 4 tons of food to occupied Oleshky by drones, according to regional authorities
Ukrainian forces have delivered around four tons of food to residents of the occupied front-line town of Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, distributing supplies to 100 locations across the city with the help of drones, the Kherson Oblast Military Administration head said on Sept. 27.
The operation was carried out in cooperation with several Ukrainian military and law enforcement units, according to Kherson Oblast Governor Oleksandr Prokudin.
Residents of Oleshky have reported that the town is running critically low on food due to a lack of supplies, while only a small number of residents have managed to evacuate.
The drone delivery is part of an effort that has been supplying food to Oleshky residents by drone since March 2026, according to the governor.
A local resident who left Oleshky in April told the Kyiv Independent that drones had previously delivered food.
"(Drones) dropped the packages in several places. (The packages) contained a little bit of medicine and food. I don't know whose drone it was, but I reckon it was Ukraine that dropped them for us," the resident said.
Prokudin said Russian forces have attempted to disrupt the deliveries, including by shooting down the drones carrying food. He also accused Russian forces of confiscating or reselling humanitarian supplies and detaining residents who receive aid.
"The occupiers are detaining residents of Oleshky for receiving humanitarian aid parcels, throwing them 'into the cellar', beating them brutally and resorting to violence," Prokudin said.
Volunteers who used to organize the evacuation from Oleshky raised concerns about such deliveries in local Telegram groups, saying they feared this might lead to checks from the Russian side and a "nightmare for people".
The last successful food delivery to the city by vehicles was on May 26. Further attempts to supply the city on June 2 and Sept. 1 were disrupted by Russian drone attacks that killed two and injured others.
Oleshky lies on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, less than 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) from the regional center of Kherson. The town has been under Russian occupation since Feb. 24, 2022.
Oleshky's population has fallen from around 24,000 to approximately 2,000 as of spring 2026, according to the Foreign Ministry.
While Russian troops occupy Oleshky and the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in Kherson Oblast, the Ukrainian military controls the western bank. Russian troops use towns and villages on the eastern bank to launch attacks across the river, including on the liberated city of Kherson.
Russian forces have placed guns, mortars, and mines in and around residential neighborhoods due to the city's proximity to Ukrainian-controlled territory, Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration, told the Kyiv Independent.
Tolokonnikov said Russia shields its positions from Ukrainian strikes through the continued presence of civilians.
"Oleshky and its people are necessary for Russian troops so that Ukrainian troops cannot actively attack them in these settlements," he said.
In spring 2026, evacuation volunteers still managed to help people from Oleshky leave for other occupied settlements in Kherson Oblast or Ukraine-controlled areas in exhausting multi-day trips. Now, they said, the high risk made evacuation impossible.
In recent weeks, some residents have started walking out of Oleshky to the neighboring village of Radensk alone or in pairs, on roads mined by Russian forces.
Russian forces are preventing Ukraine and international humanitarian organizations from accessing the occupied territories to provide aid.
On Sept. 25, the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O'Flaherty, raised concerns about the worsening humanitarian situation in Oleshky. O'Flaherty said civilians, including children, were struggling to access adequate food, medicine, medical care, clean water, and electricity, warning that some could face a serious risk to their lives.
O'Flaherty said international humanitarian law requires occupying authorities to ensure civilians have access to food and medical supplies and to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid.
"The hardship and suffering of people caught along the frontlines of the war and in occupied territories demand international attention and action," O'Flaherty said.
read also
Russia plans to spend $12 billion on jet-powered drones, loitering munitions next year, Zelensky says
Russia plans to spend $12 billion next year on the production of jet-powered drones and loitering munitions, Zelensky said in his evening address on Sept. 26, citing Ukrainian military intelligence.
Zelensky said Ukrainian intelligence had obtained Russian internal documents showing the volumes of weapons Russia is preparing to produce next year and the funding allocated for them.
In recent months, Russia has increasingly relied on jet-powered drones in attacks on Ukrainian cities. In some attacks on Kyiv, jet-powered drones have accounted for around two-thirds of all drones launched.
"Next year, just for the production of jet-powered drones and loitering munitions, Russia plans to spend $12 billion on this one category of weapons," Zelensky said.
Zelensky said Ukraine is scaling up production of interceptor drones to counter Russia's increasingly widespread use of jet-powered drones. Several interceptor prototypes are already being tested in combat, he said, with some identified as potential primary means of defense against the weapons.
"We are scaling up production and components. There will be a response," Zelensky said.
The remarks come as Russia has intensified its attacks against Ukraine in recent days, despite renewed international efforts to secure a ceasefire. U.S. President Donald Trump called for an end to the war during his address to the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Sept. 22, while Zelensky said following their meeting that Ukraine was ready to accept a ceasefire covering attacks on energy infrastructure if Russia agreed to the same terms.
Zelensky said Russia's planned spending on attack drones shows that Moscow is not preparing to halt the war "at least for now."
He also said Ukraine's partners need to increase pressure on Russia through sanctions and strengthen joint efforts to defend against drones.
Ukraine currently intercepts about 55% of Russia's jet-powered Shahed-type drones, according to Zelensky. More than 2,730 jet-powered Shaheds were launched against Ukraine in September, he said.
Zelensky said Ukraine aims to raise the interception rate to the level achieved against conventional Shahed drones, which he said is above 90%.
Ukraine has already signed 11 drone deals, according to Zelensky. The 11th, with Finland, was signed this week in New York on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
He said Ukraine is preparing a 12th agreement, which it expects to sign with another country in the coming weeks.
"For Ukraine, this means more production capacity, more funding, and more technological advantages," Zelensky said.
Zelensky also said Russia is conducting a campaign targeting Ukrainian data centers, infrastructure, and communications. He said the goal is to leave Ukrainians without internet access, communications, and digital services.
Earlier, Russia's attacks on Kyiv on Sept. 26 caused internet outages across the capital and disrupted access to some online services.

articles.title: Ukraine’s disclosure of secret North Korean POW transfer sparks South Korea’s demand for an apology
articles.body:
Seoul called on Kyiv to explain and apologize for making public the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war, saying Ukraine had broken an agreement to keep the move private and later denied that such an agreement existed, Reuters reported on 27 September. Seoul also said it was reviewing additional measures if necessary.
The dispute puts new pressure on ties between Ukraine and South Korea as Seoul supports Kyiv while also dealing with growing military cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow.
Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said Seoul "expresses strong regret over Ukraine's unilateral disclosure and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a nondisclosure agreement," according to the Korea Herald.
Seoul said Ukraine had requested that the transfer remain confidential, citing fears of a backlash at home for passing up a chance to trade the two soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners held by Russia, though a presidential official called the handover humanitarian, not a prisoner exchange, the Korea JoongAng Daily reported. Seoul went along with the request to protect the soldiers and their families and for diplomatic and security reasons, Seong said, according to the Korea Herald.
Ukraine had denied that the two countries had agreed to keep the transfer private. Dmytro Lytvyn, an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, replied to a critic on Facebook that "there was no agreement to remain silent" and that hiding the prisoners' destination "would also be wrong," the Korea JoongAng Daily reported.
How the dispute unfolded
Zelenskyy announced the transfer on 23 September during a speech at the UN General Assembly. He said Ukraine had recently sent two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea. He also described one soldier's attempt to kill himself after realizing he would be captured and accused North Korean leader Kim Jong Un of using his soldiers "like currency," pointing to Pyongyang's improved ballistic missiles and drone capabilities as what it gets in return.
The next day, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung said the transfer should not have been disclosed and that the two sides had agreed to keep it private. A South Korean presidential official said Ukraine had told Seoul in advance that Zelenskyy might mention the transfer and Seoul had asked that the soldiers' destination not be disclosed, though it was unclear how he would phrase it, the Korea JoongAng Daily reported.
Who the two soldiers are
The two soldiers—Ri, 26, a reconnaissance sniper, and Baek, 21, a rifleman—were captured by Ukrainian forces in Russia's Kursk Oblast in January 2025, according to their interview with South Korea's Chosun Ilbo. Both had served in North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau and later asked to go to South Korea in media interviews and handwritten letters to defector groups.
The two countries' foreign ministers discussed the prisoners' status in March and June, reaching a shared understanding that the case should be resolved under international law and humanitarian principles, according to South Korea's Foreign Ministry. On 8 July, at the NATO summit in Ankara, Lee and Zelenskyy agreed to handle the case on humanitarian grounds while respecting the soldiers' wishes.
The two soldiers arrived in South Korea the weekend before Zelenskyy announced their transfer at the UN General Assembly, opposition lawmaker Yu Yong-weon said.
North Korea's role in Russia's war
North Korea began sending troops to support Russia's war in late 2024, with initial estimates putting the deployment at more than 10,000 soldiers. Many were sent to Russia's Kursk Oblast. The two countries signed a strategic partnership pact with a mutual defense clause in Pyongyang in June 2024.

articles.title: Russia is launching a faster Geran-5 at Ukraine that satellite jamming may no longer knock off course, a monitoring channel says
articles.body:
Russia has fielded a Geran-5 variant that can steer by images of the ground below without satellite navigation, the Ukrainian monitoring channel Polkovnyk GSh reported. A second Russian jet drone also filmed a strike on Kyiv live and relayed control signals to the drone that hit it, presidential adviser on defense technology Serhii Beskrestnov, known as Flash, said.
Russia's air war on Ukrainian cities has turned into a race of adaptations. As Ukraine got better at catching slow drones, Moscow made them fly faster, and now its jet drones also see for themselves and talk to each other.
A Geran-5 that reads the ground
The channel labels it the Geran-5 K5. Its DSMAC-type module corrects the drone's route by matching images of the ground below against stored references, like the one on Russia's Kh-101 cruise missile. The K5 also has a new fuselage, the channel said.
Because it flies faster than the Geran-4 and the standard Geran-5, it is often mistaken for Dan-T cruise missiles, the channel said. Official Ukrainian sources have not confirmed the K5 designation or the DSMAC-class system, Militarnyi noted.
The base Geran-5 carries a warhead of about 90 kg and cruises at 450–600 km/h, Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) found in January. It relies on a jam-resistant Kometa-M12 satellite navigation system and a mesh modem. HUR's component list includes no terrain-matching optics.
800 jet drones in four days: Russia is now firing type Ukraine’s interceptors cannot catch
One drone struck, another filmed and relayed
Russia published footage of its 25 September strike on the Inkom business center in Kyiv, which killed four people, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. The video was filmed from high above the target and fueled speculation about how it was shot. Beskrestnov dismissed the theories.
"Let me say right away: no secret satellites, no FPV from a Shahed, no Russian agents, no mysterious drones," Beskrestnov wrote.
Russia hit the building with a Geran-5, a jet-powered drone that functions as a small cruise missile. At the same time, a jet Shahed flew into Kyiv and circled the target at almost 3 km altitude, he said. It served as a mesh relay, passing radio signals to the Geran-5. It also filmed the attack and transmitted the video immediately. The Shahed then left Kyiv and destroyed a McDonald's warehouse.
Mesh networking lets Russian drones relay control signals through one another. Russia already flies its jet Shaheds under mesh control.
Status-6, an X account that monitors the war, reposted the Russian video and suggested a Gerbera-type drone had filmed it. Beskrestnov identifies the camera as the second jet Geran.
"This is certainly a complex Russian drone operation that requires precise calculations and coordination between pilots. I'm even sure they were sitting next to each other," he wrote.
New sensors across the Geran family
Russia's jet Shaheds sometimes switch off their engines before an attack and glide toward the target, Beskrestnov wrote. It is still unclear whether that is a malfunction or a deliberate move to approach slowly and precisely. In the same post, he showed a Geran-4 Seeker, a jet drone that hunts for targets with a front camera. It carries two mesh antennas on its tail, one pointing down and one up.
With colder weather, warm objects will become prey for Geran Seekers equipped with thermal cameras, Beskrestnov warned. He posted a thermal image of a locomotive that a Shahed operator filmed from 5–6 km away.
Ukraine catching up again
Ukraine's interceptors are catching just over half of Russia's jet drones. Beskrestnov confirmed on 19 September that a Ukrainian jet-powered interceptor works and has enough speed margin for different targets, calling it "functional, real, and ready for refinement." Separately, drone maker Wild Hornets says its STING interceptor is heading toward mass production after its first kills against jet Gerans.
Speed alone will not catch them, Beskrestnov argued earlier. Interceptors need machine vision to lock on and guide themselves in.
The threat is in the skies daily. On 28 September, a Russian jet drone hit the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv in the middle of the working day, killing a woman.

articles.title: How the Iran war has rewritten the Gulf's security calculus
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How the Iran war has rewritten the Gulf's security calculus
The US-Israeli war on Iran and its chaotic spillover effects across the Middle East and beyond have forced the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) members to come to terms with new realities.
Calculations about the Gulf’s security architecture are being reassessed, and Gulf states have been seriously questioning longstanding assumptions about the United States’ commitment to their security in the face of regional threats, chiefly from Iran, which retaliated against US and Israeli attacks by firing missiles and drones at the GCC states since the outset of this conflict on 28 February.
Looking ahead, what will emerge from this conflict is unclear. There will not be imminent reconciliation between Gulf Arab monarchies and Iran. Nor will the Gulf Arab monarchies make a straightforward move away from Washington.
What appears likely is a complicated transition whereby the GCC members reduce their dependence on the United States, bolster their own military capabilities, further diversify defence partnerships with alternative powers, and explore ways to manage tensions with the Islamic Republic diplomatically.
What could emerge is a more fragmented Gulf order whereby GCC states seek greater autonomy from Washington while still counting on the United States to remain an indispensable military force in the sub-region.
Dr Mehran Kamrava, a professor of government at Georgetown University in Qatar, does not envision Washington reducing its commitment to GCC members.
“There has been talk that some of the US military bases that dot the region are damaged beyond repair and that the US may not rebuild them after the war is over. Still, it seems doubtful that at least in the short to medium run, the United States would reduce its security commitment to the Persian Gulf states in any significant way,” he told The New Arab.
Any new Gulf security order must include Iran
The Gulf Arab monarchies clearly recognise that Iran is their permanent neighbour, and it is impossible to simply exclude Tehran from the Gulf’s future security architecture, as demonstrated by recent statements from high-ranking officials.
In his address to the United Nations General Assembly this month, the Emir of Qatar Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani called for a “regional system of collective security” and said that “we remain convinced that the crisis in the Gulf can be resolved through diplomatic means, through reopening the Strait of Hormuz to maritime navigation, in order to avert war”.
Similarly, Anwar Gargash, UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed’s Diplomatic Adviser, recently argued that there needs to be direct dialogue between Arab states and Tehran about the region’s future and a “new mindset” in how Arab states approach Iran.
Efforts to pressure Iran have produced limited results, explained Dr Kamrava. Pointing to a “realisation that the effort to marginalise and isolate Iran, not just economically but also in military and security matters, has yielded little success,” he told The New Arab that “the GCC impetus to assume a confrontational posture in relation to Iran, as was the case in the 2010s, has clearly backfired”.
Dr Kamrava stressed that the Islamic Republic has posed much less of a threat to its GCC neighbours when these Arab states engaged Tehran diplomatically compared to the times when they sought Tehran’s isolation.
“Moreover, Iran has long called for the articulation of a regional security arrangement that takes into account all regional actors instead of only a select group of them. If Iran does indeed become part of a broader security arrangement with its GCC neighbours, there is far greater likelihood of stability and reduced tensions than has been the case so far,” he added.
Dr Ghoncheh Tazmini, author of ‘Power Couple: Russian-Iranian Alignment in the Middle East’, explained that statements such as those made by the Emir of Qatar and Gargash do not suggest that a “reset” in GCC-Iran relations is coming soon.
Such statements appear to be acknowledging the basic geopolitical reality that whatever GCC members’ differences are with Tehran, Iran is a major regional actor whose interests and capabilities cannot be wished away.
“What these statements suggest is a recognition that Iran cannot be excluded from any durable security order in the Persian Gulf. Qatar’s emphasis on collective security and Gargash’s call for direct Arab-Iranian dialogue point to greater regional agency: the states of the Persian Gulf cannot leave the terms of their security entirely to negotiations between Tehran and Washington,” she told The New Arab.
More than seven months after the United States and Israel began this war on Iran, GCC states are making different assessments about what can be done to realistically achieve stability, economic diversification, and secure trade routes. Each of these is extremely difficult to achieve without engaging the Iranians diplomatically and relying excessively on external powers.
This does not mean that GCC members are anywhere close to trusting Iran or overcoming their grave concerns about Tehran’s regional foreign policy. This is especially so for the Gulf Arab states which have suffered the most from Iranian missile and drone strikes since late February.
This change in GCC states’ assessments about how to deal with Tehran “brings them closer to an idea Iran has promoted for years, namely that the region's security should be managed by regional actors,” said Dr Neil Quilliam, an associate fellow in the Middle East and North Africa programme at the London-based think tank Chatham House, in an interview with The New Arab.
“Gulf Arab states resisted that proposition in the past because they feared it would legitimise Iranian influence. Increasingly, however, there is a recognition that any durable regional order will have to include Iran and that dialogue may offer a more realistic path to stability than continued reliance on an uncertain external security architecture,” he added.
Pushing for regional mechanisms to prevent the next war
Calls for a “regional system of collective security” and advocacy of direct Arab-Iranian dialogue are understood within the context of GCC states increasingly seeking ways to manage regional security beyond traditional deterrence.
The absence of an inclusive framework in which rivals can address disputes before they escalate has become increasingly problematic.
“The GCC, for all its limitations, managed this well among its members between 1981 and 2017 when various combinations of members defused bilateral tensions and potential clashes through GCC channels,” Dr Rory Miller, a professor of international politics at Georgetown University in Qatar, told The New Arab.
“Of course, such calls for these conflict resolution and management mechanisms are going to be more common now than ever because when you have a security vacuum you have two options: fill it through offensive actions, such as the militarisation of differences, and defensive engagement, such as conflict management through negotiation,” he added.
“In these terms, these calls by [the Emir of Qatar and Gargash] strongly signal that the defensive route is what Gulf countries are considering now.”
Diversifying defence partnerships without replacing Washington
As Gulf Arab states call for more regional diplomacy, there is also a growing recognition of their need for more robust drone and missile capabilities, along with greater interest in domestic defence industries and diversified weapons procurement.
Gulf governments will seek to reduce their exposure to changes in Washington’s foreign policy by enhancing regional defence cooperation, strengthening indigenous military capabilities, and developing relationships with a wider range of international partners to gain greater autonomy from the United States, albeit without attempting to replace Washington.
While this trend is not new and was set in motion by past episodes, including the 2019 Aramco attacks and Israel’s attack on Doha last year, the ongoing regional crisis has served to accelerate it, with events of this year highlighting how exposed the GCC states are to insecurity while so dependent on the United States as a security guarantor.
Lessons learned
As a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran, Gulf Arab governments have been forced to learn important albeit painful lessons about both Iran and the United States.
For starters, as Dr Kamrava explained, GCC states can no longer shrug off Tehran’s threats to attack US military installations in the Gulf.
“Iranian warnings of attacking American assets in the Persian Gulf, of which there were plenty before the war, should not be ignored. This is something that Iranian visitors to the Arab states would often repeat, and they were repeatedly ignored. That can no longer be the case,” he told The New Arab.
Dr Quilliam pointed out the extent of Tehran’s means to hit GCC states hard, particularly in their vulnerable areas.
“Iran has shown that it retains the capacity to inflict considerable economic and security costs on the region despite years of sanctions and attempts to constrain its behaviour,” he said in an interview with The New Arab.
“At the same time, Gulf leaders have been reminded that Washington’s priorities are not always aligned with their own. The US can enter or escalate a conflict and then leave regional states to deal with many of the consequences,” added Quilliam, who sees these dynamics encouraging GCC members to coordinate more closely with each other.
Economic ambitions depend on a more secure region
The Gulf Arab monarchies can no longer treat economic security and national security as separate concerns. Disruptions to maritime trade, energy exports, investment flows, and critical infrastructure can quickly undermine the ambitious and grandiose economic diversification agendas such as Saudi Vision 2030, which have become central to the Gulf’s future.
“For governments focused on economic transformation, the protection of supply chains, maritime routes, critical infrastructure and investor confidence is now as important as conventional defence,” Dr Quilliam told The New Arab.
The Strait of Hormuz clearly highlights this vulnerability, bringing us to the fact that geography itself can become a strategic instrument.
Although the GCC states possess vast financial resources and increasingly advanced military capabilities, these countries lack the means to eliminate the strategic importance of a narrow maritime passage through which a substantial share of global energy trade transits. This comes with significant implications.
The future Gulf security architecture will have to protect the infrastructure, trade routes and economic relationships on which the region’s prosperity depends.
“The overriding lesson is vulnerability. The war has demonstrated how quickly the states of the Persian Gulf, their infrastructure and their economies can become exposed to a conflict involving Iran and external powers. It has also demonstrated the continuing importance of Hormuz: geography itself can become a strategic instrument, and military superiority cannot entirely remove that reality,” Dr Tazmini told The New Arab.
“Hormuz has for centuries been a space in which Iran, the Arab states of the Persian Gulf and external maritime powers have encountered one another. What has changed strikingly is Iran’s position within that geography: a Strait that once exposed the limits of Iranian maritime power has today become an important instrument of Iranian strategic influence. That historical reversal will form part of the context in which any post-war regional order takes shape,” she added.
Between Washington, Tehran, and greater autonomy
Looking at the bigger picture, what seems to be emerging is a Gulf that has lost its willingness to remain so dependent on the United States for security.
Nonetheless, throughout the foreseeable future, Washington is set to continue serving as the dominant external military actor in the Gulf even as GCC states pursue their efforts to diversify their defence relationships beyond the United States by turning to states such as China, France, Pakistan, Turkey, and Russia.
Not lost in the equation is the fact that the experience of being attacked by Iran has likely strengthened the case for GCC states to directly engage Tehran and seek to establish regional mechanisms capable of preventing disputes from escalating into wider conflicts.
“I think the dilemma for these Gulf states is on the one hand there is a desire for dialogue, for reaching some sort of an accommodation with Iran to explore possibly a new security architecture with Iran that includes Iran’s concerns in terms of security for the entire Middle East,” Dr Nader Hashemi, the director of the Prince Alwaleed Center for Christian-Muslim Understanding at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, told The New Arab.
“But, on the other hand, all of these countries are still deeply dependent in terms of their military relationship, their intelligence cooperation, their political relationship with the United States,” he explained.
“So, it’s not easy for these Gulf states to move in the direction of a new relationship with Iran when they will be pressed by the United States to maintain the status quo.”
Ultimately, the order that emerges following the current US-Iran crisis will probably not be a return to the pre-28 February model, nor a total break from it.
In all likelihood, a new balance will be struck whereby Washington’s power remains important, but the Gulf Arab states are increasingly serious about greater self-reliance, diversification of defence partnerships, and diplomacy with Iran.
A key question for the post-war Gulf will be whether the GCC members can successfully establish durable institutions that permit them to mitigate, manage, and contain their tensions with Iran while maintaining their close partnerships with the United States.
“My own view is that nothing is going to change as long as Donald Trump is in the White House. The next president might create more space and room for these Gulf states to renegotiate a new relationship with Iran in terms of the region’s security architecture while at the same time maintaining a close alliance with the United States,” said Dr Hashemi.
“One thing is clear is that long-standing assumptions within these Gulf states regarding their national security strategy have completely unravelled and come undone. We’re in the process of transformation and it’s unclear what’s going to happen next.”
Giorgio Cafiero is the CEO of Gulf State Analytics
Follow him on X: @GiorgioCafiero
