articles.title: Dark models: AI is making Chinese cyberattacks harder to detect and punish
articles.body:
In mid-September, Donald Trump announced the creation of a new agency called AI Force — his response to statements from industry leaders about the need to slow the pace of the technology’s development. However, opponents of implementing a voulntary slowdown are fearful of the effects such a step could have on competition with China, whose technology is becoming increasingly popular among hacker groups due to its low cost and weaker security safeguards. Moreover, cyberattacks and other operations using Chinese AI are harder to trace and stop than those involving models by Anthropic or OpenAI, as the companies behind the Chinese models do not report on criminal incidents involving the use of their products. As a result, hackers evade the attention of the authorities, and the number of cyberattacks continues to grow. So far, no concrete countermeasures have been taken to address the problem. In the meantime, the competitiveness of Chinese AI is on the rise, according to Kang Lee, deputy director for technology and geopolitics in Asia at the Institute for Security and Technology (IST).
 
In meetings across Taiwan in July — with chipmakers, the American business community, government agencies, and the island's leading technology researchers — one number surfaced in almost every room: the 2.4 million intrusion attempts a day that Taiwan’s National Security Bureau logged against government networks in 2024 (to say nothing of the 2.63 million a day in 2025.) The number was raised in an almost pedestrian manner, without any real sign of alarm. If the ministry responsible for cyber policy was moving slowly to respond, nobody in these discussions behaved as though the slowness would ultimately prove fatal. Regardless of the seemingly “pressing” nature of Chinese cyberattacks and its larger, evidently ballooning cyber campaign, a rapid, commensurate government response, whether within the Ministry of Digital Affairs or the Administration for Cyber Security, was simply not materializing.
What China does to Taiwan through its networks is espionage on an industrial scale — and even if the hackers switch nothing off, it is still espionage. Most importantly though, I argue that artificial intelligence is entering the contest between Washington and Beijing through that gap, and two broader developments this August establish the framework for my contention. 
Artificial intelligence is entering the contest between Washington and Beijing
The first story arrived mid-August, when the Financial Times reported what the Israeli firm Dream described as the first-ever near-autonomous AI attack on a government. Assembled from two open-source agent frameworks, the tool ran up to eight agents over the course of four days in early July, mapping 21 Taiwanese government systems, compromising at least 85 accounts, and exfiltrating more than 2,500 personnel records before turning toward the nuclear safety agency and several energy companies. The AI model’s safeguards were bypassed by falsely labeling the attack as an “authorized penetration test.” Dream could not determine which model was used, and Taiwan’s digital ministry likewise confirmed that an AI-agent intrusion targeting government agencies had taken place, but without naming a source (or reporting any disruption).
Twelve days later, Bloomberg reported that the Taiwanese threat-intelligence firm TeamT5 had watched state-affiliated Chinese groups more than double their attack volume after handing reconnaissance and malware development to DeepSeek and other open-source models, which generated exploit code and harvested one thousand IP addresses. This second story, the more consequential of the two, demonstrates just how easily AI could alter who can “see” the attacker. TeamT5's chief analyst called DeepSeek “relatively powerful with very low cyber guardrails.”
Two days after Bloomberg’s report came a third story — one that received far less attention but, to my mind, helps explain both. On Aug. 26, the U.S. Justice Department seized the domains behind QScan and QTRouter, a scanning platform and a proxy relay built by a contractor group the FBI calls QTFY. The department’s release puts NASA and the Senate on the attackers’ target list. The group worked for China’s Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology, whose clients included Beijing’s Ministry of State Security and the People’s Liberation Army. It operated from May 2018 until June 2026, when the group scanned a U.S. election system and failed. Notable other activities included intrusions in September 2024 at Department of Energy laboratories and the National Institutes of Health.
In other words, QScan, a distributed scanner whose worker nodes reported to central domains, constituted industrialized reconnaissance made by human engineering years before anyone even thought to delegate the job to an AI agent. Still, it ended as such campaigns end: with its domains seized.
What agents change
Framed as a question of capability uplift — of whether models will find new holes or write better malware — the debate about AI in cyber operations has, I posit, missed the mark. Anthropic’s November 2025 account of GTG-1002, a first-of-its-kind Chinese state-sponsored campaign run through Claude Code against roughly 30 organizations, shows where the difference maker is: mainly that its numbers actually point away from the frontier.
What matters most is that even back in 2025, far before Anthropic’s Mythos or Kimi K3, the AI performed 80 to 90 percent of the tactical work, making thousands of requests at rates no human team could match, while humans intervened at four to six decision points per campaign. The tools were overwhelmingly open-source penetration-testing utilities rather than custom malware. The model repeatedly overstated its findings, hallucinating credentials and presenting public data as secret. The ratio of operators to operations changed, and consequently, so did the tempo. The choice of target and the decision to act still rested with humans.
AI is capable of simplifying already-known methods of cyberattack, but it can’t yet independently discover new vulnerabilities
The academic evidence runs the same direction: a University of Illinois team showed in 2024 that a GPT-4 agent could exploit 87 percent of a set of real, already-disclosed vulnerabilities when handed the description, and 7 percent without one. Executing a known attack has become cheap in a way that discovering the breach simply has not. In August, the Chinese-speaking operator Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 documented that running DeepSeek-driven autonomous exploitation attempts mostly failed for that reason, succeeding only once a human took over to exploit a Citrix flaw by hand.
However, Anthropic’s Sept. 10 report supplies a notable, partial exception. Chinese-speaking operators in Hunan (two of them undergraduates) ran Claude as a round-the-clock vulnerability-research loop and came away with previously unknown flaws in a major security product — one that had been validated in their own lab and was working exploits for several families of network and security appliances. The company’s own judgment is that the larger change sits across the kill chain rather than in exploit discovery.
North Korea, the purest case because its hackers work for revenue, gained fluent English and durable fake personas from generative models, and nothing new by way of technique. The scheme itself of course predates the models. In fact, that is the pattern my own research on Pyongyang's operations finds across cases: the models industrialize the deception layer and leave exploitation itself about where it was.
Again, none of this makes Chinese cyber activity innocuous, but Volt Typhoon, which U.S. intelligence describes as pre-positioning inside American critical infrastructure for a future conflict, has never been triggered. Agents only shorten the path to access without pulling the trigger. No Chinese leader will decide whether to pull it based on how cheaply that access was obtained.
However, one case — I concede — cuts the other way. This July, models that OpenAI was running through an internal cyber evaluation found a zero-day in their test environment and used it to reach the open internet, where they broke into Hugging Face’s production servers to cheat on the exam — all without human intervention or decision-making. METR, the outside evaluator that OpenAI let in afterward, counted about 700 agents in the attack.
Anthropic’s chief executive Dario Amodei cited the imbroglio on Sept. 12 when urging the industry to slow down. As warnings go it is a fair one. Yet it was also a laboratory accident: OpenAI had switched off the cyber classifiers for the test and launched tens of thousands of agents at once. The public can recite the result in such detail only because it happened inside an American company, which published a post-mortem and opened the transcripts to outside investigators. “Many external models, including open-source ones, will soon reach comparable capabilities,” the same report warns.
The window that is closing
Everything the public knows about state hackers using AI comes from a small number of disclosures. For nearly all of them, the provenance is the American company whose model was abused. The first, in February 2024, came from OpenAI and Microsoft, which found five state-linked groups, two of them Chinese, using ChatGPT for research and scripting. GTG-1002 followed from Anthropic’s watch over its own platform, as did the Hunan group in September.
This February OpenAI disrupted a Chinese influence operation against Japan’s prime minister Sanae Takaichi. The interesting detail was that ChatGPT had refused the request, so the operation went ahead without it. The operators came back only to polish status reports, and the operation surfaced because someone just so happened to touch an American model once. That is the whole mechanism, since visibility into adversary AI use has been a byproduct of adversaries using American AI. Every 2026 case that centered on a Chinese model (Unit 42’s operator, Dream’s agents, TeamT5’s three groups) came from a third party rather than a provider, because no American provider saw the traffic.
Every 2026 case that centered on a Chinese model came from a third party rather than a provider, because no American provider saw the traffic
In a lower key, influence operations tell the same story, with the same one-sided disclosures. Four of the ten cases in OpenAI’s June 2025 threat report likely originated in China. Among them, the covert influence networks generated comments by the hundred and, by OpenAI’s own accounting, drew quite little authentic engagement.
The Japan operation is a classic case here: in essence, the move to locally run Chinese models once ChatGPT refused was the migration happening in miniature. In one update, the unit behind the influence operation recorded over 50,000 posts across 200 Western platforms, fewer than 150 of which drew over 300 shares or comments. Reach matters less than plumbing. Whatever lives in the weights travels into every product built on the Chinese models. A NewsGuard audit in January 2025 found DeepSeek’s chatbot framing its answers from Beijing's perspective 60 percent of the time on prompts about foreign false claims, most of them predictably not about China.
As such, the migration to Chinese models has very plain causes. None of them is a mystery to the operators themselves. Foremost are the guardrails, or rather, the want of them. DeepSeek’s R1 failed every one of fifty harmful prompts in Cisco’s testing. Criminals moved to it and to Qwen within weeks of release. Then, the price difference easily does the rest. The models run at a fraction of what their American rivals charge — up to 90% cheaper by one marketplace's estimate.
The customer base runs beyond China, as Google’s threat researchers found a tool of the Russian state-backed group APT28 — used against Ukraine — that queried Alibaba’s Qwen through Hugging Face at runtime for its commands. It was the first malware Google had seen call a model in live operations: in short, Chinese open models are becoming infrastructure for everyone’s operators. And to my knowledge, no Chinese provider has ever published a threat-intelligence disclosure about misuse of its models.
The user base for Chinese AI models extends far beyond China, including into Russia
The loss of visibility is only half of it, because the same shift removes the lever that has ended every campaign to date. When QTFY’s nodes all reported to three domains, the FBI could seize them and the platforms went dark. GTG-1002, because it ran on Claude, ended when Anthropic cut the accounts. The campaign was contained in about ten days.
A separate campaign run on DeepSeek weights downloaded onto the operator’s own servers would have no domain to seize and no provider to call. Dream never determined which model attacked Taiwan. On August 20, The Insider argued that developers such as OpenAI and Google should monitor API requests for state hackers and that regulators should extend know-your-customer rules to cloud-based AI services. Both are right, and both just so happen to apply only to operators who stay on American platforms.
Attribution, escalation, and what the formula gets wrong
Does espionage that arrives faster make war likelier? The standard forecast holds that AI makes cyber operations faster and cheaper and harder to attribute, and therefore more escalatory. Faster and cheaper are true, but the rest survives only in a form so narrow that its proponents would hardly recognize it.
Thomas Rid and Ben Buchanan argued more than a decade ago that attribution is a layered judgment (it runs from the tactical through the operational to the strategic) and never a reading of the toolkit alone. The 2026 record, remarkably, bears them out. Where I depart from them is at the provider level. They wrote before any operator could conceive of delegating tactical work to agentic AI, and before any company held the prompts such delegation leaves behind, which preserve each instruction in the operator's own words. Obviously, no such source could have been conceived in their scholarship, yet it informs all three of their levels simultaneously. Once operators run Chinese open weights on their own hardware, those prompts and their process never leave the machines. The source is gone, and attribution falls back only on what the operator leaves behind.
Dream pointed to a Chinese-language operator from the Simplified Chinese of the framework’s internal reports. The FBI, working from Ministry of State Security payment records and the operators’ former service in the PLA, tied QTFY to Beijing. Ergo, agentic operations are, if anything, noisier than human ones, since a campaign making several requests a second is an anomaly that behavioral monitoring is designed to catch.
Agentic operations are, if anything, noisier than human ones, since a campaign making several requests a second is an anomaly
As for escalation (the even weaker claim), the evidence sits in how the United States has answered Chinese campaigns. Washington dealt with an eight-year PLA-linked campaign against its own agencies with a domain seizure. Earlier campaigns drew indictments of people who will never be arrested. My research on North Korean cyber operations finds the same shape: attribution now arrives later than it did, and a remedy does not arrive at all. The median lag from theft to government attribution lengthened from 59 days for cases from 2022 and 2023 to 111 for those in 2024 and 2025. The recovery rate for such operations sits near one percent.
The state’s toolkit against espionage is legal and dilatory. That accords with what Sarah Kreps and Jacquelyn Schneider found in a survey experiment that showed Americans were less willing to escalate over a cyberattack than over a conventional one of similar effect (the cyber firebreak), and with Jon Lindsay’s reading of Stuxnet. This reading has aged well. Espionage that arrives faster is still espionage, and states have absorbed espionage without going to war for as long as there have been states.
Where the balance moves
While cyber operations have not changed the outcome of any international dispute — and nothing in the August record portends that agents will — the balance between Washington and Beijing now turns on who owns the plumbing, and faster espionage has little to do with it. Donald Trump told reporters at his golf resort in Ireland on Sept. 13 that America is leading China in AI and that “whoever wins AI wins.”
He has a case: on Sept. 8 the FBI, the NSA, and CISA named six Chinese labs — DeepSeek and Alibaba among them — for distilling American models at industrial scale, a practice the agencies called “the critical core” of how those labs build. Anthropic’s report of Sept. 10 counted more than 151 million such exchanges from Alibaba alone between May and July.
Chinese open-weight models carried a weekly peak of 46% of enterprise token traffic on the OpenRouter marketplace by early July, up from below 5% a year earlier, and DeepSeek’s V4 was trained in part on Huawei’s chips. The operators who follow that traffic of course take their prompts with them.
Chinese open-weight models carried a weekly peak of 46% of enterprise token traffic by early July, up from below 5% a year earlier
An American provider cannot report what it never sees, and the FBI cannot seize weights that sit on the operator’s own hardware. The provider has been Washington’s best sensor, more by accident than by design, and the very hackers it was watching are now leaving its platforms. As a result, the daily cyberattack count in Taipei will keep climbing, and the attempts it counts will still switch nothing off. In the end, fewer will know who is behind them.

articles.title: NATO article 5 is not what you think it is
articles.body:
NATO article 5 is not what you think it is
There are few myths as captivating and durable as that of Article 5 of the 1949 Washington Treaty. Proponents of the myth are convinced that, thanks to this provision, NATO is like Alexandre Dumas’s Three Musketeers, in which an attack against one is an attack against all, and the US would automatically come in full force to the rescue of any of the allies under attack.
It’s debatable and essentially unknowable to what extent that would have worked in the situation of the Cold War, when the US genuinely feared the Soviet/Communist threat, because the bloc was never tested to that extent. But it certainly is utterly false under present conditions and likely future circumstances, and America’s allies and partners need to pay attention and be careful.
The wording of the article itself is deliberately ambiguous. Clearly, there’s no automaticity there in the use of force, and such careful formulation was a condition for the treaty’s ratification by the US Senate because American policymakers at the time abhorred entering into entangling alliances.
So much for the automatic use of US military force.
Later, after the Soviet Union developed intercontinental ballistic missiles in the mid-to-late 1950s, American military strategy sought to avoid a direct nuclear exchange. Nuclear war, if it were to be fought, was to stay limited, confined to Europe, east and west.
So much for the US nuclear umbrella.
During the Cold War, recurrent crises around West Berlin were considered in Washington as a likely casus belli, but West Berlin was formally an occupied territory, rather than an allied country. It was safeguarded by American, British, and French military garrisons, and a move against the city (which was never attempted) would have been an attack on US military personnel. The situation along the German-German, Czechoslovak-West German, or Norway’s and Türkiye’s borders with the Soviet Union, though tense, was invariably stable. Elsewhere, NATO and the Warsaw Pact were separated by wide swaths of neutral territory.
So much for the likelihood of military conflicts which would have triggered Article 5.
The current US National Defense Strategy doesn’t view Russia as a major threat, with the Trump administration busy shifting the focus of US forces to East Asia and the Pacific. President Donald Trump has shifted the burden of NATO’s defense onto the European members themselves. If his performance in the Ukraine conflict is a gauge, he has no wish and no inclination to commit US forces to defending America’s allies and clients. Selling arms to them and sharing intelligence is the limit.
Washington also probably takes seriously Moscow’s warning that a NATO-Russia war would be different from the Ukraine conflict, and that it “would be short.” This logically means, in plain English, that it would be nuclear. Americans who studiously avoided a nuclear war with the Soviet Union when they felt genuinely threatened cannot be expected now to allow themselves to be dragged, on behalf of their European allies, into a nuclear conflict with Russia – still the only country in the world that has the capability to annihilate the US.
In his time, President Joe Biden said the US would defend Taiwan if China tried to achieve national reunification by force, but Trump is far more circumspect. To contain China, as with Russia, his administration pushes its allies to the fore, and the Philippines and Japan are the top candidates. As for Taiwan, after its semiconductor industry is safely relocated to America, the island’s significance for America will greatly diminish.
US security guarantees, though admittedly not Article 5-type, have been exposed as less than hollow in the ongoing US war against Iran. Instead of protecting the Gulf Arab countries, the American bases in the region acted like magnets, drawing Iranian drones and missiles which damaged the host countries’ infrastructure. Those in Eastern and Northern Europe who think they will be better off hosting American (or French, for that matter) nuclear facilities should think again.
Ukraine lost its way and brought untold calamities upon itself when its leaders made NATO membership their goal. They didn’t realize that Washington never intended to give them even a symbolic guarantee of protection. Security in the 21st century world can’t be delegated to foreign powers, it can only rest on one’s own resources and stable relations with neighbors. This is the lesson not just for Ukraine and Europe, but also for the Gulf Arab states and East Asia.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy says Moscow terrorising Ukrainians as fresh strikes kill eight
articles.body:
- 
  As Russian drones struck Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia was showing no signs of de-escalating the war despite assurances to the US that it would. In a statement on X, Zelenskyy accused Russia of terrorising Ukrainians with its latest attacks, which he said included setting on fire a market outside Kyiv, and striking kindergartens, schools, homes and communications facilities. “Anywhere in the world, this choice of targets would be called by one word – terrorism. Russia has no military objective whatsoever in doing this – it is purely an attempt to break people and inflict as much harm as possible on our society,” Zelenskyy said. “If Russia were truly preparing for any real steps toward de-escalation – as it claims, particularly to American negotiators – this wave of … terror would not be happening,” he said, calling on the US to fully implement the Lindsey Graham Act, which enables sweeping sanctions on Russia aimed at pressing it into ending the war.
- 
  Zelenskyy’s comments came ahead of the conclusion of the UN general assembly in New York on Monday. On the weekend, the foreign ministers of Russia and Germany met in New York on the sidelines of the assembly to discuss the war but Russia’s top diplomat dismissed Germany’s calls to ease off its “dangerous path of escalation” towards Europe. Zelenskyy said on X that Ukraine was relying on “effective decisions” being made by other countries and stronger pressure from its partners in the G7 and G20, “so that Russia sees that manipulating diplomatic signals will not allow it to keep winning more and more time for war and terror”.
- 
  New sanctions packages targeting financial networks, supply chains and companies and individuals helping produce Russian weapons “must take effect as early as October” Zelenskyy said also, to provide a stronger foundation for changing the situation and “pushing Russia toward real diplomacy”.
- 
  Russian strikes killed eight people across Ukraine on Sunday, according to authorities while Zelenskyy said Russia had fired about 3,900 drones, aerial bombs and other missiles at Ukraine over the past week. Ukrainian prosecutors said a drone attack hit a market in Sofiiska Borshchahivka on the western outskirts of Kyiv, killing two and injuring about 10 people. Others died in strikes in different regions and Kyiv also came under attack, local officials said. In the capital, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said nine people were injured, including a child.
- 
  Russia also hit the headquarters of Kyivstar – Ukraine’s largest mobile service provider – on Sunday, the company told local media. On Monday a guided Russian aerial bomb injured 22 people, including children, as it struck an apartment building in Ukraine’s second-biggest city of Kharkiv, mayor Ihor Terekhov said on Telegram. Moscow has recently waged a sustained bombardment of Ukrainian datacentres and communications infrastructure.
- 
  Peter Beaumont and Artem Mazhulin have reported on the dire living conditions inside Oleshky, across the Dnipro River from the southern city of Kherson. Life in the city – once home to 24,000 people but now with only 2,000 remaining – has become “a hell on earth”, according to Ukrainians familiar with conditions there.
- 
  South Korea has demanded an official explanation and apology from Ukraine, accusing Kyiv of disclosing the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea and then falsely denying that the two sides had agreed to keep the move confidential, according to a report from Reuters. “The presidential office expresses strong regret over Ukraine’s unilateral disclosure and its subsequent false announcement that there had not been a non-disclosure agreement,” Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said in a statement on Sunday. According to the statement, President Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer in his address to the UN general assembly. Ukraine’s embassy in Seoul did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

articles.title: Russia Calls It “Iva”—But Its Mystery Air Defense Missile Looks Iranian or Chinese
articles.body:
- Category
- Defense Tech
Russia Calls It “Iva”—But Its Mystery Air Defense Missile Looks Iranian or Chinese
Russian mobile air defense teams may have begun using Chinese-made QW-18 or QW-19 or Iranian copies of shoulder-fired surface-to-air missiles, according to footage aired on Russian television and analyzed by OSINT researcher TheDeadDistrict on September 28.
The unidentified weapon appeared during training with a mobile fire group from Russia’s 51st Air Defense Division in the Rostov region.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian personnel referred to the system as “Iva,” but its appearance does not match any known man-portable air defense system currently fielded by Russia.
Instead, the launcher closely resembles either Iran’s Misagh-3 or China’s QW-18A/QW-19 family, Militarnyi notes.
MANPADS are compact shoulder-fired surface-to-air missile systems designed primarily to engage low-flying aircraft, helicopters and other aerial threats. Russian mobile fire groups increasingly use such weapons as part of layered defenses against Ukrainian drones.
One particularly notable detail in the footage is the apparent absence of identifying markings on the launchers, potentially obscuring the systems’ origin.
A closer examination of the weapon’s nose section appears to strengthen the case for a Chinese system. An additional component visible on the Russian launcher is consistent with features seen on Chinese QW-series weapons but does not appear on available imagery of Iran’s Misagh-3.
It remains difficult to determine whether the system is specifically a QW-18 or QW-19. An Iranian connection cannot be ruled out either.
Iran manufactures its own Misagh family of MANPADS based on Chinese designs and has also continued purchasing Chinese air defense weaponry.
In July 2026, reports emerged of an Iranian deal with China covering as many as 400 MANPADS, including QW-12 and FN-16 systems, with the package valued at approximately $60 million to $70 million.
That raises the possibility that any Chinese-origin systems reaching Russia could potentially move through an intermediary rather than arrive through a publicly acknowledged direct transfer.
The appearance of an apparently foreign MANPADS with a Russian air defense formation would also raise questions about Moscow’s ability to produce enough short-range air defense weapons domestically to meet growing wartime demand.
Earlier, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence has pulled apart Russia’s RM-48U ballistic missile, revealing a weapon assembled from repurposed S-300 and S-400 missile components and packed with foreign electronics, including dozens of parts from US-based manufacturers.

articles.title: Wes Streeting: Britain and Europe must get out of ‘defensive crouch’
articles.body:
Wes Streeting speaking at the POLITICO Pub Event on September 28, 2026 at the Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, England. | Baldo Sciacca for POLITICO
LIVERPOOL, England — Britain and Europe need to get out of their “defensive crouch,” Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said Monday, as he argued that U.S. pressure on European allies will ultimately result in a stronger Europe.
Speaking at the POLITICO Pub at Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, Streeting added that he believes that America’s frustration over “European over-reliance” on the U.S. has “not been unique to the Trump administration.”
The defense secretary said that, contrary to “the perception that the U.S. is somehow disengaging from Europe,” he has “experienced the exact opposite” — despite the ongoing U.S. review into pulling various troops and capabilities from across the continent.
Advertisement
British-American relations soured towards the end of Keir Starmer’s tenure as prime minister, after Britain refused to give the U.S. military support for its war with Iran, including the full use of British military bases for strikes on Iran. New Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s Labour government is now seeking to repair the alliance.
Part of the challenge from Donald Trump’s administration to Britain is to raise defense spending to record post-World War II levels. Britain doesn’t currently have a costed plan to reach its NATO commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defense by 2030.
Ahead of next month’s budget, he said that Chancellor John Healey doesn’t need persuading about the importance of raising defense spending as he previously resigned on this issue as a point of principle, Streeting said.
“I don’t want any complacency,” Streeting continued, adding: “We can’t just send in John Healey’s resignation letter as our submission to the spending review.”
However, he noted that he no longer gets asked how he is cutting waste and bureaucracy since leaving his position of Health Secretary for the Ministry of Defence, despite the fact that procurement challenges have “plagued the MoD.”
Fairford latest
Streeting also declined to elaborate on Donald Trump’s comments regarding the arrest of five Britons under suspicion of preparing a terrorist attack near RAF Fairford on Sunday, except to thank the farmer who reported suspicious activity to the police.
Advertisement
“I would also say respectfully to her [the farmer] she has only a partial view about what was going on, and so in that spirit, I want to underscore my thanks, the thanks of the government and the thanks of the president of the United States for the work that our police, Counter Terrorism Policing, and security services do to keep us safe, and the actions they’ve taken at RAF Fairford.”
He also rejected suggestions that Britain’s closeness to the U.S. has made the U.K. the target for potential attacks: “That alliance makes us more safe, not less safe. Having the Americans at RAF Fairford makes us more safe, not less safe.”
Elsewhere in the interview, Streeting rejected reports that the U.K. is involved in negotiations with Germany over Berlin potentially helping fund Britain’s nuclear weapons program.
“I’ve not taken part in those sorts of discussions at this stage,” he said.

articles.title: U.S. Embassy Issues Security Alert to Citizens in U.K. Amid Suspected Terror Plot
articles.body:
The U.S. embassy in London has issued a security alert for American citizens in the U.K. following a suspected terror plot near an RAF airbase used by the U.S. military, which led to the arrests of five men who have since been released on bail.
“U.S. citizens are encouraged to exercise caution and be mindful of personal security,” read the notice responding to the Sunday incident near RAF Fairford. “U.S.-associated facilities, gatherings, and organizations may be at heightened risk. U.S. citizens are advised to follow instructions of local authorities for their personal safety and security.”
The alert reminded Americans that the U.K. in April raised its national terrorism threat level to “severe” from “substantial,” a decision made after an antisemitic attack in London was declared a terrorist incident by police. The “severe” level, according to the Metropolitan Police, means “an attack is highly likely.”
The warning came after British police arrested five men on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses after they were detained near RAF Fairford in southwest England, an airbase used by the U.S. to strike Iran, in the early hours of Sunday. Officers made the arrests after receiving a tip-off that three "suspicious vehicles" appeared to be heading toward the direction of the base, which Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) previously said could be a target on account of its use by the U.S. military.
The U.K.’s Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) confirmed in a statement to TIME that the five arrestees were British nationals in their 20s who live in London. They were all released on bail Monday afternoon, local time. "They are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others. They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of enquiry," according to the CTP.
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme early Monday that it is too soon to speculate over the motives during a live investigation. Questioned about a potential Iran link, he said: "We know that Iran and their proxies wish to do us harm. We know that they hate our democracy, and we know that we regularly have to thwart Iranian attempts to threaten either our interests or indeed our allies."
CTP’s deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans said she was “very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident, and the geopolitical questions that are being raised,” but stressed more time is needed to work through the case.
Additionally, the head of CTP Laurence Taylor emphasized his officers are considering this case from "every possible angle," including the potential that this "may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state."
The Iranian embassy in London has said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" any attempt to "link Iran to" the arrests made near RAF Fairford. "The circulation of such fabricated speculations... will serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the U.K.," it said Monday.
What we know about the arrests at RAF Fairford
RAF Fairford is a NATO-designated standby deployment and a U.S. forward operating base for U.S. Global Strike Command, according to U.K. government records. It has been used extensively by U.S. military aircraft in previous conflicts, including "Operation Iraqi Freedom" in 2003.
Gloucestershire Police, the local authority responsible for the area, received a call from a concerned resident at 12:45 a.m. local time on Sunday, regarding three suspicious vehicles traveling toward the airbase.
The local resident, a farmer, told police she had found the road blocked by three white vans. “I saw a large group of hooded and masked men. When they saw me, they ran ahead of me… I then realised that something highly unusual was taking place,” she later told the BBC.
Armed officers responded to the call and five men were arrested on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act, as well as section 5 of the Terrorism Act.
Police evacuated residents from around 85 nearby households and put a cordon in place while the British Army’s specialist explosive ordnance disposal team examined the vehicles.
While the farmer who alerted police has been hailed for their actions, Streeting has indicated they only had a “partial picture” of the matter and appeared to suggest U.K. security forces had been aware of a suspected plot involving RAF Fairford.
U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday claimed the suspects had been “under view for a long time.”
"Working with Britain, it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort, and working with the British worked out great… and we got them,” Trump told reporters.
When asked if Trump had been correct, Streeting did not reject the assertion.
“Our security services and our police, they don’t ask for praise, but I think it was a proud moment yesterday to see the President of the United States recognize the extraordinary work that our police and our security and intelligence services do every day throughout the year and throughout the world to keep us safe,” he said. “That’s all I want to say this morning on that.”
TIME has asked the Ministry of Defense and Downing Street whether the British authorities were already investigating a potential plot.
Speaking at the Labour Party conference later Monday morning, Streeting celebrated the U.K. and U.S. alliance as “the closest of any two nations on Earth” and vowed the two countries “will always stand together against those who hate our freedom and those who wish us harm.”
British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband, meanwhile, referred to the incident near RAF Fairford as a “reminder of the threats our country faces.”
The U.K. must be prepared to “confront” all the security threats facing Europe and the world, he told conference attendees, adding that “we will act against the proxies of Iran.”
Concerns over the risk Iran poses to the U.K.
The U.K. government gave authorization in March for the U.S. to use bombers based at RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites used to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz. The base’s role in the U.S. military’s seven-month operation against Iran may have made the site a target.
While British police and lawmakers have said it's too early to determine who was behind the suspected terror plot, the U.K. government has repeatedly issued stern warnings regarding the threat the Iranian regime poses to the U.K.
On Feb. 28, former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer addressed the nation, explaining the U.K. had no involvement in the initial U.S.-Israeli strikes against Iran, but emphasizing the government’s belief that Iran cannot be allowed to possess a nuclear weapon.
“Even in the United Kingdom, the Iranian regime poses a direct threat to dissidents and the Jewish community,” he said. “Over the last year alone, they have backed more than 20 potentially lethal attacks on U.K. soil."
In March, four men were arrested on suspicion of conducting surveillance of locations and individuals linked to the Jewish community in London to assist Iran. One man was an Iranian national and the other three were British-Iranian nationals. The CTP said the arrests were “part of a long-running investigation and part of our ongoing work to disrupt malign activity where we suspect it.”
A separate investigation resulted in a man being charged in May with assisting a foreign intelligence service relating to Iran.
Earlier this month, a man and woman were arrested in London as part of National Security Act investigation. They were apprehended on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service. Again, the country to which the investigation was linked was Iran.
The IRGC was designated a threat to national security in the U.K. under new powers in July, after a series of antisemitic attacks across England., including arson offenses against Jewish ambulance services.
“These new powers will make it easier to prosecute and lock up anyone carrying out [Iran’s] dirty work here in Britain,” said Starmer at the time.

articles.title: Putin is testing NATO on Norway’s remote Arctic islands
articles.body:
BARENTSBURG, Norway — For the best part of a century, the biggest threat to the residents of Svalbard was polar bears. Increasingly, it now comes from Russia.
Fears are growing that Moscow could use the sprawling Arctic archipelago — a part of Norway with an unusual legal status — to test NATO militarily amid growing uncertainty over the U.S. commitment to European defense.
Allies suspect Russia of probing crucial undersea cables in the waters off Svalbard and staging military-style events that test the limits of the rules governing its presence there. As Russia ramps up hybrid attacks across Europe, Oslo is racing to boost its naval and surveillance capabilities to protect its northern flank, while local authorities on Svalbard are investing in critical infrastructure — and even have an evacuation plan in place.
Advertisement
“There is more tension in the Arctic and in the north, and of course also Svalbard is a part of that,” Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik told POLITICO. “We know that Russia ... uses a lot of ways to try to provoke or find ways to do hybrid threats.”
Despite its status as Norwegian territory, the archipelago's main island, Spitsbergen, is home to a Russian town.
“Russian leadership is highly unpredictable and more and more risk prone,” said Kari Aga Myklebost, a Russian history professor and Svalbard expert at Norway's Arctic University. “I wouldn't close out any scenario when it comes to the Kremlin's will to confront NATO.”
High North, high tension
For decades, Svalbard symbolized the Norwegian maxim “High North, low tension,” which saw efforts to build cooperation among Arctic countries, including Russia.
Beyond its remoteness — lying over 900 kilometers from mainland Norway — and its glacial temperatures, that was down to the archipelago's unique status. Under a 1920 international treaty, countries recognized Oslo’s sovereignty over the islands and in return gained resource exploitation rights — with the Soviets buying the town of Barentsburg to mine local coal deposits soon after.
Advertisement
The treaty also forbade any nation from using Svalbard for “warlike purposes” including the construction of naval bases and fortifications, but Norway does visit the archipelago with coast guard and military vessels.
At its Cold War peak, 2,400 Soviet citizens lived on Spitsbergen, the only populated island, making up around 70% of its population.
Moscow has little incentive to upend the treaty because it could rebound against its own interests. With Russia’s northwestern Kola Peninsula — home to two-thirds of its nuclear second-strike submarines — sitting around 1,000 kilometers away, “Russia has been cautious to avoid any kind of escalation,” Myklebost said.
A Soviet-era placard in Barentsburg. | Victor Jack/POLITICO
That makes it strategic for NATO, too. “In a military conflict … this is where the Russian submarines could enter the North Atlantic and hide at greater depths and pose a threat to NATO and the U.S.,” she argued.
Yet tensions have grown following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Moscow also began direct boat trips from Russia in 2024 and last year set up a chapter of the Russian Geographical Society, which is led by former Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu.
“We call them gray zone provocations,” Myklebost said. “It’s a very cost-efficient way of asserting Russian presence and … challenging Norway's jurisdiction.”
As a result, Norway’s intelligenceservices this year warned the Kremlin “aims to increase Russian scope for action in Svalbard.”
British, American and Norwegian forces this spring reportedly caught Russian vessels testing a secret subsea cable-cutting weapon off Svalbard’s coast.
Although Barentsburg’s coal reserves are dwindling, Moscow is not abandoning the town. Moscow provided state-owned Trust Arktikugol, which administers Barentsburg, with about 1.89 billion rubles (€20 million) in federal subsidies in 2025, according to its accounts.
Russia’s ambassador to Norway, Nikolay Korchunov, told POLITICO he wanted to see a “transformation of the economic activities” from coal to services in Barentsburg, and said Arktikugol was investing in maintaining the town.
Advertisement
Cranes and scaffolding adorn many of Barentsburg’s Soviet-era buildings, which lie scattered across a jagged hill facing the imposing snow-specked Vøringen glacier — a sign of Russia’s continued interest.
But “we are not questioning any sovereignty of Norway,” Korchunov insisted. “We stress the necessity and importance of fulfilling all the Svalbard Treaty,” he said, accusing Oslo of contributing to a “negative trend towards NATO militarization of entire Baltic-Arctic region.”
On thin ice
Vice Adm. Rune Andersen, the chief of the Norwegian Joint Headquarters, said his priority was “striking that balance between deterrence but maintaining stability” on Svalbard, and remaining “calm and collected” on hybrid threats.
Svalbard Deputy Governor Katharina Rise. | Victor Jack/POLITICO
But given the “risks” of escalation, the military is investing to reinforce its surveillance capabilities, he said, including launching three new maritime mapping satellites next year — alongside “a renewal of the navy and coast guard … to have a continuous presence” nearby.
NATO countries “are more often up in our waters,” said Sandvik, the minister. Defending Svalbard is also a part of NATO’s planning process, he said.
Advertisement
Locally, the strategy is to keep a lid on tensions. Svalbard’s Deputy Governor Katharina Rise said her office meets with Russia’s local consulate four times a year. “We have good and constructive dialogue,” she said. “It's our responsibility to secure the stability and … low tension here.”
Terje Aunevik, the mayor of Longyearbyen, the main Norwegian town on Spitsbergen, said authorities had plans in place to rapidly evacuate the settlement if tensions flare.
With just two subsea internet cables, one airport, one water reservoir and one diesel-run power plant in Longyearbyen that depends on imports, Aunevik said “major investments” are underway, including the construction of two new water reservoirs by around 2029. “We are quite vulnerable in that perspective,” he said.
Out in the cold
Up close, Barentsburg doesn’t look particularly threatening. Few locals venture outside the several dozen crumbling buildings. A plume of smoke escapes the aging coal plant and a lonely hammer-and-sickle Soviet flag flaps in the wind. Barentsburg feels like an abandoned relic of a bygone era.
Some of the recent hybrid activity is also down to a local push for attention from Moscow, said Arild Moe, a research professor and Russia expert at the Fridtjof Nansen Institute think tank. “They’re playing on nationalist strengths … to get priorities and to get finance.”
But Putin’s unpredictability and Trump's repeated wavering on NATO remain wild cards.
Anxiety is also palpable on Spitsbergen. In Barentsburg, “we don’t speak about [political] topics,” said a waitress from St. Petersburg who asked that her name not be used, while acknowledging locals fear a potential NATO-Russia war. “Of course this worries us,” she said.
“There is of course this constant chatter about if the Russian government wants to push a NATO member and Svalbard is the place where they would do it,” said Jonatan Svensson, an expedition guide who has lived in Longyearbyen for five years.
Jonatan Svenssson. | Victor Jack/POLITICO
To assuage those fears, NATO should consider air patrols over Svalbard, shift defensive air assets to the north of mainland Norway and hold joint exercises nearby, the two NATO diplomats said, provided Oslo agreed and the measures complied with the Svalbard Treaty.
However, so far NATO has no public plans to boost its naval or air presence around the islands. But some worry the alliance's current posture won't be enough to deter Moscow.
In theory, it would be “really easy” for Russia to occupy Svalbard, said Ståle Ulriksen, a lecturer at the Royal Norwegian Naval Academy, if it flew in special forces from northern Russia and seized the airport. However, he argued such a scenario is unlikely.
Yet Moscow wouldn’t need to launch a full occupation. According to Myklebost, the analyst, Russia could stage an emergency affecting its local citizens and send in crisis management forces, a move that may not clearly trigger NATO’s Article 5 mutual defense clause.
“A worst-case scenario is a situation where Moscow sees an opportunity to test NATO cohesion,” she said. “Maybe Norway's shouting for help from allies, and then you have Donald Trump saying: ‘No — we are not risking our good deals with Russia over this tiny island.’”

Ukraine Goes After Russia’s Air Defense and Drone Network, Hitting Pantsir-S2 and UAV Sites
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Pantsir-S2 air defense system, drone command and launch sites, ammunition depots, and other military facilities during operations on September 27 and overnight into September 28, Ukraine’s General Staff reported.
According to the General Staff, Ukrainian Defense Forces targeted a Pantsir-S2 surface-to-air missile and gun system near Seltso in Russia’s Bryansk region.

The latest strikes came alongside separate Ukrainian operations targeting Russian radar, communications, aviation, and maritime assets. articles.title: North Korean hackers suspected in €332.8m crypto heist as it leads global hacks
articles.body:
North Korea, one of the world’s most closed-off countries, has been linked to some of this year’s largest cryptocurrency thefts. Proceeds from such attacks help fund its nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programmes, according to the US government.
North Korean hackers are suspected of stealing $387.5 million (€332.8mn) in cryptocurrency from major global cryptocurrency exchange Bitget in what appears to be the biggest crypto theft of the year.
In a statement, Bitget said it detected unauthorised transfers from some of its hot and warm wallets on Thursday.
Hot wallets are connected to the internet so an exchange can process transactions quickly, while warm wallets have more limited online access.
The company said its cold wallets, which are kept more isolated, were not affected.
The company identified IP addresses whose VPN usage appeared to match that of a North Korean group, making a North Korean connection “very likely,” CEO Gracy Chen said in a livestream.
“We’ve identified IP addresses that match the VPN choices by a certain [Democratic People’s Republic of Korea] DPRK group. We think this is very likely to be attacked by North Korea,” Chen said in a post on X.
The attackers did not obtain the private keys used to access Bitget’s hot, warm or cold wallets, Chen added, meaning they could not use those keys to take direct control of the wallets.
Instead, the hackers breached an internal system and entered false transaction information that made fraudulent transfers appear legitimate to Bitget’s approval system.
Bitget says its user protection fund, which it said held more than $464 million (€398.5mn) at the time of the attack, is sufficient to cover the loss.
The customer account balances remain accurate, while deposits and trading have continued to operate.
However, Bitget temporarily suspended withdrawals as a precaution while it checked its systems. It has announced plans to restore withdrawals in stages from 28 September.
The company said it had notified law enforcement and was working with security firms to investigate the attack and trace the stolen funds.
Chen said in a livestream on Friday that people she identified as members of Lazarus, a North Korean state-linked hacking group known for stealing cryptocurrency, had previously approached her by posing as a journalist to arrange a Zoom interview.
This is the largest cryptocurrency theft reported so far this year, according to a report from the blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs.
Stolen assets are used to fund nuclear weapons and missiles
North Korea has previously been identified as responsible for large-scale virtual asset thefts.
Money stolen by North Korean state-linked hackers helps fund the country’s nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programmes, according to the United States (US) Treasury Department.
According to another report from TRM Labs, North Korean groups accounted for 76% of the value stolen in cryptocurrency hacks through April this year. The figure predates the Bitget incident.
In February 2025, North Korean hackers stole approximately $1.5 billion (€1.28bn) in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit, according to the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).
The FBI said the hackers made the funds harder to track by rapidly converting some of the stolen assets into other cryptocurrencies and distributing them across thousands of addresses.
While North Korea has developed sophisticated cyber capabilities, its government severely restricts ordinary citizens’ access to the global internet.
According to the United Nations Human Rights Office Seoul in South Korea, most citizens can use only a controlled domestic network.

articles.title: Russian attacks kill eight in Ukraine after Moscow vows to continue war
articles.body:
Russian attacks kill eight in Ukraine after Moscow vows to continue war
Russian strikes killed eight people across Ukraine on Sunday, authorities said, a day after Moscow vowed to continue the war. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had launched about 3,900 drones, aerial bombs and missiles over the past week. Kyiv accused Moscow of deliberately targeting civilians as winter approaches.
Russian strikes killed eight people across Ukraine on Sunday, a day after Moscow vowed to pursue the war, authorities said Sunday.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Russia had fired about 3,900 drones, aerial bombs and other missiles at Ukraine over the past week.
Russia has stepped up attacks on Kyiv, with Ukraine charging that Moscow is deliberately hitting civilian targets as the country braces for another tough winter.
Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi announced that Russian strikes hit a children's centre in the northern city of Sumy, killing three people, including a 16-year-old girl.
Zelensky said three people had been killed in night-time strikes on the southern Zaporizhzhia region and a Russian drone strike had killed one man in Kyiv.
Authorities in the Odesa region said a "massive strike" on the south of the Black Sea region had killed one more person.
Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klitchko said a woman and two 16-year-olds had been wounded and hospitalised in the capital.
"The enemy continues to relentlessly attack the Kyiv region with strike drones," the city's administration said.
"Sixteen sites have been damaged," including 12 houses, a warehouse and production facility, it added.
Russian strikes in the Odesa region damaged housing, a shop, a hotel, a medical building and a grain warehouse, regional head Oleg Kiper said.
Read morePoland fears Ukraine war could spill over
Targeting 'civilian infrastructure'
"This past week, the Russians launched more than 2,200 attack drones against Ukraine, as well as around 1,650 aerial bombs and 38 missiles of various types, a significant number of them ballistic missiles," Zelensky posted on social media.
The latest strikes had targeted two kindergartens, two schools, housing "and other civilian infrastructure" in various parts of the country, he added.
"If Russia were truly preparing for any real steps toward de-escalation – as it claims, particularly to American negotiators – this wave of 'shahed' terror would not be happening," Zelensky said in later comments.
In Moscow, Russia's defence ministry said it had bombed a Kyivstar data centre in Kyiv and another belonging to the Omega Telecom company, claiming that the firms were providing services to the Ukrainian army.
It also released an image of a drone bearing the ironic message "Digital Detox", confirming that the strikes were aimed at disrupting internet access in Ukraine.
On Saturday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov told the UN General Assembly his country intended to continue its military campaign "to the end".
Read moreRussia accuses Europe of seeking to thwart Ukraine talks
Russia denies that it aims at civilian targets.
The defence ministry also said that Russian forces had seized the border village of Khrypuny in Ukraine's eastern Kharkiv region, where Russia controls pockets of land.
Russia does not claim the Kharkiv region as its own, unlike the Donetsk, Lugansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions. Throughout the war however it has attacked the region and seized land there.
The Kremlin has repeatedly said it intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine.
US-led talks to end the war have failed to produce a breakthrough and the UN has highlighted the growing civilian toll as the two sides become more entrenched.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Poland to ease rules for shooting down drones, missiles entering from Russia
articles.body:
Poland will change procedures for military aircraft and helicopters that engage objects entering from the direction of Russia, Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk said on Sept. 28.
Under the current peacetime procedure, Polish pilots must fly close enough to visually confirm a target in Polish airspace before firing at it.
The new procedures will replace this visual identification with so-called positive identification, meaning the radar reading alone will be enough for the pilot or the operational commander to authorize shooting down the object, Polish broadcaster RMF24 reported.
This procedure would allow Polish forces to shoot down missiles or drones entering Polish airspace from the direction of Russia faster than previously.
"Until now, we have not used such options, because they are usually reserved for a state of war or martial law," Tomczyk said. "However, given the threat, and given that Poland today faces the possibility of drones entering our territory every day, we must introduce such changes, both for the pilots and for the security of the state."
Amid rising tensions between Russia and Poland, Russia has repeatedly violated Polish airspace.
On Sept. 23, a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter briefly violated Polish airspace near the country's northern border, Poland's Operational Command of the Armed Forces (DORSZ) said.
The helicopter crossed into Polish airspace north of Braniewo at around 11:08 a.m. local time after flying from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, the command said.
The helicopter entered Polish airspace to a maximum depth of around 300 meters and remained there for 42 seconds, according to the statement.
The aircraft was tracked by Polish military radar systems, while fighter jets were scrambled and ground forces were placed on standby. Polish air defense crews remain on round-the-clock watch and at "constant readiness" to protect the country's airspace, according to the statement.
On the morning of Sept. 16, Poland scrambled fighter jets and temporarily halted operations of the Lublin Airport and Rzeszow-Jasionka Airport as Russia launched drones against Ukraine, Polish authorities announced.
Around 7:00 a.m. local time, military aircraft took off, and ground-based air defense and radar reconnaissance systems were readied in response to Russian drone attacks on Ukraine, DORSZ announced on social media platform X.
This was a preventive measure to protect Polish airspace, particularly in the regions bordering Ukraine, DORSZ said. Shortly after 8:00 a.m., DORSZ announced the operation had ended.

articles.title: Iran says it ‘has no plans to negotiate with US’ despite Trump claims – US politics live
articles.body:
Iran has 'no plans to negotiate with US' despite Trump claims in media
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
State media in Iran has reported that Iran’s delegation to the UN General Assembly had no talks planned with the United States, after US president Donald Trump said he expected more negotiations.
“Iran’s delegation in New York has no plans for negotiations with the United States,” said the official IRNA news agency, citing an unnamed source close to the group.
Trump told media outlet Axios on Sunday that he expected talks to resume soon, a day after he rejected a proposal by Tehran to reopen the strait of Hormuz within seven days.
“Iran’s views and positions were conveyed clearly and explicitly to the US side... via a Qatari mediator,” IRNA said, adding that the Iranian delegation would return to Tehran on Tuesday.
Iran says it presented seven conditions for ending the war and reopening the strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway through which roughly 20% of the world’s oil and gas flowed before the war.
The strait lies at the heart of the conflict that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February. Following that attack, Tehran placed a chokehold on the waterway, and Washington responded with a blockade of Iranian ports.
Axios said indirect talks mediated by Qatar could take place as early as today, less than a week after similar discussions between US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi.
Iran demands a seven-day ceasefire across the Middle East, including in Lebanon, where its ally Hezbollah is regularly bombarded by Israel.
It also demands the unfreezing of its foreign assets, lifting sanctions on its oil sector, and an end to the US naval blockade. Trump rejected their demands on Saturday.
In other developments:
The Trump administration on Monday plans to release new fuel economy standards that would relax regulatory requirements for automakers to control pollution from gasoline-powered cars and light trucks. President Donald Trump said on his Truth Social media account on Saturday that the less stringent mileage requirements would “take the waste out of building cars in America” and save families “thousands on a new, beautiful and safe car,” while boosting auto production in the US.

Russia Revives Secret Nuclear Bunker Built to Launch Retaliatory Strike. Here’s What We Know
Russia has carried out a major modernization of a secret underground command complex in the Ural Mountains linked to Perimetr, the Cold War-era nuclear command system known in the West as “Dead Hand.”
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to a joint investigation by Danwatch, The Sunday Times, and the Dossier Center published on September 26, thousands of Russian military procurement records indicate that large-scale work at Object 1335, buried inside Mount Kosvinsky in the Sverdlovsk region, began in 2018.
The investigators reviewed more than two million Russian military procurement documents and found orders for construction materials, excavation equipment, ventilation systems, electrical infrastructure, and protective equipment associated with the facility.
The purchases included around 22,000 tons of steel, more than 56,000 tons of cement, roughly 600 kilometers of electrical cables, as well as specialized filtration systems designed to protect against chemical, biological, and radioactive contamination.
The Sunday Times separately reported that procurement documents refer to at least 24 underground chambers and show that the distance between the facility’s main and emergency exits is approximately 2.5 kilometers. Satellite imagery also shows extensive excavation and new construction around the mountain.
Object 1335 is believed to serve as a protected command center for Russia’s Strategic Missile Forces. Former personnel described the underground network as extensive enough for buses to move between different sections of the complex.
The facility has long been associated with Perimetr, a Soviet-designed backup nuclear command system intended to preserve Russia’s ability to order a retaliatory strike if its senior leadership and normal communications channels were destroyed in a nuclear attack.
Pavel Podvig, a nuclear disarmament expert and head of the Russian Nuclear Forces project, told The Sunday Times that “Perimeter is actually a communication system,” designed to ensure that a retaliatory order can still be transmitted after an attack.
Details of Perimetr’s current operation remain classified. However, Russian military publications uncovered by the investigators indicate that the system has undergone further modernization.
Retired Major General V. G. Khalin, who participated in its development, wrote that its automation system and technical capabilities had been upgraded, including through mobile command posts and space-based communications.
Another Russian military veteran wrote that Object 1335 was placed on combat duty in 2023, while Khalin later referred to the facility as having the technical capability for an automatic retaliatory strike.
Danwatch said the expansion of Object 1335 forms part of a broader modernization of Russia’s nuclear forces and command infrastructure. The Kremlin and presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov did not respond to requests for comment from the investigative outlets.
Russia has also continued exercising other parts of its strategic nuclear forces. On April 2, Russia conducted drills in Siberia involving mobile RS-24 Yars intercontinental ballistic missile systems, with crews practicing dispersal, combat duty, protection from simulated air attacks, and operations under conditions of radioactive contamination.
The Yars is one of the core systems in Russia’s nuclear arsenal, with a reported range of up to 11,000 kilometers and the ability to carry multiple independently targetable warheads.

articles.title: A Ukrainian Hornet drone hit a Russian radar 120 km behind the front. It was likely a $100 million Nebo-M
articles.body:
A Ukrainian Hornet drone struck a Russian radar system about 120 kilometers behind the front, Taras Myshak, senior communications officer of the 59th Separate Assault Brigade of Unmanned Systems, said on Suspilne on 28 September, ArmyInform reported. The brigade's Signum unmanned systems battalion carried out the strike about a week earlier, he added.
Russia's air defenses depend on radars to see Ukrainian drones and missiles coming. Every radar it loses weakens that watch and gives the next Ukrainian strike a better chance of getting through.
According to Myshak, the target was a "quite expensive" Russian radar system.
A radar system is effectively the "eyes" of the Russian air defense system: it detects aerial targets, determines their coordinates, and transmits information to other elements of the system.
Russians continue probing Ukrainian defenses
Russian forces in the brigade's zone, roughly along the Donetsk Oblast border, continue to operate in small infantry groups and use infiltration tactics, Myshak says. At the same time, the Russians are trying to cut Ukrainian logistics, he adds, saying that the brigade is effectively holding the Russian army back from infiltrating into Dnipropetrovsk Oblast.
The Russians' main means in this sector remain drones and infantry, the serviceman says. The number of infantry has decreased somewhat compared with previous periods, but the pressure from the enemy has not stopped, he adds.
"Of course, they will try, they will constantly probe, so to speak, our defense with their infiltrations. And likewise with drones, of various ranges, working on logistics, making it impossible for us to enter positions, to deliver everything necessary to the positions, in order to make our defense impossible," Myshak emphasized.
At the same time, Ukrainian troops are trying not only to defend against these actions but also to deprive the Russians of radars, electronic warfare systems, and other equipment, the serviceman says. "We likewise don't let them relax," he said.
Russians tried to prevent the strike, but Ukrainian forces hit the target
This was likely the same strike that Ukrainian volunteer fundraiser Serhii Sternenko reported on his Telegram channel on 18 September. Operators of the Signum unit of the 59th Brigade, together with the First Separate Unmanned Systems Center, hit a Russian Nebo-M radar about 120 kilometers from the front line, he wrote.
The radar, which Sternenko valued at about $100 million, was damaged over two drone sorties, which also wounded two Russian servicemen, according to his post. During the operation, the Russians tried to jam the drone's video feed with electronic warfare, but the operators flew on using only flight data and their own experience, he added.
Ukraine systematically knocks out the "eyes" of Russian air defense
In October 2024, Ukraine's military said it had hit a Russian Nebo-M radar station with ATACMS ballistic missiles to blunt Moscow's ability to spot and shoot down aircraft and missiles, Reuters reported. The military estimated each such system at more than $100 million.
Ukraine is systematically increasing its use of medium-range strike drones, which can hit targets up to 200 kilometers deep inside enemy territory, the Ukrainian Defense Ministry reported in May this year. Russian air defenses and radars are among the main priorities of such operations, as their destruction weakens the system for detecting and intercepting aerial targets, the ministry said. Medium-class drones, including the FP-2, Hornet, and Bulava, play a critical role in such strikes, the ministry noted.
According to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, Ukrainian forces struck at least 25 major Russian air defense and radar systems during April, about 12 of which were radar systems, the Ukrainian Defense Ministry also wrote in May this year.

articles.title: Satellite Imagery: Strike Damaged Five Workshops at Plant Involved in Kh-101 and Oreshnik Production
articles.body:
Satellite imagery shows damage to the Azov Optical and Mechanical Plant (AOMZ), which is involved in the production of Kh-101, Kh-35U, and Kh-59/Kh-69 cruise missiles, as well as Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missiles.
The Absolutely Reliable Source Telegram channel published the satellite imagery.
Judging by the imagery, six buildings were hit. According to the channel, they house five production workshops.
Workshop 022, a foundry comprising two buildings, was hit. A fire and significant damage were recorded at the site.
Workshop 024, the machining workshop, also sustained significant damage, with part of its roof collapsing.
In addition, workshop 008, which produces optics; workshop 009, an assembly workshop; and workshop 010, an electroplating workshop, were damaged.
The Ukrainian Navy and the SSU’s Special Operations Center Alpha launched the strike on the night of September 26.
The attack involved Ukrainian Neptune cruise missiles as well as RUTA, Palianytsia, and Bars jet-powered drones.
The Azov Optical and Mechanical Plant joint-stock company is part of Russia’s Tactical Missiles Corporation and is one of its key optoelectronic production facilities.
The plant produces, among other things, radar and infrared seekers for guided missiles, thermal imaging devices, and electronic systems for precision-guided artillery.
The plant also supplies components for anti-tank weapons production, weapon stabilization systems for armored vehicles, navigation and laser equipment for aircraft and UAVs, and electronic warfare systems.
The enterprise also manufactures optomechanical and optoelectronic products and equipment for Russia’s aerospace industry.
Following a document leak, researchers found that AOMZ is involved in producing Kh-31P anti-radiation missiles, short-range R-74 and long-range R-37M air-to-air missiles, Kh-101 and Kh-35U cruise missiles, Kh-59/Kh-69 cruise missiles, and Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missiles.
Open-source information also indicates that the enterprise is involved in producing KAB-250, KAB-500, and KAB-1500 guided aerial bombs and the Kh-38ML short-range air-to-surface missile.

articles.title: Iranian missile strike injured eight US Marines – NBC
articles.body:
Iranian missile strike injured eight US Marines – NBC
Eight US Marines were injured when an Iranian anti-ship cruise missile struck a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz that they were operating on earlier this month, NBC News reported on Sunday, citing sources. The Pentagon has not offered an account of the incident and is facing scrutiny over whether it is downplaying the number of casualties and costs in the war with Iran.
The Marines – seven enlisted personnel and one officer – were operating as part of a landing team when the missile hit, unnamed US officials told the network. The personnel suffered smoke inhalation and possible traumatic brain injuries, but none were seriously wounded, the report claims.
NBC sources said the Marines were not aboard a US Navy ship but did not identify the type of vessel.
The Pentagon did not provide an explanation for the incident. It took it nearly ten days to quietly add the Marines into the Defense Casualty Analysis System, a database that tracks injuries and deaths in the conflict.
Just last week, the tally abruptly rose by 37, bringing the acknowledged number of US troops wounded since the hostilities began to 861, with more than half categorized as casualties of ‘Overseas Operations’ rather than specifying the unpopular war against Iran.
Earlier this month, the Washington Post also reported that at least 22 service members died in the Middle East since the war began, compared with 18 acknowledged by the Pentagon at the time.
While it is unclear whether the Trump administration was deliberately downplaying the toll, or the discrepancy was caused by bureaucratic procedures, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth denounced the report as “DISGUSTING and FAKE.”
The dispute over the human toll has been accompanied by questions over the financial costs of the conflict. CENTCOM estimates the costs of military operations against Iran at around $43.6 billion, but the figure does not include the potential multi-billion-dollar cost of repairing US military facilities hit in retaliatory strikes.
NBC reported in July, citing people familiar with Pentagon assessments, that the overall cost could already be $80 billion to $100 billion when repairing bases, replacing destroyed aircraft, and fully replenishing weapons are included.
Iran has warned that it has “unforgettable lessons” in store for the US if it continues the escalation, saying it will only lead to “heavier costs and further humiliation.” Last week, President Masoud Pezeshkian told Fox News that Iran “does not seek to kill Americans” but will resist the pressure campaign.

Zelenskyy urges US to implement Graham Act: Russia is manipulating diplomacy
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called on the US to implement Lindsey Graham's sanctions law against Russia, saying Russia is manipulating diplomatic signals and has no intention of ending the war.
Source: Zelenskyy on social media
Quote: "If Russia were truly preparing for any real steps toward de-escalation – as it claims, particularly to American negotiators – this wave of 'Shahed' terror would not be happening. And we need to take a sober view of the situation. Russia knows how to send the kind of encouraging diplomatic signals that the world simply wants to hear… It knows how to send such signals in order to delay tough steps by the world in response to the war.
In America, the important Lindsey Graham sanctions and tariffs law has already reached the implementation stage. It is a law that can change a lot for the better if fully implemented. This law needs to be implemented – and everyone in the world can see that there is EVERY REASON to apply it and A CLEAR PURPOSE for doing so. We are counting on effective decisions from the world and stronger pressure from our partners, so that Russia sees that manipulating diplomatic signals will not allow it to keep winning more and more time for war and terror. It is important that our other partners in the G7 and G20 also take a principled stance."
Details: Zelenskyy said that new sanctions packages are also being prepared, including measures targeting financial networks, schemes for supplying components and equipment used to produce Russian weapons, as well as specific companies and individuals, particularly those involved in the production of Russian ballistic missiles.
"The new sanctions must take effect as early as October to provide a stronger foundation for changing the situation and pushing Russia toward real diplomacy," he stressed.
Background:
- On 18 September, Trump signed the Russia sanctions bill, which was co-authored by the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
- On 16 September, the US House of Representatives passed the Russia sanctions bill on the introduction of tariffs on countries that buy Russian energy. The bill was passed by the US Senate on 7 August.
- On 22 September, Trump said that, if necessary, he was ready to implement the Graham Act on sanctions against Russia.
- On 25 September, Zelenskyy said that during his conversation with Trump, he had raised the issue of implementing the Graham Act, which concerns sanctions against Russia and punitive tariffs on buyers of Russian energy.
- On 26 September, amid Russian strikes on Ukrainian oblasts, Zelenskyy called on Trump to implement the Graham Act and urged the European Union to introduce additional sanctions against Russia.
