articles.title: Britain leads Europe in new defence factory investment
articles.body:
The United Kingdom has taken the largest single share of Europe’s defence manufacturing expansion since the start of 2024, attracting 34 of the 197 facility investments announced or opened across the continent in that period, according to research published by Cushman & Wakefield.
That share of 17 per cent puts Britain ahead of Germany, which accounted for 27 investments, France with 26 and Spain with 12. The property consultancy tracked announcements and openings between January 2024 and August 2026 covering drones, missiles, munitions, combat air systems and other advanced defence technologies, treating each as a driver of demand for industrial and logistics space.
The Defence Investment Plan committed an additional £15 billion between 2026-27 and 2029-30, taking planned defence investment to around £298 billion across the four-year period, and annual defence funding is expected to approach £80 billion by 2029. Governments across Europe are expected to spend more than €625 billion on defence equipment between 2026 and 2029.
The concentration of that money in Britain, France and Germany reflects their standing as the three largest defence producers in Europe, and Spain, Italy, Sweden, Turkey, Belgium and the Netherlands have also drawn significant new investment. Central and eastern Europe, led by Poland, accounts for a substantial share, weighted heavily towards artillery and munitions, which the researchers attribute both to proximity to the war in Ukraine and to those countries ramping up their own defensive capabilities while contributing to wider EU and NATO initiatives.
Artillery and munitions is the largest single category across the continent at 52 facility announcements, bolstered by the European Union’s Act in Support of Ammunition Production, and almost half of that activity is in central and eastern Europe. Aircraft and ships account for 43 commitments, driven in particular by Airbus, Safran and Leonardo, while investment in vehicles has come from BAE Systems, Patria, Rheinmetall, Iveco, Escribano and KNDS. Companies in systems and components have invested heavily as well, across radar and sensor systems, communications and navigation.
Ten of the 21 drone and autonomous vehicle production facility openings and investment announcements recorded since 2024 have been in the United Kingdom, the largest concentration anywhere in Europe. The research counts aerial, surface and ground systems together in that total, and describes their deployment in Ukraine and the Middle East as having driven substantial investment in development and production. Eight aircraft and naval manufacturing investments have also come to Britain, the second-largest share in that category.
Tim Crighton, head of logistics and industrial for the UK and EMEA at Cushman & Wakefield, said: “The UK is exceptionally well positioned to capture this next phase of defence-led industrial growth. Alongside established strengths in aerospace and naval manufacturing, we are seeing increasing investment in drones, autonomous systems and other advanced defence technologies. These sectors are creating demand across a broad range of industrial assets, from purpose-built production facilities to existing industrial buildings that can be adapted and brought into operation swiftly. Working across a range of these projects, we can see the significant investment going into these facilities which in turn is driving economic growth and new skilled employment opportunities.”
More than half of the investments across Europe, 54 per cent, involve newly created facilities, and 36 per cent are being delivered as new-build developments. The average unit size committed to is around 20,000 square metres, and the most frequently demanded buildings fall between 10,000 and 25,000 square metres. Converted buildings feature more heavily in the existing space taken, typically legacy industrial assets taken over wholesale for new production lines.
Many manufacturers can work from conventional industrial buildings adapted for production rather than purpose-built plants, though the research sets out where defence differs from an ordinary industrial letting. Some buildings require blast proofing, internal partitioning or segmentation, and depending on the machinery involved, reinforced floors or larger doors. Sites generally need enhanced security, including higher fences, advanced access systems and surveillance. Lease negotiations run longer because of security checks on the asset, the landlord and neighbouring occupiers, and because government approvals can form part of the conditions for contracting space. Tenants tend to seek greater rights to alter buildings from the outset rather than during a tenancy, and may ask for restrictions on access or enhanced security around a landlord’s inspections.
Industrial estates aimed squarely at the sector have begun to appear, among them Telford Defence and Business Park in the West Midlands, which received development permission in 2024 and has funding in place, marketing what it calls defence-ready opportunities within the established West Midlands cluster. Elsewhere, Estonia has developed the 204-hectare Ermistu Defence Industrial Park, which has secured four manufacturers and has room for more, and a 200-hectare scheme is proposed at North Kiviõli with an emphasis on energetic materials. Turkey’s Kırıkkale weapons industry zone, established in 2014 on land belonging to the state manufacturer MKE, has drawn private firms to build factories on the site.
Sally Bruer, head of EMEA logistics and industrial research at the firm, said: “What is particularly notable is how quickly defence manufacturers’ investment is translating into real estate requirements. More than half of the facility commitments we tracked involve new sites, reflecting manufacturers’ need to increase capacity and secure long-term production capability.
“As large procurement programmes move through the supply chain, we expect this to drive increasing demand for smaller and mid-sized industrial facilities across the broader supplier ecosystem as businesses expand production capacity to support the next phase of defence growth.”
Investment so far has been led by the prime contractors and their tier one suppliers, while Europe’s defence ecosystem takes in more than 2,500 specialist small and medium-sized firms. Expansion is harder for those businesses until orders are placed further up the chain and income starts to arrive, and survey work by GLOBCOM cited in the research found that fewer than half of tier two, three and four suppliers have seen the demand growth the primes and tier ones have enjoyed.

articles.title: Chinese shoulder-fired anti-aircraft missiles appear in Russian service
articles.body:
- Russian state TV footage shows a Russian air defense unit with unmarked shoulder-fired missiles resembling China's QW-18A and QW-19, Militarnyi reported.
- The launchers were filmed with a mobile fire group of the 51st Air Defense Division in the Rostov region.
Russian air defense troops appear to be using Chinese-designed shoulder-fired anti-aircraft missiles, according to an analysis by Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi of footage aired on Russian state television.
The launchers were shown during an exercise by a mobile fire group of Russia’s 51st Air Defense Division in the Rostov region, in a segment broadcast by the state channel Rossiya 1 and shared on X by the account TheDeadDistrict. Mobile fire groups are small teams, often riding in pickup trucks, that Russia uses to hunt Ukrainian drones with machine guns and short-range missiles.
The soldiers in the report called the weapon “Iva.” But the launcher does not match any man-portable air defense system, or MANPADS, known to be in Russian service, Militarnyi reported Sept. 28. Russia’s own shoulder-fired missiles in current use include the Igla-S and the newer Verba.
Militarnyi said the launcher most closely resembles Iran’s Misagh-3 and China’s QW-18A and QW-19. Neither the launchers nor the missiles shown on camera carried any visible markings, which the outlet said could point to an effort to hide where they came from.
A closer look at the footage favors a Chinese origin, according to Militarnyi. The Russian launchers have an extra fitting on the front section that does not appear in available photos of the Iranian Misagh-3. The outlet did not rule out that it could be a newer Iranian version, but said no photos of Misagh launchers with that feature have been published. Militarnyi said it could not determine whether the system is a QW-18 or a QW-19. China’s state-owned CASIC showed the QW-19 at the DSA 2024 defense exhibition in Kuala Lumpur.
The weapons may have reached Russia through Iran, Militarnyi said. Tehran buys Chinese arms, including shoulder-fired missiles, and in July 2026 reports emerged that an Iranian deal with China covers up to 400 MANPADS, including the QW-12 and FN-16, at an estimated cost of $60 million to $70 million. Iran’s Misagh family is itself derived from China’s QW series, and Pakistan builds a similar missile under the name Anza-2.
Militarnyi said Russia’s use of foreign-made shoulder-fired missiles may indicate that its own industry cannot produce enough to meet the military’s needs. Mobile fire groups have become a main line of defense against the long-range drones Ukraine sends against Russian refineries, airfields and weapons plants, which increases demand for short-range missiles.
Ukraine has previously said it confirmed Chinese supplies of gunpowder and artillery systems to Russia, and Ukrainian intelligence services believe military cooperation between the two countries includes producing Chinese-designed weapons inside Russia. China has repeatedly said it does not supply lethal weapons to either side in the war.

articles.title: Seoul seeks apology after Ukraine 'breached' confidentiality agreement over transfer of North Korean POWs
articles.body:
North Korean soldiers were among the foreign contingent conscripted to fight alongside Russian troops on various frontlines in the war on Ukraine, after the Kremlin sought assistance from its close allies to bolster its deployments amid struggles with domestic conscription.
South Korea's President’s Lee Jae Myung’s office demanded an apology from Ukraine for denying an agreement to keep the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war from its territory to Seoul confidential.
The row was ignited by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's disclosure last week that his country had sent two North Korean soldiers to the South, adding that they were "not easy to capture alive".
The intensifying dispute risks complicating Kyiv's efforts to obtain weapons from allies, including South Korea, to fight off bombardments from Russia.
Hours after Zelenskyy's disclosure, South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung criticised the action.
"I do not know why the Ukrainian side broke the agreement and made the matter public, but it is very disappointing," he wrote on X.
Zelenskyy's aide Dmytro Lytvyn sought to play down the disclosure, saying that the president had only made public the fact that the soldiers were handed to South Korea. Ukraine is an "open country", noted Lytvyn, saying that it would be “unusual” to hand over the soldiers in secret.
But Seoul condemned it as a breach of trust.
Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said in a statement late on Sunday that South Korea was "considering additional measures that may be necessary regarding this matter".
"It is in itself a very serious matter that the Ukrainian side violated the confidentiality agreement between the two countries and made the disclosure unilaterally,” he said.
"But the Ukrainian presidential press office's false statement that there had been no confidentiality agreement, seriously undermines trust between the two governments and gravely damages friendly relations between the two countries," he added.
The South Korean Presidential office demands "an official explanation and apology," said Seong.
Ukraine captured early last year two North Korean soldiers among Pyongyang's troops fighting for Moscow. One of them said he served in a reconnaissance unit and while some North Korean soldiers had been trained to use Russian military equipment, he had not.
The soldier said he was conscripted to the military aged 17 and had been serving since then. A South Korean lawmaker had previously said the pair wanted to live a "normal life" in the South of the Peninsula.
Analysts believe Lee Jae Myung’s angry reaction to the confidentiality agreement risks sparking intense feuds with the nuclear-armed north, which could translate into further hostility towards Seoul.
"North Korea has been using the deployed soldiers to create a heroic narrative for regime propaganda, and the South Korean government appears concerned that confirming the prisoners' return to the South and publicising it could further fuel hostility towards Seoul," said Park Won-gon, a professor at Ewha Womans University.
Beyond the ramifications within South Korea, the row also risks complicating Kyiv's requests to the ally for armaments supplies.
South Korea has so far not provided lethal weapons to Ukraine, citing a domestic ban on militarily aiding countries at war. Nevertheless, it had been considering requests for defensive weapons, especially since North Korea deployed troops to support Russia.

articles.title: Iran rules out new US talks after Trump rejects Hormuz offer
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran rules out new US talks after Trump rejects Hormuz offer
Iran has denied plans to take part in new negotiations with the US this week after President Donald Trump said he had expected further talks.
"Iran's delegation in New York has no plans for negotiations with the United States," state-run news agency IRNA said on Monday, citing an unnamed source on the Iranian negotiating team.
Trump told US news outlet Axios on Sunday that he expected new talks this week, a day after rejecting an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days and return to peace talks.
"Iran's views and positions were conveyed clearly and explicitly to the US side … via a Qatari mediator," IRNA said, adding that Iran's negotiating team would return to Tehran on Tuesday.
The two sides held their first discussions in three months on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York last week. The indirect talks saw Qatari officials mediate between an Iranian negotiating team led by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
"I expect more talks with Iran [this week]," Trump told Axios's Barak Ravid. "They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal I want to make. It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand."
Two regional sources also told the outlet that indirect talks could resume as soon as Monday.
Iran has proposed reopening the disputed waterway and restarting nuclear talks within seven days if the US agrees to meet a list of conditions.
They include an end to the US naval blockade, the lifting of oil sanctions, the unfreezing of Iranian assets and a permanent end to the war across the region.
The framework is similar to the memorandum of understanding agreed in June, which produced a short-lived ceasefire.
Trump rejected the proposal on Saturday.
"They made a proposal but I rejected it," he said. "They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they're losing so badly."
Since the collapse of the MoU, the US has ramped up economic pressure on Tehran, reimposing the blockade on Iranian ports and pressuring countries to cut ties with Iranian airlines.
Iran has seen its control of the strait challenged in recent weeks, as a US military effort to escort vessels through the waterway has helped oil and gas shipments reach their highest levels since the war began on 28 February.
Meanwhile, Iran's Revolutionary Guard has continued to attack ships in the strait. Iranian media reported that almost 20 ships came under attack on Friday and Saturday.
In a statement carried by state television, Khamenei said Iran had emerged "stronger and more resilient" from the war.
"Today, having suffered painful blows at the hands of valiant fighters and the guardians of the Strait of Hormuz, they (the enemies) do not venture beyond the Arabian Sea," the statement read. "Whenever they have braved this risk, they have only brought harm upon themselves. It will not be long before the Arabian Sea, too, would rid itself of their presence," he added.
Eight US Marines injured in Iran missile attack
Eight US Marines were injured in an Iranian missile attack in the strait earlier this month, NBC News reported on Monday, citing three US officials.
The Marines were not seriously injured but suffered smoke inhalation and possible traumatic brain injuries, according to the officials.
The attack took place on 14 September and had not previously been reported. All the personnel returned to duty shortly afterwards.
The Defence Department has come under increasing scrutiny over its disclosure of casualty figures during the seven-month war, with multiple US news reports raising questions over whether the publicly released figures capture the full toll of the conflict.
The Washington Post reported last week that at least 22 US service members had been killed in the conflict, citing six US officials. That is four more than the Pentagon has publicly announced.
At least 861 others have been wounded, according to the Pentagon's public database.
Qatar extends force majeure on gas shipments
QatarEnergy has extended force majeure on gas shipments to Asia and Europe by another month amid continued disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Bloomberg.
The state-owned company has notified Bangladesh and Pakistan that affected shipments would remain suspended through November, while Italy's Edison said deliveries had been cancelled until early December. At least one Indian buyer was also told that force majeure would remain in effect.
Qatar has been able to increase shipments in recent weeks as more vessels have navigated the strait, but flows remain well below pre-war levels.
The disruption has piled pressure on Qatari state finances and pushed gas prices in Asia and Europe to around their highest levels since late 2022.

articles.title: 9 injured as Russian drones, missiles continue to batter Kyiv for fourth consecutive night of strikes
articles.body:
At least 2 killed, 8 injured in Kyiv as Russia drones, missile strike market, gas station in hours-long attacks
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Russia continued its onslaught of hours-long attacks on Kyiv throughout the evening and into the early morning of Sept. 27-28, striking civilian targets while killing and wounding multiple people.
On the evening Sept. 27, two people were killed and four others injured by a Russian strike on the Stolichny food market just outside of the capital, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. The strike caused a fire at the wholesale food market.
Eyewitness footage from the scene of the strike on the market shows flames engulfing vehicles in the parking lot. Over central Kyiv, air defense systems were reported to be active, filling the city with sounds of blasts and explosions amid a nine-hour-long air raid alert. 
According to a Kyiv Independent journalist, authorities also halted trains set to depart during the attack, evacuating passengers to underground shelters.
Later in the overnight hours of Sept. 28, amid a newly issued air raid alerts, drones reportedly had damaged an unspecified "non-residential building" in the Podil district of Kyiv. Eyewitness reports by a Kyiv Independent reporter detail a Russian drone striking a building in the neighbourhood.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service said that three people injured were injured in the area, while another person was injured in the Holosiivskyi district after a drone struck a two-story home.
Additional fires were reported throughout the city amid the attack including office buildings in the Pecherskyi and Shevchenkivskyi districts.
Klitschko also reported that a gas station had been set ablaze in the Obolonskyi district of the city.
The attack comes amid a day of devastation in Kyiv with multiple hours-long attacks reported across the capital. An additional nine people sustained injuries in attacks on Kyiv throughout the day, said Klitschko. Six of the injured victims were hospitalized, including one child.
Unrelenting attacks on the capital occurred immediately prior on the night of Sept. 26-27, when Russian strikes on Kyiv killed one and injured at least five.
Across Ukraine on Sept. 26-27, attacks by Russian forces further killed 14 and injured at least 57.
"This past week, the Russians launched more than 2,200 attack drones against Ukraine, as well as around 1,650 aerial bombs and 38 missiles of various types, a significant number of them ballistic missiles," said President Volodymyr Zelensky.

articles.title: 197 combat engagements at front in past day, most in Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka – General Staff
articles.body:
Since the beginning of the day, Russian troops have attacked the positions of the Defense Forces of Ukraine 197 times, with Russians being most active in Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka directions, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine has reported.
"In total, since the beginning of this day, 197 combat engagements have occurred. Russians launched 64 airstrikes, dropped 196 guided aerial bombs. In addition, it deployed 5,565 kamikaze drones for strikes and carried out 2,132 shellings of settlements and positions of our troops," the message reads.
Throughout the day in South Slobozhanske direction, Russians storming the positions of Ukrainian units five times near Starytsia, Kozacha Lopan, Volohivske, and Prykolotne; another two combat engagements are still ongoing.
In Kupiansk direction, the Defense Forces repelled two Russians assaults in the areas of Kivsharivka and Kolisnykivka.
In Lyman direction, Ukrainian defenders repelled five attempts by Russia to advance in the areas of Zarichne, Lyman, and Dibrova; another combat engagement is ongoing.
In Sloviansk direction, the Defense Forces stopped three attempts by Russia to move forward near Mykolaivka.
In Kostiantynivka direction, the Defense Forces repelled 20 Russians assaults in the areas of Kostiantynivka, Novoselivka, Illinivka, Dovha Balka, and Rusyn Yar; another combat engagement is ongoing.
A total of 15 attacks were repelled in the Pokrovsk direction. Russia tried to advance in the areas of Vilne, Bilytske, Chernihivka, Myrne, Serhiivka, and Molodetske. Three combat engagements are ongoing.
"According to preliminary estimates, 33 Russians were eliminated and 6 wounded here today; two units of automotive equipment, 10 units of special equipment, two unmanned aerial vehicle control posts, and one Russian ammunition depot were destroyed. Four units of automotive equipment, five unmanned aerial vehicle control posts, and 52 enemy shelters were damaged. Twenty-four unmanned aerial vehicles of various types were destroyed or suppressed," the report says.
Ukrainian defenders repelled four attacks by Russia in Oleksandrivka direction in the areas of Sichneve and Verbove.
Eleven attacks by Russia were recorded in the Huliaypole direction in the areas of Rizdvyanka, Kopani, Yehorivka, and Myrne.

articles.title: Air defense downs 112 of 165 enemy targets, hits recorded at 14 locations
articles.body:
The Defense Forces of Ukraine neutralized 112 enemy targets overnight Monday, though enemy air attack weapons hits were recorded at 14 locations, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine has reported.
"According to preliminary data, as of 07:00, air defense shot down/suppressed 112 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera, and other types of drones," the statement reads.
In total, on the night of September 28 (from 18:00 on September 27), the enemy attacked with 165 Shahed-type strike UAVs (79 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parodiya type decoy drones from the directions of Oryol, Millerovo, Primorsko-Akharsk, Shatalovo in Russia, and temporarily occupied Donetsk and temporarily occupied AR Crimea – Hvardiiske.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
Meanwhile, hits by the adversary's air attack weapons were recorded at 14 locations, as well as the fall of downed targets (debris) at 7 locations.
The attack is ongoing, with several enemy UAVs remaining in airspace, the command added.

articles.title: UK counter-terrorism police probe Iran link to suspected bomb plot at RAF base
articles.body:
Since March, RAF Fairford has been used by the US military to launch air strikes on Iran as the war in the Middle East rumbles on.
Five men arrested on suspicion of terror offences in the UK on Sunday are to be released on bail, police have announced.
Laurence Taylor, the head of UK counter-terrorism policing, said on Monday that the men were to be released on police bail following "extensive interviews and inquiries."
"This does not mean that the investigation is over," he said, adding that they would be "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others."
"They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of inquiry," he went on.
British counter-terrorism police are investigating whether there is a link to Iran after police found explosives on three vans near an RAF base in Gloucestershire on Sunday.
Speaking to the BBC on Monday morning, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting cautioned that it would be "irresponsible to speculate."
"As soon as we can keep the public informed, we will. I would just ask people for a bit of forbearance to give the police and security services the time and space to do their job," he said.
Since March, RAF Fairford has been used by the US military to launch air strikes on Iran as the war in the Middle East rumbles on.
In July, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it was aware that the base was being used by US bombers and warned the UK that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces.”
Armed officers detained the group of five men on Sunday after a call to emergency services about three "suspicious vehicles which appeared to be travelling towards the air base," London's Metropolitan Police said in a statement.
Counter-terror police said on Monday that all the men are British nationals in their mid-20s.
US President Donald Trump told reporters they had been "looking to do big damage" at the base in southwest England.
"We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," he said, adding the US and UK had been working together on the incident.
A local resident who said it was known locally that the base was on lockdown due to a "terror threat" alerted emergency services after seeing three vans blocking the road and a large group of men wearing hoods and balaclavas.
She told the PA news agency she found it "astonishing" it had been effectively down to a "plucky amateur" spotting unusual activity to raise the alarm.
Some 85 households in the nearby village of Whelford were advised to evacuate and army bomb disposal experts called in to examine three large white vans stopped on a rural road.
Incident 'contained'
"Counter Terrorism Policing can now confirm they are leading an investigation into an incident which took place overnight near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire," the Met statement added.
Broadcast aerial footage showed a bomb disposal robot moving around the vans, two of which had their rear doors open.
Police believed the incident had been "contained" and a 400-metre cordon had been put in place.
Armed officers could be seen guarding the entrance to the base.
In March, then prime minister Keir Starmer granted permission for "defensive" US action against Iranian missile sites from two UK bases including Fairford.
New Prime Minister Andy Burnham was being kept updated on the incident, a government spokesperson said.
Burnham, who was in the northwestern city of Liverpool along with other senior ministers for his Labour Party's annual conference, thanked the police, armed forces and residents who had been asked to leave their homes "while precautionary checks are carried out."
Attacks by proxies
Fairford is the UK base of the 501st Combat Support Wing, a US air force administrative support wing, which said in a statement that no US air force personnel had been involved in the incident.
"The 501st Combat Support Wing appreciates the swift response and continued support of our local law enforcement partners," it said.
"We remain in close coordination with our UK partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities," it added.
The incident comes amid concerns about the actions of hostile foreign states.
Interior Minister Shabana Mahmood has accused Iran and Russia of using proxies to carry out criminal activities on their behalf on UK territory.
Earlier this month, reports said British military sites had been targeted by drones more than 300 times over the past year.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Drone Launch Site in Donetsk and Ammo Depots in Luhansk
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Strikes Russian Drone Launch Site in Donetsk and Ammo Depots in Luhansk
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian facility used to store, prepare, and launch attack drones in temporarily occupied Donetsk, as well as ammunition and logistics sites across the occupied parts of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The strikes were carried out on September 26 and overnight into September 27, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on September 27.
In Donetsk, Ukrainian forces targeted a site used by Russian troops for the storage, preparation, and launch of attack UAVs. The General Staff said such facilities remain a priority because strikes against them are intended to reduce Russia’s ability to deploy unmanned strike systems.
Two Russian ammunition depots were also hit in Krepenke and Luhansk in the temporarily occupied Luhansk region, according to the military.
Ukrainian forces additionally struck a Russian logistics warehouse in Rovenky, Luhansk region, and a fuel and lubricants storage facility in Novoamvrosiivske in the occupied Donetsk region.
The General Staff did not provide details on the extent of the damage or the types of weapons used in the strikes.
“Work on key military targets of the Russian aggressor continues. More to come!” the General Staff said.
Earlier, on September 26, Ukrainian forces struck the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant in Russia’s Rostov region, damaging several production facilities at a site that manufactures components for Russian missiles, artillery, and anti-tank weapons.

articles.title: Iran, US send mixed signals over talks to end war
articles.body:
Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian holds an image of late Iranian supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at United Nations headquarters, September 23, 2026. (AP Photo)
Iran and the United States sent mixed signals on Sept. 28 over negotiations aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, as reports indicated that mediators were pressing Tehran to make certain concessions.
State media in Iran on Sept. 28 reported that Iran’s delegation to the U.N. General Assembly had no talks planned with the United States, after US President Donald Trump said he expected more negotiations.
Trump told media outlet Axios on Sept. 27 that he expected talks to resume soon, a day after he rejected a proposal by Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days.
“Iran’s views and positions were conveyed clearly and explicitly to the U.S. side... via a Qatari mediator,” the official IRNA news agency said, adding that the Iranian delegation would return to Tehran on Sept. 29.
Iran says it presented seven conditions for ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway through which roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil and gas flowed before the war.
The strait lies at the heart of the conflict that began with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
Following that attack, Tehran placed a chokehold on the waterway, and Washington responded with a blockade of Iranian ports.
Axios said indirect talks mediated by Qatar could take place as early as on Sept. 28, less than a week after similar discussions between U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
Iran demands a seven-day ceasefire across the Middle East, including in Lebanon, where its ally Hezbollah is regularly bombarded by Israel.
It also demands the unfreezing of its foreign assets, lifting sanctions on its oil sector, and an end to the US naval blockade.
Trump rejected their demands on Sept. 26.
Meanwhile, the Wall Street Journal reported that mediators are pressing Iran to make concessions on its nuclear program in an effort to revive ceasefire negotiations with the U.S.
Mediators described the effort as a long-shot attempt to secure movement from Tehran on its nuclear program, while Iran has so far given little indication that it is prepared to discuss the issue.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sept. 27 that Tehran remained open to negotiations but would respond to renewed military action.
“We are fully prepared for the war to resume,” Araghchi told NBC News when asked about the Journal report.
“We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war. But at the same time we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose,” he added.
Arab mediators said Iran had made no concessions since Trump rejected its ceasefire proposal, while Gulf officials said Tehran wants Washington to offer concessions before negotiations advance.

articles.title: Russia lacks forces for 'major attack on NATO,' Poland says
articles.body:
Russia lacks the forces to launch a major attack on NATO while its military remains tied up in Ukraine, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said in remarks reported on Monday.
Speaking to public broadcaster TVP Info, Sikorski elaborated on his warning last week that Warsaw had information from multiple sources indicating Russia was “preparing something big this year.”
Asked what form Moscow’s plans might take, he said “of course only Putin knows that, but we must be ready, we must not let ourselves be manipulated, and we must be vigilant, so that as an alliance we can react immediately to any provocation.”
“Russia doesn’t have the forces for a major attack on NATO,” he said. “All its forces are tied up in Ukraine.”
Sikorski suggested Moscow could attempt “something on a smaller scale that might cause some controversy among allies.”
An incident that divided European and US members over whether NATO’s Article 5 mutual defence clause applied would suit the Kremlin, Sikorski added.
“Russia might do more aggressively what it’s already doing,” he added.
Last week Polish authorities temporarily evacuated the Hrubieszow and Dorohusk border crossings after intense Russian drone and missile strikes targeted Ukraine’s western regions bordering Poland.
Separately, Polish fighter jets were scrambled and air defences placed on standby after a Russian Mi-8 helicopter crossed into Polish airspace from Kaliningrad.
Western governments have accused Moscow of conducting sabotage and airspace incursions as part of a campaign of hybrid warfare against NATO and EU countries.

articles.title: Several Men Detained Near RAF Fairford in Britain as Police Investigate Possible Terror Plot
articles.body:
British police detained several men near RAF Fairford on suspicion of illegally possessing or using explosives.
Gloucestershire Police reported this.
The U.S. Air Force uses RAF Fairford as a main forward operating base for deploying strategic bombers in Europe. U.S. B-52H, B-1B, and B-2A bombers regularly arrive there as part of Bomber Task Force missions.
Counterterrorism police have joined the investigation. Law enforcement officers are examining the circumstances of the detentions and any possible links between the suspects and preparations for a crime.
A major incident was declared in the Whelford area following the detentions. British police cordoned off part of the area, while bomb disposal teams are examining several vehicles.
Local residents from several houses were evacuated to a community center. Armed police officers are stationed near the main gate of RAF Fairford.
Authorities have not said that they prevented a terrorist attack or confirmed that the detainees were planning an attack on the air base. Investigators are also determining the possible motives and links of the suspects.
Recently, attacks on defense industry facilities in Britain by pro-Palestinian activists have increased. British law enforcement agencies have also stepped up their focus on possible sabotage activities by Russian agents in the country.
For example, executives of British defense companies supplying weapons and drones to Ukraine were warned of an increased risk of espionage by Russia.
The British government is increasing its focus on the security of the defense industry amid a series of incidents in Europe. Previously, Western law enforcement agencies stated that Russian intelligence services may have been planning attacks on executives of German defense companies.
According to British intelligence, the threat posed by Russian intelligence services has increased significantly since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In 2024, the number of MI5 investigations related to state threats increased by 48%.
The GRU plays a particularly important role in these operations. British authorities have officially linked units 29155, 26165, and 74455 to Russian military intelligence, saying they are involved in sabotage activities, cyber operations and information attacks.
As of July 2026, London had imposed sanctions on three GRU units and dozens of Russian intelligence officers.
Russia also uses criminal financial networks to support its operations. As part of Operation DESTABILISE, Britain’s National Crime Agency recorded 129 arrests and seized more than £25 million in cash and cryptocurrency in the United Kingdom.
Investigators established links between Russian-speaking money-laundering networks and people connected to Russian intelligence services.

articles.title: Iran will respond to any aggression with new weapons
articles.body:
Iran will respond to any aggression with new weapons
TEHRAN — Iran has warned the United States against any intervention in the Strait of Hormuz, while stressing that its Armed Forces have developed new military technologies and capabilities to respond to any potential aggression.
Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi, spokesman for Iran’s Armed Forces, issued the warning on Saturday night, saying that any U.S. attempt to interfere in the strategic waterway would face an Iranian response.
“If the United States intervenes in the Strait of Hormuz, it will get slapped,” Shekarchi said, using a colloquial expression to underline the consequences Washington would face in the event of direct intervention.
He also said that the United States had “no way out other than leaving West Asia,” arguing that the sooner American forces withdrew from the region, the lower the losses they would suffer.
Shekarchi described the Islamic Republic as a “global power” and said Iran would not allow the United States to return to its former position in a “new world order.”
Iran’s military doctrine and new technologies
The senior military spokesman said Iran’s Armed Forces had sought to strengthen their combat capabilities and incorporate advanced technologies since the Iran-Iraq War in the 1980s, also known as the “imposed war.”
He cited the beginning of Iran’s indigenous missile production during the conflict with the former Ba’athist regime in Iraq as a tangible example of the country’s efforts to develop defense capabilities under wartime conditions.
According to Shekarchi, one of the most significant changes in Iran’s military doctrine following the Islamic Revolution was the shift from conventional warfare toward asymmetric warfare.
He said conventional military methods could be vulnerable when confronting an adversary equipped with costly and technologically sophisticated heavy weapons.
“Asymmetric warfare means standing up to the enemy’s expensive heavy weapons and achieving victory with lower costs and simpler but more effective and practical defense equipment,” Shekarchi said.
’A surprise in store for the enemy’
Shekarchi said Iran’s adversaries had miscalculated the country’s resilience and defensive capabilities.
He argued that if the enemy had properly assessed Iran’s capabilities, it would not have chosen to attack the country.
The general also emphasized information security as a key principle within the Armed Forces, saying that safeguarding military information was essential to preserving the element of surprise.
He said Iran possessed unique elements of national power and pointed to the participation of the Iranian people both on the streets and on the battlefield as a fundamental factor in the country’s ability to withstand attacks.
Referring to recent threats against Iran, Shekarchi said the Armed Forces would employ newly developed military technologies in responding to any future aggression.
“The powerful Iranian Armed Forces are many times stronger than they were at the outset of the second and third imposed wars,” he said, describing the current condition of the Armed Forces as “very good.”
He said Iran’s missile and drone capabilities had become more advanced and powerful and warned that Tehran had capabilities that had not necessarily been publicly disclosed.
“This time we have a surprise in store for the enemy,” Shekarchi said, adding that Iran would respond to any potential aggression with new military technologies.
Hormuz at the center of the dispute
Shekarchi also reiterated Iran’s position on the Strait of Hormuz, saying that the strategic waterway was under Iranian management.
“Management of the Strait of Hormuz is in Iran’s hands,” he said. “Any ship that wants to pass outside the Iranian route will not have security.”
The comments come as control and security arrangements in the Strait of Hormuz have emerged as a major point of contention between Tehran and Washington.
In recent indirect negotiations in New York, Iranian officials presented conditions under which Tehran said it could facilitate the reopening of the waterway and the resumption of nuclear talks. According to Axios, U.S. negotiators told their Iranian counterparts that Iran did not control the strait and therefore could not impose conditions concerning it.

articles.title: Staff killed and wounded in Russian strike on Kyiv’s science academy
articles.body:
Russia has hit the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv with a drone, killing at least one person in the latest daytime attack on Ukraine’s capital.
Flames tore through the historic building on Monday as people clambered out of first- and second-floor windows to escape, in dramatic scenes increasingly familiar in the heavily bombarded city.
At least one person was killed and three others were wounded, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, who said the injured had been taken to hospital.
The 19th-century building stands close to the German embassy, the National Opera, St Volodymyr’s Cathedral and several government buildings.
Anatoliy Zagorodny, the president of the national academy, said the blast struck while many staff members were inside. Standing outside the burning building, he said he did not know why Russia had targeted a leading centre of scientific research. “We are not connected with the military. This is an attack on science. It is terrorism,” he said.
He said he feared some of his colleagues could still be trapped inside the academy.
While the sciences building is a civilian scientific institution, it has longstanding ties to Ukraine’s defence sector. Among those injured in Monday’s strike was Volodymyr Horbulin, the academy’s first vice-president and a former high-ranking security official.
Another Russian drone struck a nearby private medical centre, killing at least one person.
Russian strikes over the past week involving missiles and increasingly sophisticated jet-powered drones have hit apartment blocks, offices, warehouses and datacentres across the capital, killing and wounding civilians almost daily and giving Kyiv an increasingly frontline feel as it faces some of its most sustained bombardment since the early stages of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.
The drone and missile campaign is designed to grind down public resilience and damage the economy. Monday’s double strike is likely to raise fresh concerns over Ukraine’s ability to protect even the most heavily guarded parts of the capital.
The newer jet-powered drones fly faster and are harder to intercept than the older Shahed or Geran-2 models that were the backbone of Moscow’s air campaign. Ukraine is racing to develop and manufacture interceptors capable of bringing them down.
Moscow has also changed its tactics, launching more attacks in daylight hours so that residents in major cities have to spend more of the day under air raid alerts.
Buildings hit during daytime strikes are often occupied because many Ukrainians work through drone alerts rather than spend hours in shelters.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, called on western countries to intensify their pressure on Russia.
“Every Russian terrorist attack is a loss of life that could have been prevented if pressure on Russia had finally become total,” he wrote on X on Monday. “The world must understand that terrorists will go further if they are not stopped here, in Ukraine. And we cannot turn a blind eye to such brutal strikes.”
Russia has signalled that its attacks on Ukraine could intensify and US-brokered efforts to end the war show little sign of progress.
“Ukraine will have to pay a price for the actions that have taken place in recent months,” the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, told reporters on Monday, referring to Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russian territory. “That is happening right now.”

articles.title: Russian Forces Begin Using New Geran-5 Version With Autonomous Optical Navigation
articles.body:
Russian forces have begun using a new modification of the Geran-5 jet-powered UAV, which features an autonomous optical navigation system and a modified fuselage design.
The monitoring channel Colonel GSh reported this, referring to the new version as the Geran-5 K5.
According to the channel, the UAV is equipped with an electro-optical correction system that allows it to navigate using images of the ground surface.
Its operating principle is similar to that of OEKС (DSMAC) systems, which use terrain image matching for navigation and allow the flight path to be corrected without satellite navigation.
The new version also has a higher speed than the standard model. As a result, it may be mistakenly identified in flight as other jet-powered strike assets, including the Dan-T.
At the same time, the K5 designation and the installation of a DSMAC-class system have not been officially confirmed by Ukrainian sources.
An indirect indication that autonomous optical navigation has appeared on Russian Geran-series drones came from a statement by Russian military correspondent Andrei Filatov. He said that Russian drones of this series already use an autonomous optical navigation system called Susanin.
Filatov claims that the system navigates using images of the underlying terrain, allowing the UAV to continue along its route without radio beacons.
However, the Russian source does not specify which Geran modification is equipped with the system and does not identify it as DSMAC.
According to official data from Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence, the baseline Geran-5 is 6.5 meters long, has a wingspan of 3.2 meters and a maximum takeoff weight of up to 850 kilograms.
It is equipped with a warhead weighing about 90 kilograms, has a cruising speed of 450–600 km/h, a range of about 950 kilometers and can reach an altitude of up to 6 kilometers.
The Geran-5 examined by Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence was found to contain a Kometa-M12 jam-resistant satellite navigation system, an inertial navigation system, a tracker with cellular modems, a mesh modem and a Chinese TELEFLY TF-TJ2000A turbojet engine. The current public list of components maintained by Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence does not include a separate DSMAC system.
Russia is known to have already modified the Geran-5’s design by moving the turbojet engine inside the fuselage from an external nacelle, reducing aerodynamic drag and potentially increasing the UAV’s speed and flight range.

articles.title: Trump expects new Iran talks despite rejecting deal offer
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump expects new Iran talks despite rejecting deal offer
US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that he expects talks with Iran to resume in the coming week, despite his rejection of a truce proposal put forward by Tehran.
Iranian officials brought a plan to the UN General Assembly in New York for a seven-day truce, followed by the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz shipping channel.
Trump dismissed the plan and has mused on resuming full-scale air strikes on Iranian targets, but he told the news platform Axios that he expects negotiations to resume.
"They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make," Trump told Axios. "It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago."
"They overplayed their hand," Trump said, in the interview published Sunday.
Citing sources familiar with the matter, Axios reported that indirect talks between Washington and Tehran could take place as early as Monday.
On Sunday, Iran was still standing by its conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, leaving the Gulf front of the Middle East war locked in a stalemate, while fighting rages in Yemen.
'We will not back down'
Hormuz is a key chokepoint for the world's energy supplies and is now central to the conflict between Washington and Tehran, which was started nearly seven months ago when the US and Israel launched a wave of strikes against Iran.
Iran's plan called for a cessation of all hostilities in the Middle East, including in Lebanon, according to Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, and a return to the conditions in an earlier ceasefire deal that fell apart.
That agreement, which collapsed during fighting over Hormuz, called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.
"Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz is contingent upon these conditions being fulfilled. We will not back down from them," Araghchi said on Sunday, state broadcaster IRIB reported.
"We have never closed the door to diplomacy or negotiations, but at the same time, we have never backed down from our rights."
Washington's ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, accused Tehran of demanding too much in exchange for a return to the negotiating table.
"This was, I think, a pretty cynical attempt to put something on the table that they knew was unacceptable. To ask for the release of the blockade, the sanctions, international sanctions and access to billions in assets, just to talk," he told NBC News in an interview broadcast Sunday.
"I think it's kind of common sense that the president doesn't have a lot of confidence this time after we just tried a few months ago."
Iran's Revolutionary Guards meanwhile said that they seized an American submersible drone on Sunday in the Strait of Hormuz.
It said the underwater vehicle was being used "for espionage purposes", adding that it was "now in the hands of the force's specialists for data recovery".
'Tool for pressure'
Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in June aimed at ending the war, reopening the strait and launching talks on Iran's nuclear programme.
But the deal broke down shortly afterwards when Iran fired on commercial ships in Hormuz that it accused of deviating from its approved route through the waterway.
Iran requires ships to obtain authorisation before passage, citing security and sovereignty reasons.
Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the United States sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation.
Araghchi said at the UN that Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan, adding: "The choice now rests with the United States."
Hossein Mohebi, a spokesman for Iran's Revolutionary Guards, was quoted by Tasnim news agency as saying: "We will not cease punishing the US until Iran's seven conditions are met."
Mohebi had told AFP in an exclusive interview on Tuesday that ending hostilities in Yemen was also among Tehran's demands.

articles.title: UK: five arrested on suspicion of preparing 'terrorist act'
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UK police arrest five on suspicion of preparing 'terrorist act' near air base
British counter-terrorism police were Sunday probing "a major" incident near a base used by the US air force after arresting five men on suspicion of "preparing a terrorist act", police said.
Armed officers detained the group in the early hours after a call to emergency services about three "suspicious vehicles which appeared to be travelling towards the air base", London's Metropolitan Police said in a statement.
US President Donald Trump told reporters they had been "looking to do big damage" at the Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford air base in Gloucestershire, southwest England.
"We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," he said, adding the US and UK had been working together on the incident.
A local resident who said it was known locally that the base was on lockdown due to a "terror threat" alerted emergency services after seeing three vans blocking the road and a large group of men wearing hoods and balaclavas.
She told the PA news agency she found it "astonishing" it had been effectively down to a "plucky amateur" spotting unusual activity to raise the alarm.
Some 85 households in the nearby village of Whelford were advised to evacuate and army bomb disposal experts called in to examine three large white vans stopped on a rural road.
Incident 'contained'
"Counter Terrorism Policing can now confirm they are leading an investigation into an incident which took place overnight near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire," the Met statement added.
Broadcast aerial footage showed a bomb disposal robot moving around the vans, two of which had their rear doors open.
Police believed the incident had been "contained" and a 400 metre (1,300 feet) cordon had been put in place.
Armed officers could be seen guarding the entrance to the base.
In March, then prime minister Keir Starmer granted permission for "defensive" US action against Iranian missile sites from two UK bases including Fairford.
New Prime Minister Andy Burnham was being kept updated on the incident, a government spokesperson said.
Burnham, who was in the northwestern city of Liverpool along with other senior ministers for his Labour Party's annual conference, thanked the police, armed forces and residents who had been asked to leave their homes "while precautionary checks are carried out".
Defence Minister Wes Streeting said in Liverpool he had been in contact with US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and the UK was "working closely with our American friends".
Asked if there was any Iranian involvement, he said it would be "irresponsible to speculate".
Gloucestershire police said earlier it had declared a "major incident" with several men arrested "on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act".
Villagers evacuated
Residents from Whelford were evacuated to a nearby leisure centre.
"My understanding is that the whole village was evacuated in the early hours of this morning," district councillor Tristan Wilkinson told AFP.
"Most people got in their cars, so when the police knocked on the doors and told them to go, most people were able to kind of drive away."
They were now waiting to see if the cordon would be relaxed later Sunday, as many were worried about pets which had to be left behind. "I'm hoping that the police will actually reduce the cordon quite quickly," Wilkinson said.
Villager Julian Tudsbery said it was his fellow villager who had alerted police first after they "phoned the airbase police who didn't answer the phone. It just rang out so she dialled 999".
Fairford is the UK base of the 501st Combat Support Wing, a US air force administrative support wing, which said in a statement that no US air force personnel had been involved in the incident.
"The 501st Combat Support Wing appreciates the swift response and continued support of our local law enforcement partners," it said.
"We remain in close coordination with our UK partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities," it added.
The incident comes amid concerns about the actions of hostile foreign states.
Interior Minister Shabana Mahmood has accused Iran and Russia of using proxies to carry out criminal activities on their behalf on UK territory.
Earlier this month, reports said British military sites had been targeted by drones more than 300 times over the past year.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits 4 Russian Oil Depots, 2 Defense Plants in Massive Overnight Strikes
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) said on Monday that its drones struck four oil depots in Russia’s Krasnodar Krai overnight, while President Volodymyr Zelensky reported additional Ukrainian strikes on defense plants and other military-related targets across Russia.
The SBU said drones operated by its Alpha Special Operations Center hit the Edelweiss-95 and Din-Yug-Oil depots in the stanitsa of Novotytarivska, where two separate fires were reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Another strike targeted the Lukoil-Yugnefteprodukt oil depot in the stanitsa of Pavlovska, where the SBU said a fire was still burning.
The fourth reported target was the Angelinska oil depot in the stanitsa of Staronyzhestebliivska, where another fire was reported.
The SBU said the facilities are part of Russia’s fuel infrastructure and that disabling them could complicate fuel supplies for Russian forces.
Russian outlet Astra also reported that the Edelweiss-95 oil depot in Novotitarovskaya, Krasnodar Krai, caught fire following the drone attack.
According to Astra’s analysis of eyewitness accounts and information about the company’s employees, the facility was identified as the Edelweiss-95 oil depot. The company specializes in wholesale supplies of diesel fuel and gasoline, including AI-92, AI-95, and AI-100 grades.
The depot has a reported storage capacity of 4,500 cubic meters (159,000 cubic feet) and its own railway spur for receiving and shipping fuel.
Lavrov Says Turkey Must Guarantee S-400 Systems Won’t Reach Ukraine
According to the company’s website, Edelweiss-95 has operated in the fuel market for 30 years and purchases petroleum products directly from major Russian refineries.
“The SBU continues to strike targets in the Russian rear that support the war against Ukraine,” the SBU said, describing the strikes as a response to Russian attacks on Ukrainian cities and civilian infrastructure.
Zelensky reports strikes on defense plants
Zelensky said Ukrainian forces also used long-range capabilities against two defense plants in Russia’s Tula and Voronezh regions.
“We are consistently responding to Russian strikes against life with our own long-range capabilities. Last night, we deployed our long-range ‘sanctions’ against two defense plants – in the Tula and Voronezh regions,” Zelensky said in a Telegram statement.
He also confirmed that SBU units had struck Russian oil facilities in Krasnodar Krai.
According to Zelensky, Ukrainian forces also targeted facilities in the Kaluga and Oryol regions that Russia uses for drone attacks against Ukraine. In the Bryansk region, he said, operations targeted Russian forces directly.
He also reported that a target in the Black Sea had been hit, without providing further details.
“Russia must stop the escalation,” he added.
Russia reports 254 drones overnight
Russia’s defense ministry said its air defenses intercepted and destroyed 254 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones between 8 p.m. Moscow time on Sunday and 8 a.m. on Monday.
The ministry said the drones were detected over Belgorod, Bryansk, Smolensk, Kaluga, Tula, Kursk, Voronezh, Lipetsk, Tambov, Ryazan, Oryol, and Rostov oblasts, as well as the Moscow Region, Krasnodar Krai, occupied Crimea, and the waters of the Azov and Black seas.
Russian officials also reported damage and casualties in several regions.
Voronezh Governor Alexander Gusev said four people, including three children, were injured in the region and that a house and three garages were destroyed by fire.
In the Bryansk region, acting Governor Yegor Kovalchuk said part of a railway bridge collapsed and 10 rail cars derailed on the Dyatkovo-Lyudinovo line. He also reported the derailment of 18 empty semi-trailers in the Unechsky district.
No injuries were reported in the railway incidents, according to Russian officials.

articles.title: Russia Wants Ukraine to 'Pay the Price'
articles.body:
The Kremlin threatened Ukraine by saying Kyiv would have to “pay a price” for “actions that have taken place in recent months” in a statement on Monday.
Dmitry Peskov, spokesperson for Russian leader Vladimir Putin, made the remarks at a press briefing but did not specify which “actions” he meant.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“This is also something the president has spoken about – Ukraine will have to pay a price for the actions that have taken place in recent months,” Peskov said.
While Peskov has been vague in his remarks, Kyiv has stepped up attacks on major logistics warehouses and Russian refineries in 2026, forcing the world’s third-largest oil producer to import automobile fuel from overseas amid a sprawling crisis.
Peskov added that the Russian armed forces were given the choice to hit targets they “consider appropriate” as attacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure escalate.
“Our armed forces continue the special military operation and consistently strike targets they consider appropriate,” Peskov added, referring to the Ukraine invasion using the Kremlin-approved term.
The statement came amid intensified Russian strikes on civilian objects such as trains, data centers, educational institutions, and gas stations throughout September, with particular ferocity seen in recent days.
Kyiv Post correspondents have reported a series of explosions on Monday in and around the city center, at a frequency unseen for months.
Russian Drone Hits Odesa High-Rise, Injures 4
The strikes also included fatal attacks on border crossings with Moldova, and forced shutoffs at those along the Polish border that prompted visiting Western officials to seek shelter.
On Monday, a Russian drone struck the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine and trapped locals inside a burning building in central Kyiv – just meters away from a junction also hit by a Russian missile in October 2022.
For weeks, Russia has also struck data centers in Ukraine, including but not limited to an attack on the Comsonova data center on Saturday morning and four others on the same day a few days earlier, with Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi cautioning that Kyiv is bracing for the “worst possible scenario.”
On Sept. 21, Peskov also ruled out progress in US-mediated peace talks.

articles.title: Ukraine Carrying Out Airdrops of Food Via Drone to City Besieged by Russian Forces, Official Says
articles.body:
Ukraine’s military has for months been using drones to deliver food to a city facing a humanitarian crisis amid its continued occupation by Russian forces, Ukrainian officials have said.
The city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region is in a dire humanitarian situation, with Ukrainian authorities saying that remaining residents have been forced to eat dogs and weeds as Russian forces prevent them from leaving and block supplies from entering the city.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
An abundance of anti-personnel mines on the ground and drones in the sky make any escape attempt risky, but some are nonetheless making that journey, according to reports.
Kherson regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said on social media on Sunday that, since March, Ukraine’s defense forces have been carrying out airdrops to deliver food across the city via drone, with the most recent such operation being carried out on Saturday night.
Prokudin said: “In Oleshky, the Russians are holding around 2,000 of our people hostage. Among them are nearly 50 children. They are forced to survive without food, electricity or water.
“Most horrifyingly, the Russians have effectively deprived them of the opportunity to leave this hell,” he added.
🇺🇦 Last night, Ukraine’s Defence Forces delivered food to residents of occupied Oleshky to save people from hunger.
Using drones, they dropped around 4 tonnes of food at 100 locations across the city.
We will continue doing everything we can to support the residents of Oleshky. pic.twitter.com/78Ki8BbpvY
The governor of Kherson also said that Russian forces detained and “brutally” beat several people who went to collect food delivered by Ukraine’s military, adding that occupying Russian forces have taken some of the supplies for themselves.
Russia Strikes Kyiv, Kharkiv Again as Weeks of Attacks Kill Dozens
Moscow has long denied that it targets civilians in its ongoing war in Ukraine, with Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov blaming Kyiv for the lack of supplies in Oleshky, which had a population of around 24,000 people before the war.
Kherson is one of four Ukrainian regions that were unilaterally annexed by Moscow after sham referendums in September 2022, despite Russia lacking full military control of the areas following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February that year.
The Russification of the four Ukrainian regions annexed by Russia in 2022 – Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson – has been a key strategic goal for the Kremlin since the beginning of the war.
Kremlin-backed occupation authorities have pressured Ukrainian nationals in the regions to take up Russian citizenship, reportedly making it a condition for access to basic services such as healthcare and education, and have long been accused of conscripting Ukrainian residents into the Russian armed forces.

articles.title: EU intensifies defense and military buildup push
articles.body:
EU intensifies defense and military buildup push
The EU has greenlit a slew of new joint defense-industrial initiatives, with Ukraine joining most of them, as Brussels presses ahead with its defense buildup despite Russia’s warnings against the bloc’s “rabid” militarization.
The initiatives are part of the European Defense Projects of Common Interest (EDPCIs), large-scale industrial programs pitched as a way for groups of countries to jointly develop, manufacture, and deploy military capabilities too big or complex to tackle alone. The projects fall under the €1.5 billion European Defense Industry Program (EDIP), one of the EU’s mechanisms for expanding weapons production.
The Council formally endorsed the first five megaprojects within the framework on Monday, including:
- Drones and counter-drone systems (DECODER): scaling up and deploying military drones, along with systems to detect and neutralize UAVs;
- Maritime and seabed defense (IMSD): creating joint systems to detect and respond to threats at sea and on the seabed;
- SPACE: expanding military space capabilities, including missile-launch early warning, satellite communications, intelligence, and surveillance;
- Integrated air and missile defense (EU-FIAMD): linking participating countries’ air and missile defenses, early-warning capabilities, and command systems;
- Eastern Flank Watch (EFW): strengthening defenses along participating countries’ eastern territories.
On average, 18 member states will be involved in each project.
The European Commission has already earmarked €325 million to support the five initiatives. While the money has not yet been handed out, the decision on Monday makes the projects eligible to apply for this funding and opens the door to further EU financing later.
The initial sum is only a fraction of Brussels’ longer-term ambitions: EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius earlier put their combined funding at around €190 billion ($216 billion) by 2036. He hailed the decision as a “major breakthrough” aimed at closing critical gaps in the EU’s defenses.
Ukraine will take part in four of the five initiatives despite not being an EU member, only sitting out the space initiative. Brussels has been steadily drawing Kiev deeper into its defense-industrial system, arguing that European manufacturers should use Ukraine’s battlefield experience to develop new weapons and technologies.
The European Commission said it will help participating countries get the projects running and coordinate their work. Brussels has also left the door open to more initiatives under the framework in the future.
The EU believes its military buildup is needed to counter what it describes as a growing ‘Russian threat’. Moscow has dismissed the claims as “nonsense,” accusing European governments of using them to justify bloated military budgets and continued weapons supplies to Ukraine. Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev slammed the EU’s militarization as “rabid.”
At the UN General Assembly last week, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov dismissed speculation that Russia plans to attack NATO or EU states, accusing European governments of preparing for a conflict with Russia, pointing to their stated goal of boosting military readiness by 2030 and the vast sums being poured into weapons production.

articles.title: AI threat ‘not a hoax’ – Bill Gates
articles.body:
AI threat ‘not a hoax’ – Bill Gates
Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has rejected US President Donald Trump’s dismissal of artificial intelligence safety concerns, arguing that Washington should impose mandatory safeguards on the rapidly advancing technology.
Trump has resisted calls to slow AI development, arguing that restrictions could allow China to overtake the US and dismissing fears surrounding the technology as a “hoax.”
Gates, however, has criticized what he described as a “nationalistic” approach to the issue and said safeguards would not undermine Washington’s technological advantage.
“No. It’s not a hoax at all,” Gates said when asked about Trump’s position in an interview with NBC News’ Meet the Press aired on Sunday.
Earlier this month, Trump dismissed warnings that AI could escape human control and destroy humanity. “WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!” he wrote, adding that the US is leading China and other countries.
Gates argued that treating the technology primarily as a geopolitical competition was encouraging a potentially dangerous rush to develop increasingly powerful systems.
“Because it’s cast in this nationalistic, you know, us-versus-them type thing, you have people who are saying, ‘Well, let’s just go full-speed ahead,’” he said, calling it “completely irresponsible” not to require AI systems to have safeguards and monitoring capabilities.
Gates acknowledged that the US government has “so little expertise” regarding some of the capabilities recently developed by private AI companies, but nevertheless insisted that government involvement is necessary.
“No one thinks self-regulation is enough,” he said, calling for legislation and mandatory monitoring of advanced models.
Gates also predicted Trump could ultimately change his position once convinced that such measures would not damage Washington’s standing against Beijing.
“I think after he hears from me and other people, including that this does not handicap us in whatever he thinks the nation-state race is, that, you know, we will come to a consensus,” Gates said.
Trump, however, doubled down on his position on Sunday. Asked about reports of rogue AI agents, he told Fox News: “I don’t worry about it.” The president argued that slowing development could sacrifice Washington’s technological advantage, which he estimated at around 18 months.
“We’re about maybe a year and a half up on China,” Trump said. “We’re leading... And why should we give that up?” He also confirmed plans to have dinner with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, one of the leading advocates of slowing development of increasingly capable AI systems.
Gates, meanwhile, disputed suggestions that Beijing would reject safeguards, arguing that China itself has an interest in preventing attacks involving advanced AI.
“Certainly, all countries should want the safeguards in place,” he said. “So anyone that says, ‘Well, you know, China won’t put these safeguards in place’ – I totally disagree with that.”
He nevertheless acknowledged that reaching an international agreement could prove more difficult than Cold War negotiations on nuclear weapons. Asked whether US-Soviet arms-control talks could serve as a model for Washington and Beijing, Gates replied: “Yeah, absolutely. This is more difficult than that was.”

Russia Reportedly Starts Using New Geran-5 Drone With Cruise Missile-Style Navigation
Russian forces have reportedly begun using a new version of the Geran-5 attack drone equipped with an optical navigation system that allows it to navigate using reference images of terrain, according to the Ukrainian Telegram channel Polkovnyk HSh on September 27.
The modified version, identified as the Geran-5 K5, is fitted with an electro-optical DSMAC (Digital Scene Matching Area Correlation) module. The system compares images of the terrain below with stored reference imagery to determine the drone’s position and guide it along its route.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Polkovnyk HSh, a similar navigation principle is used by Russia’s Kh-101 cruise missile. The Geran-5 K5 has also received a redesigned fuselage and reportedly flies faster than both the Geran-4 and the standard Geran-5.
Its higher speed has reportedly led to the new variant being mistaken for Dan-M-type missiles in some cases.
Militarnyi noted that a statement by Russian correspondent Andrei Filatov provided indirect evidence that autonomous optical navigation has been introduced on drones from the Geran family.
Citing Russian media outlet Gazeta.ru, Filatov claimed that Geran drones are already using an autonomous optical navigation system called “Susanin.” According to him, the system navigates by analyzing images of the ground, allowing a drone to continue along its route without relying on radio beacons.
However, the Russian source did not specify which Geran variant is equipped with the system and did not identify the technology as DSMAC, Militarnyi reported.
Geran-5 is a Russian strike unmanned aerial vehicle with a maximum takeoff weight of approximately 850 kilograms and a cruising speed of between 450 and 600 kilometers per hour, making it considerably faster than the Geran-3. Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate estimates its flight endurance at around two hours and its maximum range at up to 950 kilometers.
The drone can reach an altitude of six kilometers, although its documented combat use has so far occurred at altitudes ranging from 200 meters to three kilometers.
The reported emergence of the K5 variant comes days after Ukrainian border guards intercepted and destroyed a Geran-5 on September 23. The drone was downed by operators from the 105th Separate Border Detachment, named after Prince Volodymyr the Great, according to ArmyInform.
