articles.title: Seoul summons Ukraine envoy over North Korean prisoner-of-war row
articles.body:
Seoul summons Ukraine envoy over North Korean prisoner-of-war row
- Published
South Korea has summoned Ukraine's acting ambassador after President Volodymyr Zelensky last week announced his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul.
Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo lodged a formal complaint with Andrii Vieshkin and expressed "strong regret" that Zelensky had revealed the transfer, which Seoul says was supposed to be a secret.
The two North Koreans, who were among thousands of soldiers supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.
President Lee Jae Myung called the disclosure "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security.
Ukraine's foreign ministry declined to comment when approached by the BBC.
In early 2025, Ukraine said its forces had captured two North Korean soldiers as prisoners of war in Russia's Kursk Oblast.
After more than a year of negotiations between Seoul and Kyiv, Zelensky announced they had been transferred to South Korea at the UN General Assembly last Wednesday - adding they had not been "easy to capture alive".
Seoul confirmed the news but sharply criticised Zelensky for allegedly breaking an agreement to keep the transfer a secret.
This was partly to protect the North Koreans' families, President Lee's office said in a statement, which added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.
Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer.
The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement.
Seoul demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations.
Lee faced heavy criticism at home after Zelensky's disclosure. The South Korean opposition accused him of covering up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.
Lee, whose party takes a conciliatory approach to the North, has been making efforts to reopen peace talks, with little success.
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.
After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks.
"When North Korea actively participates in a war in Europe, South Korea cannot remain a distant observer," said Mykhailo Podolyak, a senior adviser to Zelensky.
"The transfer of defence technologies and capabilities from Seoul to Kyiv is not just about helping Ukraine; it is about South Korea protecting its own long-term security interests by containing the expansion of an aggressive totalitarian axis."
This July, Seoul announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment.
Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take.
South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US.
Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

“If Russia were truly preparing for any real steps towards de-escalation, as it claims, particularly to American negotiators, this wave of Shahed terror would not be happening,” Zelenskyy said in later comments, referring to the Iran-developed drones Moscow has used against Ukraine.

Russian Minister of Foreign Affairs Sergey Lavrov told the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Saturday that Moscow intended to continue its military campaign “to the end”.
Ukrainian drones struck an oil depot in Russia’s Krasnodar region on Monday, according to local reports.
Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ published footage of a large fire and identified the facility as the Pavlovskaya oil depot.
No injuries have been reported so far.
Ukraine has intensified its targeting of Russian oil infrastructure in recent weeks.

articles.title: Mediators reportedly continue work with Iran, US toward likely deal
articles.body:
Mediators are still working with Iran and the United States on a deal to end fighting and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, with indirect talks expected to resume Monday, three officials told The Associated Press.
The details were revealed as the war enters its eighth month after causing widespread economic suffering. Multiple efforts to allow safe shipping on one of the world's most crucial waterways have failed.
There was uncertainty over the weekend after President Donald Trump told journalists he had rejected Tehran’s latest proposal to reopen the strait in a week if the U.S. lifts its blockade of Iranian ports, releases frozen Iranian assets and waives sanctions on Iranian oil sales, among other conditions.
Iran’s foreign minister, however, remained in New York and said he awaited word from mediators. Qatar has been mediating.
Two of the officials speaking to the AP Monday confirmed that mediators are working with both sides on a proposal that would include reopening the strait and lifting the U.S. blockade and then removing sanctions.
According to the draft text being discussed, the strait would reopen in accordance with a separate deal that Iran has been discussing with Oman, on the other side of the strait, and it would include no tolls – something Tehran has pursued.
That deal seeks to temporarily manage shipping traffic on what was seen as an international waterway before the war.
The two officials also said that despite Trump’s public comments, the U.S. has not officially rejected the current proposal, indicating that his remarks may have been a negotiating tactic.
The third official said the U.S is seeking Iranian concessions on its nuclear program, including allowing inspectors to enter the country. Under the Memorandum of Understanding the two sides signed in June that collapsed within days, Iran's nuclear program was meant to be discussed over a 60-day period.
All three officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss behind-the-scenes diplomatic negotiations.
One official reported positive signals coming from both sides. A second reported "slight progress" over the weekend. The third said mediators are still trying "to soften" the positions of both sides.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
While Iran’s latest proposal echoes the June deal, a key difference is speed.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told a closed-door meeting on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly last week that Tehran had pitched the deal as benefiting Trump in the midterm elections.
Araghchi later told journalists that "the seven-day timeline will start as soon as the United States accepts this plan."
Both the U.S. and Iran have been hurting economically – the U.S. from high oil prices as Iran attacks ships on the strait, and Tehran from the naval blockade and a growing number of U.S. sanctions that bottle up its oil sales. Brent crude, the international standard, is above $108.
For months, the two sides have been trying to outlast the other, while regional countries put up with missile and drone attacks as Tehran claims to target U.S. military assets in the region.
Reflecting Iran's impatience, a rare statement Monday attributed to the theocracy's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei noted the "painful blows" that enemy forces have received near the strait. "Before long, the Arabian Sea, too, will be rid of them," the statement added.
The latest proposed deal again seeks to end the fighting on all fronts, including in Lebanon. But a new front has emerged in recent weeks as Iran-backed rebels in Yemen are now perched on another crucial waterway, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern entrance to the Red Sea. That has further pressured global markets.
Iran argues that the Houthis have their own demands and that their conflict with neighboring Saudi Arabia is separate from the U.S.-Iran war, but Iranian officials said they are willing to help in finding a settlement between the Houthis and the Saudis, one of the officials said.

articles.title: Iranian Missile Hits Ship with U.S. Marines in the Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
Eight U.S. Marines were injured in an Iranian cruise missile strike on a ship in the Strait of Hormuz.
NBC News reported the incident, citing three U.S. officials.
According to their data, the attack occurred on September 14, injuring seven enlisted Marines and one officer. They suffered smoke inhalation and experienced symptoms consistent with concussions.
The outlet noted that none of them suffered serious injuries, and all eight soon returned to duty.
The Marines were operating as part of a Battalion Landing Team. According to U.S. officials, the struck vessel was not part of the U.S. Navy. They did not disclose the ship’s type or ownership.
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) declined to comment on the circumstances of the attack. At the time of the strike, the U.S. defense agency had also not publicly reported the incident.
Meanwhile, a separate report by the UK’s United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) confirms that an unidentified vessel was struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on September 14.
The UKMTO report matches NBC’s data on the date and area of the incident, but does not officially establish that it involved the same vessel.
Information about the wounded Marines also appeared with a delay in official U.S. casualty statistics. According to the Pentagon’s Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS), 37 service members were added to the September tally — 29 sailors and eight Marines.
However, DCAS does not disclose the circumstances, location, or exact date on which they were wounded.
NBC notes that the eight Marines were added to the statistics about ten days after the September 14 attack. One U.S. official attributed the delay to the fact that symptoms of some injuries, including concussions, may not appear immediately.

articles.title: UK Thwarts Suspected Terrorist Plot Against Base Used by US Bombers for Strikes on Iran
articles.body:
An air base in England where American bombers used to strike Iran are based was the target of a suspected bomb plot, U.K. officials said Sept. 27.
Five men were arrested on suspicion of terrorism and explosives offenses after being stopped close to RAF Fairford, police said, and explosive ordnance disposal technicians were dispatched to the scene. RAF Fairford is a British base currently hosting a dozen B-1B Lancer bombers, which have been stationed there for around seven months for strikes on Iran.
President Donald Trump said the suspects were “looking to do big damage” to the U.S. at RAF Fairford and called the arrests “fantastic” before boarding Air Force One on Sept. 27.
“We had them under view for a long time and we got them,” Trump added. “Working with Britain, it was an amazing job. We had them under investigation.”
The base has been under increased security for days, which included the placement of vehicles around the perimeter, people familiar with the matter said. The threat level at the base was raised before the suspects were arrested. A U.S. Air Force spokesperson declined to discuss specific force protection measures, citing operational security.
Explosive ordnance teams from the British Army were called in to inspect the scene, and helicopter video footage aired by multiple U.K. news outlets showed a robot and personnel inspecting three white vans near the base fence, with B-1Bs parked on base nearby.
“The safety and security of the public is our first priority, and I want people to know that we will always take every step necessary to protect our communities and keep our country safe,” British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement.
Police said they were called by a local after receiving a report about three suspicious vehicles near RAF Fairford, which is located in Gloucestershire in southwest England.
“At around 12:45 a.m. today … police received a call relating to three suspicious vehicles which appeared to be traveling towards the air base,” the Metropolitan Police, which investigates terrorism cases in the U.K., said in a Sept. 27 statement.
The U.K. government is still investigating the incident, counterterrorism officials said.
“We are in the early stages of an investigation, and five men remain in custody,” counterterrorism policing senior national coordinator Vicki Evans said. “As you would expect, we are working closely with our partners to understand the circumstances of the incident.”
RAF Fairford does not have permanent U.S. Air Force aircraft assigned there, but it has a wing dedicated to supporting U.S. operations and is considered the main U.S. bomber site in Europe, having regularly hosted U.S. aircraft for years.
“The 501st Combat Support Wing and our other U.K.-based wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our U.S. service members, civilians, contractors, and their families,” the Air Force spokesperson said. “We constantly assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people, and their families.”
Roadblocks, large machinery, and armed police have been seen around the base. Eighty-five homes in the nearby village of Whelford were evacuated.
“The emergency services have well-rehearsed plans for dealing with major incidents,” Gloucestershire Police assistant chief constable Richard Ocone said. “A cordon is in place as a precaution and the public can expect to see an emergency services presence in the area for some time.”
The B-1Bs at Fairford were heavily used during Operation Epic Fury, the large-scale air campaign against Iran in the spring, when the base housed some two dozen bombers including B-52 Stratofortresses.
Since a shaky ceasefire in April, most of the B-1Bs have remained while the U.S. carried out occasional strikes, including at least one involving a B-1 from Fairford. The bombers have regularly conducted training sorties out of the U.K.
The U.K. government gave permission for the base to be used in strikes on Iran in March under former Prime Minister Kier Starmer, for what the U.K. considers collective self-defense strikes. Burnham reaffirmed that decision in July, and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps warned the U.K. government that it considered Fairford a legitimate target for attack. The U.K. government said in July it was prepared to use the British armed forces to defend the base.
The U.S. Air Force said it would continue to cooperate with the U.K. government to ensure the safety of its bases in Britain. Another U.K. base with U.S. aircraft is RAF Lakenheath, which hosts F-35A Lightning II and F-15E Strike Eagle fighters that have deployed to the Middle East for operations against Iran. Lakenheath is also used as a stopover location for fighters heading to the Middle East from the U.S.
“The safety and security of our Airmen, families, and surrounding communities remains our highest priority,” the Air Force spokesperson said. “We remain in close coordination with our U.K. partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities.”

articles.title: Ukraine regains territory and captures POWs in frontline push
articles.body:
KYIV — Ukraine’s army pushed back Russian forces in a key part of the eastern front with Russia and captured more than 250 prisoners, a senior Ukrainian general announced on Monday.
"Russians surrendered by entire subunits, along with officers, pilots, and artillerymen," said Gen. Andrii Biletskyi, commander of the Third Army Corps.
He said the success was the third part of Operation Vivaldi, a carefully prepared effort to recapture the initiative in the Donetsk region.

The latest phase recaptured 51 square kilometers of territory, bringing the total recovered during Vivaldi to 176 square kilometers, according to the Third Army Corps.
The operation shows that Ukraine can reuse some Russian advances. It also has significance beyond the battlefield: Kyiv sees such counterattacks as evidence to its allies — and particularly the Trump administration — that Russia's grinding advances in Donetsk are not inevitable and that Russian leader Vladimir Putin cannot simply wait for Ukraine's defenses and Western resolve to collapse.
Vivaldi has seen the integrated use of drones, armor, artillery and infantry against Russian forces attempting a pincer attack to seize control of Lyman, a lynchpin of the "fortress belt" cities that have stymied Russian advances for years.
"Russian forces had advanced right up to the Siverskyi Donets River, and holding Lyman as the primary defensive hub for the northern Donetsk region would have become significantly harder had they advanced further," said Mykola Bielieskov, a research fellow at Ukraine’s State National Institute for Strategic Studies and senior analyst at Come Back Alive Initiatives Center NGO.
"Any further enemy advances would have disrupted logistics and supply lines to Lyman, complicating the city's defense," he added.
In the operation, Ukraine emphasized the use of unmanned technology to spare its troops — from air-dropping tiny ground robots behind Russian lines to turning Soviet-era BTR-60 armored vehicles into kamikaze robots by stuffing them full of explosives and driving them into Russian fortifications.
Advertisement
Biletskyi said the Third Corps deceived Russian forces into believing the main Ukrainian thrust would come toward Shandryholove and Zelena Dolyna, drawing Russian reserves into counterattacks there while Ukraine struck toward Nove.
“This led them to senselessly burn through their reserves in counterattacks in that very sector. The Russians missed the real strike," Biletskyi added.
According to Bielieskov, the result undermines Russia's theory of victory, which he said "hinged precisely on attempts to turn local advances in the Donetsk region into strategic successes." He added: "The goal was to create the impression Russia would inevitably capture the Donetsk region, thereby raising the question: 'What is the point of the West helping Ukraine, or of Ukraine clinging to the region?'"
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy pointed to the broader battlefield picture on Sunday. "Overall, this week, across all sectors of active combat operations on the front, our units neutralized 10,660 Russian troops killed and wounded," he said. "Every such week on the front that becomes ours — Ukrainian — in terms of the overall situation prevents Russia from mounting greater offensive activity against Ukraine."
The operation also sends a signal to the Trump administration, which has revived its efforts to end the war by turning to its special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. “Even U.S. negotiators — such as Kushner, who are not exactly known for being sympathetic to [Ukraine’s] cause — pointed out to Putin that his promise to rapidly occupy the Donetsk region was not materializing,” Bielieskov said.
Although Ukrainian gains in the area have been independently documented by open-source battlefield monitors including DeepState, the Kremlin insisted it hasn't suffered any setback.
Advertisement
The Russian defense ministry called Ukraine’s announced success near Lyman a smokescreen “for Kyiv’s Western curators,” claiming nothing more than the unsuccessful infiltration of "the enemy’s small assault groups" is going on in the northern part of the Donetsk region.
Biletskyi, the Third Army Corps commander, said that the operation, named after Italian composer Antonio Vivaldi’s Four Seasons cycle of violin concerts, will continue.

articles.title: Small drone boat can land a significant hit, says NATO
articles.body:
A small uncrewed boat is now capable of inflicting serious damage on a warship, and NATO’s Mediterranean task group has been retraining its air defences to deal with drones as well as aircraft, the commander of Standing NATO Maritime Group Two has said.
Commodore Georgios Kypriotis of the Hellenic Navy, speaking in an interview released alongside the conclusion of Exercise Dynamic Guard 26-2, set out how quickly the picture has moved. “In the latest years we have seen that the unmanned, the big drones or even USVs, is an emerging threat, but we are preparing also to defend ourselves against such threats,” he said.
“Dynamic Guard is a very specific example of that. We are training to defend ourselves against the UAS, and as a matter of fact, during the first day of the exercise we showed the ability to transfer our air defence capability against jets to defence capability against drones.”
What has changed, in his account, is what a cheap hull can now do to an expensive one. “Now, with a small USV, you can accomplish a significant hit to your enemy, and this is something different,” the commodore said. “That’s why we keep training ourselves in that perspective.”
He described the group as teaching itself a new way of fighting, and said of its progress: “I am pretty sure, I’m confident that we are doing very well.”
Dynamic Guard is the alliance’s premier live exercise for electronic warfare and anti-ship missile defence, and this iteration was the first to incorporate counter-drone warfare alongside the two. The five-day event began on 21 September and concluded at Taranto in southern Italy, drawing in warships, aircraft and electronic warfare specialists from across the alliance.
Crews practised the full defensive sequence, from early detection and tracking through to coordinated responses using both soft-kill and hard-kill counter-uncrewed systems techniques, alongside electronic warfare and anti-ship missile defence procedures. The training tested how ships share information, coordinate their defensive actions and adapt when communications or sensors are disrupted, with simulated threats covering communications jamming, radar jamming, anti-ship missile attack and uncrewed aircraft.
In his formal statement on the exercise, Kypriotis said: “Exercise Dynamic Guard represents a vital opportunity for our units to rigorously test and refine their electronic warfare capabilities, in a highly realistic operational scenario which includes multi-domain threats from drones of any kind, to missiles and fighter jets. It demonstrates that NATO forces are trained and prepared to confront and, in modern naval warfare, controlling and defending the electromagnetic spectrum is crucial. Our multinational forces are fully prepared to train alongside Allied partners, strengthen interoperability, and demonstrate NATO’s collective readiness to deter and defend against any threat.”
Gerald Poppinga, an expert with the NATO Communications and Information Agency’s joint intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance branch, described the contest as one that never settles. “Electronic warfare is not new. We have a long history of operating in and understanding the electromagnetic spectrum,” he said. “But as we have developed new ways to detect and defeat systems, those systems have also evolved to overcome their vulnerabilities. It is a constant cycle of adaptation. That is why we must continue to train, learn and keep pace with the rapid development of technology.”

articles.title: Bundestag Approves Purchase of AIM-120, Meteor and Air Defense Systems for German Armed Forces
articles.body:
The Bundestag’s Budget Committee has approved a package of procurement and modernization programs for the Bundeswehr covering air-to-air missiles, air defense, armored vehicles, naval systems and strategic airlift.
The German Federal Ministry of Defence reported this following the Budget Committee’s meeting on September 23.
The Air Force will receive two additional batches of AIM-120 AMRAAM missiles for F-35A and Eurofighter fighters. The procurement will be carried out through the U.S. Foreign Military Sales program and financed from Germany’s defense budget.
The Bundeswehr will also receive two special batches of Meteor missiles for Eurofighters. They are intended to test tactics and technical solutions and to support integration work as part of the fighter’s radar modernization.
For the Navy, the committee approved a naval adaptation of the IRIS-T SLM system for F125-class frigates. The German Defense Ministry said this is intended to strengthen their self-defense capabilities against air threats.
Militarnyi previously reported that in October 2025, the naval version of IRIS-T SLM had already been tested aboard the Baden-Württemberg frigate during firing exercises off Norway. At the time, the system was installed on the ship’s deck as a separate module.
For the Army, the committee approved the integration of digital radios into Fennek 1A1 and 1A2 reconnaissance vehicles. Some surplus Fenneks will also be upgraded to the Joint Fire Support Team A5.1 standard as an interim solution until the arrival of corresponding vehicles based on the GTK Boxer.
The committee also approved the second amendment to the contract for the NNbS short- and very-short-range air defense system. Among other things, fire-control vehicle modules and air defense missile vehicle modules will be adapted to the standardized Boxer B0 chassis, while the air defense vehicle simulator will be built in a containerized configuration.
A separate procurement covers 70 mm rockets in combat and training configurations for Tiger attack helicopters and the Bundeswehr’s light combat helicopters. The committee also approved additional laser designators for Joint Fire Support Team dismounted teams.
For the Navy, one of two full-function NH90 simulators will be upgraded to integrate the NATO Frigate Helicopter German Navy Step 3 configuration. The Bundeswehr will also receive new multipurpose combat boats for the naval battalion, along with training, documentation and equipment.
In addition, a new contract under the Strategic Airlift International Solution was approved, guaranteeing the Bundeswehr access to strategic airlift aircraft for transporting oversized and heavy cargo.
As part of efforts to strengthen air defense, Germany is also increasing its procurement of IRIS-T systems.
As Militarnyi previously reported, in February 2026 the Bundeswehr ordered additional batches of IRIS-T missiles for SLS and SLM ground-based systems and combat aircraft.

articles.title: Eight US Marines injured in recent, undisclosed Iranian attack on ship in Hormuz - report
articles.body:
Eight US Marines were injured in an Iranian attack on a ship in the Strait of Hormuz on September 14, NBC reported Sunday evening, citing three US sources.
The Marines were not seriously injured by the Iranian cruise missile hit on the vessel, but they sustained smoke inhalation and showed symptoms of concussions, including headaches, according to the report.
The Marines were not on a US Navy ship, but the officials did not share what type of ship it was.
All eight service members returned to duty soon after the attack.
The Defense Department did not disclose any attack taking place on September 14 or any injuries sustained.
Pentagon accused of misrepresenting casualty count
The Pentagon's public account of US service member casualties has come under scrutiny, with a Washington Post report emerging on Friday that said that at least four service members killed in the Middle East since the start of the war were not represented in the official casualty count.
The Defense Department has also been accused of downplaying injuries by wounded soldiers who spoke to CBS News.
One soldier described suffering severe shrapnel wounds and undergoing multiple emergency surgeries in Kuwait. A US Army official told his wife that his injuries were "minor."
The US military has strongly disputed this claim, telling CBS that military designations, including “not seriously injured” and “combat casualty,” have specific definitions that have been misconstrued.
"The care and well-being of our soldiers is of the highest priority," CBS cited an army spokesperson as writing. "Any assertion that the army seeks to downplay a soldier's injuries is simply not true."

articles.title: Hezbollah marks second anniversary of Sayyed Nasrallah’s martyrdom with vows of continued resistance
articles.body:
Hezbollah marks second anniversary of Sayyed Nasrallah’s martyrdom with vows of continued resistance
Sheikh Qassem vows Hezbollah will not surrender weapons at massive Beirut commemoration
TEHRAN — The southern suburbs of Beirut transformed into a sprawling sea of black and yellow on Sunday. Tens of thousands of mourners converged on the shrine of Sayyed Hassan Nasrallah to mark two years since his assassination in an Israeli airstrike.
Crowds filled the streets surrounding the site in Bir al-Abed near the old airport road. Their chants of loyalty rose above the din of a city still bearing the physical scars of the U.S.-backed Israeli bombing campaign.
Many attendees carried portraits of Sayyed Nasrallah and his successor, Sayyed Hashem Safieddine, who was martyred in an Israeli strike mere days after his mentor.
Gathering in a neighborhood that Israeli warplanes systematically reduced to rubble was a deliberate statement of defiance. Mourners traveled from southern villages still under the threat of occupation.
Faithful to the pledge
Addressing the massive gathering in a televised broadcast, Hezbollah Secretary-General Sheikh Naim Sheikh Qassem delivered an uncompromising defense of the resistance. His speech served as both a tribute to the fallen commanders and a blunt indictment of Lebanon’s political establishment.
Sheikh Qassem spoke directly to the martyred leaders. He told Sayyed Nasrallah that while his physical body had departed, his teachings remain the driving force of the movement.
“You are the resistance and the resistance is you, and you have become its symbol for the free people of the world,” Sheikh Qassem declared. He praised Sayyed Safieddine as an indispensable pillar of the jihadist journey who never tired in his service to the cause.
The organizing theme of the memorial was “Inna Ala al-Ahd” (We remain faithful to the pledge). Sheikh Qassem defined this phrase as absolute operational continuity.
When leaders are martyred, new commanders immediately step forward to maintain the exact same trajectory, the Resistance leader explained. The pledge guarantees the continuation of the courageous, divine resistance against foreign aggression until every inch of occupied land is fully liberated.
The battlefield ledger
Sheikh Qassem then pivoted to the military realities on the ground, systematically dismantling the arguments of domestic opponents who question the utility of Hezbollah’s arms.
He turned the scrutiny back on the government. “Some, especially among our opponents, ask: what has the Resistance done?” he noted. “But it seems they forgot to ask: what has the state done?”
Hezbollah halted the Israeli aggression project, the Hezbollah leader explained.
Sheikh Qassem stated that the Israeli military deployed up to 90,000 soldiers and officers, backed by unlimited American capabilities, yet utterly failed to break the resistance. Israeli forces were physically prevented from establishing permanent occupation zones or settlements in Lebanon, he explained.
Fighters delivered legendary performances across the southern front. Sheikh Qassem listed the battlegrounds where Hezbollah forces entrenched themselves and bled the advancing brigades.
They held their ground in Bint Jbeil, Khiam, Aita al-Shaab, Naqoura, and al-Bayyada. At the Ali al-Taher ridge, resistance units maintained their defensive posture under heavy bombardment for three consecutive months, Sheikh Qassem stated.
He honored the 3,400 martyrs and 14,600 wounded from Operation People of Might. Sheikh Qassem directed special recognition to the survivors of the pager terror attacks, calling them living martyrs who transformed their wounds into active resistance.
Domestic betrayal and the disarmament illusion
The sharpest political warnings targeted Lebanon’s governing authority. Sheikh Qassem accused the state of acting as “an accessory” to the Israeli-American project by offering unforced concessions.
He argued that the current framework agreement handed Israel all of Lebanon’s negotiating leverage in a single session. Pointing to seven rounds of direct negotiations that yielded results “below zero,” he demanded an immediate freeze on direct talks.
The secretary-general ridiculed the persistent demands for Hezbollah to surrender its weapons. “You stayed two years trying to strip the weapons and you could not, so why do you ask the Lebanese Army?” he asked.
Asking the national army to serve as a disarmament tool for political factions is a delusion, the Resistance leader said.
Sheikh Qassem affirmed that Hezbollah will never forfeit a single inch of Lebanon’s 10,452 square kilometers.
Turning to the collapse of the Lebanese state, he asked where the government was regarding the ruined economy, hyperinflation, electricity blackouts, and stolen depositor funds.
Sheikh Qassem announced that Hezbollah, utilizing its own resources and donor funding, will shortly unveil a comprehensive housing and reconstruction project for displaced citizens, stepping in where the state has completely vanished.
Concluding his address, Sheikh Qassem reaffirmed that Palestine remains the absolute compass for the resistance.
He saluted the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Leader of the Islamic Revolution for their steadfast backing.
Pointing to Israel’s isolation at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, he noted that the regime has become an exposed global pariah.

articles.title: Dialogue between Russia and US essential to save arms control system — expert
articles.body:
ISTRA (Moscow Region), September 28. /TASS/. Resuming dialogue between Russia and the US, with China’s participation, is essential to preserving what remains of the arms control system, Karen Hallberg, Secretary-General of the Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs, told TASS in an interview on the sidelines of the annual meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club.
This is critically important because resuming dialogue among the nuclear powers – for example, if the US, Russia and China were to establish a high-level forum or negotiating platform to discuss ways of reducing nuclear risks – would facilitate the implementation of Article 6 of the NPT [Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons] and demonstrate the countries’ serious commitment to negotiations. This would bring greater stability to the entire system, she said.
Hallberg emphasized that renewed Russia-US dialogue, with China’s involvement, on nuclear issues would foster a deeper understanding that there is no way to control nuclear weapons without reaching a mutual understanding among all nuclear powers.
In Hallberg’s view, the process could begin with the three major nuclear powers: Russia, the US and China.
Such a dialogue could also build confidence among the other two nuclear powers, the UK and France, which could subsequently join the negotiations. Their participation is important, she noted, as it would help build trust amid the ongoing conflict in Ukraine and tensions between NATO and Russia.
European nuclear weapons – British and French – are also part of the equation, Hallberg noted.
About the Meeting
The 23rd annual meeting of the Valdai International Discussion Club, themed "Responsibility for the Future: Limits of the Possible or Limitless Possibilities?", is taking place in the Moscow region from September 28 to October 1. The club’s flagship conference brings together 120 participants from 40 countries.

articles.title: Trump left Saudi Arabia to face Houthis alone – Mearsheimer to RT (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Trump left Saudi Arabia to face Houthis alone – Mearsheimer to RT (VIDEO)
US President Donald Trump has effectively abandoned Saudi Arabia, a key ally in the Middle East, leaving it to face “almost a full-blown war” with Yemen’s Houthis, political scientist and University of Chicago Professor John Mearsheimer said in an interview with RT.
Hostilities between Riyadh and the Shiite militant group, officially known as Ansarullah, have flared up in recent weeks after several years of relative calm. The Houthis have launched missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory, while Riyadh-backed government forces have tried to hold off the group’s advances inside Yemen.
Earlier this month, the Houthis seized control over Yemen’s Red Sea coast, taking positions around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait – a key waterway which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on for oil exports since navigation through the Strait of Hormuz was reduced to a trickle amid the US-Israeli war against Iran.
In an interview with New Order host Afshin Rattansi on Sunday, Mearsheimer said that because of its “foolish” decision to “attack the Houthis and pick a fight with them,” Saudi Arabia has found itself in “really deep trouble.” He added that the “Houthis are a formidable fighting force, and the Saudis are not.”
He went on to suggest, citing media reports, that Trump encouraged Riyadh to strike an airport in the Houthi-controlled Yemeni capital, Sanaa, in mid-July. The attack, which was apparently meant to prevent an Iranian plane carrying a Houthi delegation from Tehran from landing, shattered the UN-brokered 2022 truce between the Saudis and the Houthis, triggering the current escalation.
Mearsheimer gave credence to claims made earlier this month by the New York Times, which said Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman phoned Trump on multiple occasions in recent weeks, asking for military support against the Houthis. The president decided, however, not to intervene, according to the NYT. 
Trump was reportedly close to authorizing strikes on the Houthis last weekend, but reversed his decision at the last minute.
According to Mearsheimer, “the last thing [Trump] wants to do is get into a fight with [the Houthis] to try to rescue Saudi Arabia” – not least because of how badly America’s attempt to bomb the Houthis into submission went last year.
Less than two months into the campaign, Trump abruptly announced a ceasefire, declaring victory and saying the Houthis promised not to attack US ships.
“But in fact, the Houthis beat the United States. We did not defeat the Houthis,” Mearsheimer said.
Speaking to Al-Mayadeen on Saturday, the head of the National Security Committee in the Iranian Parliament, Ibrahim Azizi, warned neighboring Arab nations against cooperating with the US and allowing it to use their territory as a launchpad for attacks.
Azizi added that the US security umbrella in the Middle East has proven to be ineffective.

articles.title: RAF 'terror plot' raises questions over UK's role in Iran war
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
RAF 'terror plot' raises questions over UK's role in Iran war
A suspected terror plot targeting a British airbase used by the US to launch operations against Iran has raised questions over whether UK involvement in the conflict has increased the risk of retaliation on British soil.
Five British men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested early on Sunday after police received reports of three suspicious vans travelling towards RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire.
They were initially detained on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and later arrested on suspicion of preparing an act of terrorism.
Counter-terrorism police are investigating a possible Iranian connection, but have yet to establish the motivation or whether any foreign state was involved.
Despite this, much British media coverage has focused on Iran, with some reports describing the incident as an alleged Iranian "bomb plot".
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said it would be "far too early to comment or speculate" about the motivations of those arrested.
Iran has denied involvement in a statement posted by the Iranian embassy on social media, saying it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations" that it had any involvement in the suspected plot.
US President Donald Trump has claimed the suspects were planning to cause "big damage" to the base, saying US and British authorities had been watching them "for a long time".
Police said the arrests followed a call from a member of the public reporting suspicious vehicles near the base, although Streeting said the witness had only a "partial picture" of the security operation.
Why is RAF Fairford important?
RAF Fairford has become an important part of US military operations during the war with Iran.
Despite its RAF designation, the Gloucestershire base is extensively used by the US Air Force and hosts the headquarters of its 501st Combat Support Wing.
It is also the US Air Force's only bomber Forward Operating Location in Europe, designed to receive and sustain America's long-range strategic bomber force. Its infrastructure can accommodate B-1, B-2 and B-52 strategic bombers.
After initially declining to allow British bases to be used for US attacks on Iran, the UK subsequently authorised Washington to use Fairford for what it described as specific "defensive" operations. American B-1 and B-52 bombers have since operated from the base during the conflict.
London distinguishes between allowing strikes against Iranian missile facilities threatening Gulf states, shipping and British interests and participating in the wider US offensive campaign.
Iran's warning to Britain
Iran does not necessarily recognise that distinction.
In July, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned Britain over the use of RAF Fairford, saying bases used by the US to launch attacks on Iran could be regarded as legitimate military targets.
Security was subsequently increased, with a local councillor telling Reuters that authorities had responded to a specific Iranian threat against the base around six weeks before Sunday's arrests.
There is currently no public evidence establishing that those arrested were working for Tehran or that Iran ordered the alleged operation. Investigators are reportedly considering several possibilities, including an Iran-linked motive, Russian involvement and an Islamist motivation.
Even if an Iranian connection is established, it would not necessarily mean the operation was directed by the Iranian state.
Has UK policy increased the risk?
Britain maintains that it is not participating in the wider US war against Iran while allowing American forces to use British territory for some military operations against Iranian targets.
This raises questions under international law over when military assistance makes a country a participant in an armed conflict.
Traditional laws of neutrality generally prohibit neutral states from allowing their territory to be used by one belligerent for military operations against another.
The UN General Assembly's Definition of Aggression also includes allowing a state's territory to be used by another country to perpetrate aggression against a third state.
This does not automatically make Britain an aggressor or party to the wider conflict.
The UK argues that the operations constitute lawful individual and collective self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter, including the defence of regional states subjected to Iranian missile attacks.
International law expert Marc Weller has nevertheless argued that Britain's position has moved it closer to direct involvement and that its distinction between different categories of US operations may be difficult to sustain.
Writing for Chatham House in March, Weller noted that Iran could not know whether a US aircraft leaving a British base was conducting an operation authorised by London under collective self-defence or participating in Washington's broader campaign.
From Tehran's perspective, Fairford is therefore not simply a British military installation, but a forward base hosting US strategic bombers operating during the war against Iran.
An Iranian connection to Sunday's alleged plot remains only a possibility under investigation.
But should one be established, the incident would raise questions over whether allowing UK territory to become part of the military infrastructure used against Iran has also increased Britain's exposure to the conflict.

articles.title: Iran Claims to Have Seized Second U.S. Underwater Drone in Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy has claimed to have seized a U.S. REMUS 600 UUV in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian media outlet IRIB reported this, citing a statement by the IRGC Navy.
According to the Iranian side, the UUV was detected while conducting a reconnaissance mission in the Strait of Hormuz.
The IRGC said the seizure operation was conducted using intelligence capabilities and electronic warfare systems.
After being seized, the REMUS 600 UUV was handed over to Iranian specialists, who are expected to examine the vehicle and attempt to retrieve information from its storage systems. The Iranian side also released video footage of the captured vehicle.
The United States has not officially confirmed the loss of this particular vehicle or disclosed the circumstances of its seizure.
The REMUS 600 is an autonomous uncrewed underwater vehicle (UUV) developed in the United States. It was designed as a multipurpose platform for underwater missions, including reconnaissance, seafloor mapping, mine detection and classification, oceanographic data collection and the search for underwater objects.
The REMUS 600 can operate at depths of up to 600 meters. Underwater navigation is carried out autonomously using an inertial navigation system, Doppler velocity log and acoustic navigation, while GPS can be used after the vehicle surfaces.
According to Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, the REMUS 600 can remain operational for about 70 hours and has a range of up to 286 nautical miles.
The Iranian side said the vehicle’s recorded routes, sonar data, navigation parameters and other information that may have remained in its memory could be of particular value.
This is the second case in September in which Iran has claimed to have seized a U.S. UUV. On September 8, the IRGC Navy reported the seizure of a Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle made by Anduril near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz.
The U.S. side then confirmed the loss of the vehicle, but said it had malfunctioned before falling into the hands of Iranian forces and did not contain classified equipment.
In July, U.S. Central Command used maritime kamikaze drones for the first time to strike Iranian military targets.

articles.title: Mediators press Iran for nuclear concession to revive ceasefire talks with US: Report
articles.body:
Merve Berker
28 September 2026•Update: 28 September 2026
Mediators are pressing Iran to make concessions on its nuclear program in an effort to revive ceasefire negotiations with the US, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The initiative follows US President Donald Trump's rejection of an Iranian proposal for a seven-day ceasefire that would have reopened the Strait of Hormuz and ended the US blockade of Iranian ports, according to the Journal.
Mediators described the effort as a long-shot attempt to secure movement from Tehran on its nuclear program, while Iran has so far given little indication that it is prepared to discuss the issue.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran remained open to negotiations but would respond to renewed military action.
"We are fully prepared for the war to resume," Araghchi told NBC News when asked about the Journal report.
"We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war. But at the same time we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose," he added.
Arab mediators said Iran had made no concessions since Trump rejected its ceasefire proposal, while Gulf officials said Tehran wants Washington to offer concessions before negotiations advance.
Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, whose country is relaying messages between Washington and Tehran, said the conflict was becoming increasingly difficult to resolve.
"This conflict is very complex," he said, earlier in New York at a special UN General Assembly edition of the Qatar Economic Forum.
Iran wants Washington to return to a memorandum of understanding reached in June that included reopening the Strait of Hormuz and eventually beginning nuclear negotiations in exchange for measures including sanctions relief, the unfreezing of billions of dollars in Iranian funds held overseas and an end to the US blockade.
US officials, however, said Trump no longer wants to return to that agreement, while Washington has tightened sanctions and maintained its blockade.
A senior Middle Eastern official involved in the talks said Iran could compromise on its nuclear program but would require explicit assurances that Israel would not attack again after any US-Iran agreement.

articles.title: A decade ago, Russian airline group S7 bet on a floating spaceport to break into the commercial launch market. Yet Sea Launch hasn’t launched a rocket in more than 12 years.
articles.body:
A decade ago, Russian airline group S7 bet on a floating spaceport to break into the commercial launch market. Yet Sea Launch hasn’t launched a rocket in more than 12 years.
On September 27, 2016, exactly 10 years ago, S7 struck one of the most ambitious deals in Russian spaceflight: the purchase of Sea Launch, a floating spaceport designed to send commercial payloads into space from the Pacific Ocean. S7 Group had ambitious plans to capture the commercial launch market, and its CEO, Vladislav Filyov, drew comparisons to Elon Musk. Science communicator Vitaly Yegorov explains what became of the project over the next decade and how the war affected its fate.
One project captures much of what went right and wrong in Russian spaceflight after the Soviet Union collapsed. Engineers from Russia and Ukraine built it from the remnants of the Soviet space program, with help from the United States and Norway. It saw successful launches and devastating accidents, lost out to commercial rivals, and fell victim to a political rift between former allies.
That project is Sea Launch, a floating spaceport for launching commercial satellites from equatorial waters in the Pacific Ocean. It now sits idle at a dock in Russia’s Primorye region, with no future in sight.
In the 1990s, Russia’s space industry was struggling to survive. State funding had fallen sharply, and the companies that had recently built the remarkable Energia rocket and Buran spacecraft had to scramble for money to pay their employees and keep their factories running. The international commercial market offered a lifeline. The United States and Europe needed relatively inexpensive launches, while Russian and Ukrainian companies needed foreign contracts. The U.S. interest was not purely economic; it also wanted former Soviet rocket technology to remain with those who already had it and not spread to countries Washington sought to keep it from.
Joint programs followed that would have seemed unthinkable just 10 years earlier. American space shuttles began flying to the Mir space station, Russian rocket engines went to the U.S., and Russian space companies formed joint ventures with European and American firms. One was the international Sea Launch consortium, established in 1995.
The engineering logic was elegant: put a spaceport on a vessel and take it to the most energy-efficient place to launch rockets. The equator is particularly well suited to launching commercial telecommunications satellites into geostationary orbit. There, Earth’s rotation gives a rocket up to 465 meters per second of extra speed at liftoff. More important, an equatorial launch avoids the need to adjust the orbit’s inclination relative to the equator. Together, these advantages increase a rocket’s payload capacity by about a quarter — a kind of gift from the planet. There is another benefit: in the middle of the Pacific, falling rocket stages pose less of a concern, reducing disposal costs.
The project began with a used, Japanese-built semi-submersible oil platform called Ocean Odyssey. It was converted for space launches and renamed Odyssey. The platform carried rockets to the launch site and served as the launchpad.
The second part of Sea Launch was Sea Launch Commander, an assembly and command ship built for the project. Rockets underwent final assembly and launch preparations aboard the ship while it was still in port. During a launch, the ship served as mission control and a tracking and command station. The original plan was to carry rockets to the launch site aboard Sea Launch Commander and transfer them to Odyssey at sea, allowing more than one launch per voyage. But the vessels’ motion at sea forced the consortium to abandon the idea.
The vessels were based in Long Beach, California, near Los Angeles. From there, they sailed to the equator, where the platform took up its launch position and the rocket was prepared for liftoff. The command ship then withdrew to a safe distance with all personnel aboard.
Boeing was the U.S. partner in the project, with a 40% stake. It handled overall management, financing, and commercial operations. On the technical side, Boeing was responsible for the rocket’s fairing and for preparing its payload section, allowing the project to comply with U.S. technology nonproliferation requirements. Personnel from Russia and Ukraine had almost no knowledge of what was beneath the fairing and had no contact with the payload. Russia’s RSC Energia developed the launch infrastructure and received a 25% stake. Norway’s Kvaerner received 20% for converting Odyssey and building the command ship. Ukraine’s Yuzhmash and Yuzhnoye Design Bureau, which worked on the rocket, received 10% and 5%, respectively.
The consortium chose the medium-lift Zenit-3SL rocket, derived from the Soviet Zenit-2. From the equator, it could launch satellites that would have required heavy-lift rockets from Baikonur or Cape Canaveral. Its first two stages were made by Ukraine’s Yuzhmash but contained many Russian components, including the RD-171 first-stage engine. Russia’s Energia also supplied the DM-SL upper stage — effectively the rocket’s third stage. Building the complete rocket therefore required contributions from three countries.
The first demonstration launch took place in 1999, followed by the first commercial launch. Sea Launch was in business, but it soon became clear that its finances were falling short of expectations.
Investment in Sea Launch totaled about $3.5 billion. In the 1990s, as the telecommunications market grew and Europe’s Ariane 4 was its only launch competitor, investors saw promise in the project. By the early 2000s, however, Russia’s heavy-lift Proton rockets, Europe’s Ariane 5, and the American Atlas V and Delta IV had entered the international market. Sea Launch struggled to attract orders, and its inability to launch several rockets on a single voyage erased the economic advantage of launching from the equator.
Zenit also proved far from the most reliable rocket. In 2000, a software error cost the project the ICO F-1 satellite. In 2004, Telstar 18 was delivered to an off-target orbit, though one that could be corrected. Then, on January 30, 2007, Sea Launch suffered its most dramatic accident. The rocket carrying the NSS-8 satellite exploded almost immediately after its engines ignited, engulfing the launchpad in a huge fireball. The platform needed repairs, though they were less extensive than the explosion had initially suggested. The year of downtime during those repairs dealt a much greater blow to the project’s finances.
In June 2009, Sea Launch declared bankruptcy.
In 2010, RSC Energia’s head, Vitaly Lopota, effectively decided on his own to save Sea Launch, and the Russian company took the lead in restructuring it. Through its subsidiary Energia Overseas, it gained control of 95% of Sea Launch’s shares. Boeing retained 3%, and the Norwegian side retained 2%. Bankruptcy, however, did not wipe out the old debts. Along with the spaceport, RSC Energia inherited a multimillion-dollar legal dispute with Boeing.
For Lopota, the effort to save Sea Launch ended in criminal prosecution. In 2014, investigators began examining RSC Energia’s financial transactions connected to the project. They believed the corporation’s management had signed deals that made little financial sense and spent substantial sums propping up a money-losing business. Lopota was convinced he had saved a unique project. In July 2025, the criminal case against him was closed because the statute of limitations had expired, after he agreed to end the proceedings on those grounds. It was not an acquittal, but neither did any court find him guilty.
Taking over the spaceport also meant that the Russian side had to pay to keep it running and remain responsible for Sea Launch’s existing financial obligations.
From 2011 through 2014, Sea Launch carried out six more launches, one of which again ended in failure. Over the project’s 15-year history, it conducted 36 launches: 32 successful, one partially successful, and three failures. SpaceX had emerged as another competitor by then, but Sea Launch was already facing a different set of problems.
In 2014, Russia annexed Crimea, and Moscow’s relations with Kyiv and Western countries deteriorated sharply. For Russia’s space industry, that meant sanctions and the collapse of cooperation with Ukraine on Zenit and other projects. Sea Launch was left with no orders, no rocket, debts to Boeing, and about $20 million per year in costs to maintain its U.S. infrastructure.
For a while, the project’s future was uncertain. There was talk of selling it to Israel or the United Arab Emirates, but in 2016, the possibility of a revival emerged from Russia’s private space sector. By then, Sea Launch was an asset of RSC Energia, part of the recently formed state corporation Roscosmos. The debt to Boeing for Sea Launch stood at about $373.5 million. Meanwhile, NASA was stuck: after the shuttle program ended in 2011, American astronauts could reach the International Space Station only aboard Russian spacecraft. After 2014, the prices NASA paid for seats began to rise, while American private companies had not yet completed spacecraft to replace the Russian ones.
Under a multilateral agreement, Boeing obtained rights to five seats aboard Russian crewed Soyuz spacecraft and then offered them to NASA. The bulk of the debt associated with Sea Launch was paid off, and Roscosmos was finally able to find a new investor for the floating spaceport.
In 2016, Vladislav Filyov, co-owner of the major Russian airline S7 Group, decided to try his hand at the space business. S7 Group finalized the deal in April 2018. The company acquired the Odyssey platform, the assembly-and-command ship, equipment, and the rights to the Sea Launch trademark.
S7 was counting on Roscosmos’s new Soyuz-5 rocket. It was effectively a Zenit redesigned to use Russian-made parts and carry heavier payloads. For launches from the equator, its projected performance and price were comparable to those of its main rival, the expendable 2015 version of the Falcon 9.
Filyov’s plans were ambitious: S7 was prepared to order 80 rockets from Roscosmos at once. While Soyuz-5 was still in development, S7 ordered 12 Zenit rockets from Ukraine’s Yuzhmash. Building them, however, required Russian components, whose delivery depended on permits from the Russian authorities.
For a time, it seemed that S7’s status as a private company might allow it to work around the political disputes between Russia, Ukraine, and the U.S. There was even a proposal to assemble the rocket from major components in the port of Long Beach, where the floating spaceport was still based. The “American” Antares was being built in the U.S. at the time in much the same way, using a Ukrainian rocket body and Russian engines, so the idea did not seem far-fetched. But the Russian authorities’ determination to deny Ukraine orders ruled out that option for Zenit. Filyov was left waiting for the delayed Soyuz-5.
In 2020, S7 moved Sea Launch from the U.S. to Russia to cut maintenance costs and avoid further political risks as relations between the countries worsened. The move came at a steep price: some of the American and Ukrainian equipment had to be removed, leaving the spaceport almost inoperable even if Zenit rockets became available again.
At the same time, S7 faced two crises. Vladislav Filyov’s wife, Natalya Filyova, who was also a co-owner of the company, died in 2019; then the economic fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic hit the airline in 2020. S7 had little capacity left to pursue its space ambitions, and 2022 effectively ended all of Sea Launch’s commercial prospects. Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine brought a new wave of sanctions against its space industry, virtually shutting Russian rockets out of international competition.
Soyuz-5 did not make its first test launch from Baikonur until 2026, but that made no difference to Sea Launch. Even before the war, the cost of adapting the launchpad for the new rocket was estimated at $1 billion. Under current sanctions, the investment looks economically hopeless. What is more, the growth of low-Earth-orbit satellite constellations has diminished Sea Launch’s old advantage — launching from the equator — because those satellites instead need orbits closer to the poles.
As of September 2026, Sea Launch remains in the port of Slavyanka near Vladivostok. It has gone more than 12 years without a launch. The mothballed spaceport has yet to be scrapped, but a return to launches looks remote.
Perhaps Sea Launch’s only chance of revival today lies with Rassvet, a satellite internet project by the Russian company Bureau 1440. Competing projects Starlink and Amazon Leo are pursuing vertical integration, producing not only satellites but also rockets and launch facilities through SpaceX and Blue Origin. Bureau 1440 might be interested in launching satellites from a spaceport of its own, one beyond the reach of Ukrainian missiles. But that would take several more years and depend on many other factors — above all, the war.

articles.title: West risks falling for Kiev’s ‘nuclear terrorism’ – Moscow
articles.body:
West risks falling for Kiev’s ‘nuclear terrorism’ – Moscow
The West risks becoming a victim of the very “nuclear terrorism” it enables by backing Ukraine, Russian Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik has warned.
Miroshnik, who oversees matters tied to Kiev’s military crimes and human rights violations, was commenting on the escalation in Ukrainian attacks on the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP), Europe’s largest, and nearby Energodar, home to most of its workers. Russia took control of the facility in March 2022.
In remarks released on Monday, Miroshnik told TASS that Western governments understand Kiev’s “increasingly provocative tactics” but continue to “turn a blind eye.”
“They think that this situation, which is gradually heating up and genuinely threatens very serious consequences, will somehow pass them by,” he stated, arguing that Kiev’s progression “toward crimes, provocations, and outright terrorism” also threatens its supporters.
“Terrorism is a double-edged weapon. At some point it will come back to them... If they think they are somehow shielded from this, it’s some global naiveté.”
Miroshnik linked the escalation to the EU’s €90 billion ($102 billion) ‘loan’ package, finalized in April to bankroll Kiev’s military and failing budget. He said Ukrainian attacks had since intensified, driving residents from Energodar, targeting sensitive sites including nuclear waste facilities, and expanding to the Kursk and Smolensk nuclear plants. Ukraine’s strategy, he argued, now amounts to “manufacturing a humanitarian catastrophe” with EU money.
The diplomat also slammed Kiev’s Western backers for conveniently accepting Ukrainian denials over the attacks on the ZNPP, saying such “idiotic, twisted logic suits the West perfectly well” in its anti-Russian agenda.
The attacks have increasingly threatened the ZNPP’s safety. Its main external power line was severed in March and restored only this month, while the backup failed in August after an “incident” in Ukrainian-controlled territory, forcing the plant onto diesel generators for over two weeks. Ukraine has also recently targeted emergency fuel tankers, killing two Russian servicemen and wounding others, while a drone strike last week damaged a radiation monitoring post.
Attacks on the plant and its personnel have killed at least 13 people and injured scores more since the spring, according to site officials. The head of Russian state nuclear giant Rosatom, Aleksey Likhachev, has warned of the “real danger of a massive nuclear incident” affecting Russia, Ukraine, and the EU if the attacks continue.
Moscow has accused Kiev’s Western backers of effectively enabling the attacks by refusing to condemn them. It has particularly criticized the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which maintains a permanent presence at the plant, for documenting military activity without publicly identifying Ukraine as responsible. Earlier this month, IAEA chief Rafael Grossi again urged “maximum military restraint,” citing “reported military activity” but assigning no blame.

articles.title: Switzerland May Choose SAMP/T NG Amid Patriot Delays
articles.body:
The French-Italian company Eurosam has emerged as the leading contender to supply Switzerland with a second long-range air defense system.
Blick reported this, while Armasuisse, Switzerland’s Federal Office for Defence Procurement, confirmed that the military-industrial evaluation of the submitted proposals had been completed.
The Swiss Federal Council will make the final decision on the system selection. At the same time, Armasuisse has not officially disclosed the names of the systems that remain in the competition.
Switzerland began seeking a second long-range air defense system due to delays in the delivery of U.S.-made Patriot systems previously ordered under the Air2030 program.
In March 2026, the Federal Council instructed the Federal Department of Defence to prepare the procurement of an additional long-range ground-based air defense system, preferably of European manufacture.
At the project’s initial stage, manufacturers from France, Germany, Israel, and South Korea were invited to participate.
Switzerland set key selection criteria, including delivery speed and reliability, effectiveness against long-range aerial threats, integration with the national air defense system, and a stable supply of missiles and spare parts.
In addition, Bern wants part of missile, control-system, or critical-component production to be localized in Switzerland or other European countries.
According to Blick, the system’s European origin could be one of the advantages of Eurosam’s proposal.
This is likely referring to the SAMP/T NG, the new generation of the French-Italian air and missile defense system.
The SAMP/T NG is equipped with modern 360-degree surveillance radars and uses ASTER 30 family missiles, including the new ASTER 30 B1NT variant.
The system can detect targets at ranges of more than 350 km and engage aerodynamic targets at distances exceeding 150 km. In addition to aircraft and cruise missiles, the system is designed to counter ballistic targets.
In February, the Swiss Federal Department of Defence expressed doubts about the reliability of information on the terms and delivery dates for U.S. air defense systems and the possible delivery of SAMP/T systems to Switzerland in 2029.
